dishes.title: Eggs Benedict
dishes.summary: Poached eggs and warm back bacon on toasted English muffins, coated in hollandaise. It is here because hollandaise is the first warm butter emulsion, a sauce held between two temperatures, and because poaching, holding and reheating eggs in batches is exactly how a brunch station feeds a full room.
skills: a warm butter emulsion held at the right temperature
equipment: Heatproof glass or stainless bowl that sits snugly over a saucepan
Medium saucepan for the bain-marie
Balloon whisk
Small saucepan for melting butter
Wide deep frying pan or saucepan, at least 3 inches (8 cm) of water
Slotted spoon and a fine sieve
Bowl of iced water
Instant-read thermometer
Thermos flask or a small jug kept over warm water, for holding the sauce
Frying pan for the bacon
Kitchen paper

ingredients.note: very fresh; use pasteurised eggs for anyone vulnerable

ingredients.us: 1/2 tsp, plus a pinch for the eggs

ingredients.note: the freshest you can buy; fresh whites hold together

ingredients.item: Canadian bacon (back bacon) or thick-sliced cooked ham

ingredients.note: split with a fork, not a knife, for a craggy surface

mise: Separate the 3 yolks into the bowl; keep the whites for another day.
Melt the 12 tbsp (170 g) butter in the small pan and keep it warm, not sizzling, on the lowest heat.
Squeeze the lemon and measure the water.
Fill the saucepan with 2 inches (5 cm) of water for the bain-marie and bring it to a bare simmer.
Fill the wide pan with water at least 3 inches (8 cm) deep, add the vinegar and heat to 185°F (85°C), the water trembling but not bubbling.
Crack each poaching egg into its own small cup.
Set up the iced water bowl beside the stove, and a tray lined with kitchen paper.
Fill the thermos with hot tap water to warm it, then empty it just before the sauce goes in.
Split the muffins with a fork and lay out the bacon.

timeline.do: Melt the butter, separate yolks, heat both waters.
Poach the eggs in batches and hold them in iced water.
Make the hollandaise and transfer it to the warmed thermos.
Warm the bacon, toast and butter the muffins.
Reheat the eggs in hot water for 60 seconds.
Assemble, sauce, chives, serve on warm plates.

steps.do: Poach in batches of four. Tip one egg into a fine sieve over the sink for 20 seconds to drain the loose, watery white, then lower it into the 185°F (85°C) water. Repeat with three more, spaced around the pan. Poach 3 minutes.
steps.look: The white wraps itself around the yolk in a neat oval with no ragged tails. A lifted egg feels set on the outside and wobbles like a water balloon in the middle.
steps.mistake: Boiling water, which tears the white into rags and toughens it before the yolk warms.
steps.fix: Lower the heat until only a few small bubbles rise from the bottom. If the eggs are already ragged, trim the tails with scissors after chilling; they will still taste right.

steps.do: Lift each egg with the slotted spoon, dab the base on kitchen paper and slide it into the iced water. Poach the second batch of four the same way.
steps.look: The eggs sink and firm slightly in the cold water and stop cooking at once, yolks still liquid.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in warm water, so the yolks keep cooking and set solid by service.
steps.fix: Ice water stops the cooking; chilled poached eggs keep up to 2 days in the fridge in water, which is how a restaurant serves hundreds.

steps.do: Make the sabayon. Whisk the 3 yolks, 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water in the bowl until frothy. Set the bowl over the barely simmering water, the base not touching it, and whisk continuously, in figures of eight and around the sides.
steps.look: Within 3 to 5 minutes the yolks triple in volume and turn pale and thick. The whisk leaves trails and a ribbon lifted from it sits on the surface for 2 seconds. A thermometer reads 145 to 155°F (63 to 68°C).
steps.mistake: Stopping whisking or letting the bowl get too hot, so the yolks scramble into small curds at the edges.
steps.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat every 20 seconds while you whisk to control it. If you see the first specks of scrambling, take it off, whisk in 1 tsp (5 ml) cold water and push through a sieve before going on.

steps.do: Take the bowl off the heat and set it on a folded damp cloth so it does not spin. Add the warm melted butter a few drops at a time at first, whisking constantly, then in a thin steady stream once a third is in. Leave the milky solids in the bottom of the butter pan.
steps.look: The sauce thickens and turns glossy as each addition is absorbed, like a warm mayonnaise. It should fall from the whisk in a thick, soft ribbon.
steps.mistake: Pouring the butter in too fast at the start, so the emulsion never forms and pools of yellow fat float on top.
steps.fix: Stop pouring and whisk hard until it comes back together. If it has split completely, put 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a spoonful at a time; it will re-emulsify.

steps.do: Season with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, a small pinch of cayenne and more lemon to taste. If the sauce is thicker than double cream, whisk in warm water 1 tsp (5 ml) at a time. Pour it into the emptied warm thermos and close the lid.
steps.look: A pale yellow sauce, sharp enough to make you notice the lemon, that coats a spoon thickly and flows slowly when tipped.
steps.mistake: Holding hollandaise over direct heat or simmering water, which keeps cooking the yolks until it splits.
steps.fix: Hold it warm, never hot: about 145°F (63°C) in the thermos or over hand-hot water off the heat. Use within an hour.

steps.do: Fry the bacon in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes a side, just to warm and lightly colour it. Keep it warm on a plate covered with foil.
steps.look: Edges just golden, slices still pink and juicy, smelling of warm ham.
steps.mistake: Frying it hard until it curls and goes dry; back bacon is lean and toughens fast.
steps.fix: Warm it gently; it is already cooked. Curled slices can be pressed flat under a small pan.

steps.do: Toast the muffin halves cut side up under the overhead grill (broiler) or in a toaster until golden and crisp at the edges, then butter them lightly.
steps.look: Deep golden peaks and craggy hollows, crisp enough to hold sauce without turning soggy.
steps.mistake: Pale, soft muffins that collapse into paste under the egg.
steps.fix: Toast them a little darker than you think; the sauce and egg soften them.

steps.do: Bring the poaching water back to 150 to 160°F (65 to 71°C). Slip in the chilled eggs and leave 60 to 90 seconds to warm through. Lift out and drain well on kitchen paper.
steps.look: The eggs are hot to the touch on the outside with yolks still liquid when gently pressed.
steps.mistake: Reheating in simmering water, which cooks the yolks firm.
steps.fix: Keep the water hot but well below a simmer; test one egg first and adjust the time.

steps.do: Assemble on warm plates: two muffin halves, a slice of bacon on each, a drained egg on each. Spoon about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of hollandaise over each egg so it runs down one side. Finish with chives and a few grains of cayenne.
steps.look: Glossy sauce mantling each egg, the yolk outline visible under it, the muffin edges still crisp.
steps.mistake: Wet eggs that water down the sauce and make the muffin soggy.
steps.fix: Always blot each egg on kitchen paper before it goes on the plate.

dishes.science: Hollandaise is an emulsion of butterfat droplets suspended in a small amount of water, held there by egg yolk. Yolk carries lecithin and proteins that sit at the boundary between fat and water and stop droplets merging. Whisking the yolks over heat first makes a sabayon: the proteins begin to unfold and trap air and water, giving a thick base with enough structure to carry the butter. Heat is the risk on both sides. Below about 120°F (49°C) the butter firms and the sauce goes grainy; above about 160°F (71°C) the yolk proteins bond tightly, squeeze out water and the fat escapes. Acid from lemon loosens the proteins and helps them stay flexible. Vinegar in the poaching water helps the outer white set fast.
dishes.plating: Use warm plates with a wide rim. Set the two halves slightly apart in the centre, eggs facing the guest, so the sauce falls to the outside rather than pooling between them. Dot cayenne across the sauce in a single line and scatter chives over the egg only. A few dressed leaves or a little fruit can sit at the top of the plate; wipe any sauce from the rim.

pairing.drink: A Brut Champagne or a Crémant. Bright acidity and fine bubbles cut through butter and yolk, and the toasty, bready notes echo the muffin.
pairing.brennans: Eggs Hussarde: Brennan's own poached egg dish with hollandaise, the one to taste against yours when you describe it to a guest.

variations: Eggs Florentine: wilted buttered spinach in place of the bacon.
Eggs Royale: smoked salmon in place of the bacon, with a little dill in the hollandaise.
Béarnaise: replace the lemon and water with a tarragon, shallot and white wine vinegar reduction for a sauce that suits steak.
safety: The yolks in hollandaise are only lightly cooked. For pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system, use pasteurised eggs.
Hold hollandaise warm, about 145°F (63°C), and use it within an hour; do not keep it overnight or reheat it.
Chilled poached eggs keep up to 2 days in cold water in the fridge, below 40°F (4°C).

dishes.title: Eggs Sardou
dishes.summary: A New Orleans breakfast of poached eggs set on artichoke bottoms over creamed spinach, finished with hollandaise. It is here because it adds two classic preparations to the hollandaise you have just learned, turning whole artichokes into bottoms and making a proper creamed spinach, and because it is on the Brennan's breakfast menu you serve.
equipment: Sharp small paring knife and a serrated knife
Teaspoon or melon baller for scraping out the choke
Large saucepan for the artichokes
Medium saucepan for the creamed spinach
Balloon whisk
Heatproof bowl and saucepan for the bain-marie
Wide pan for poaching
Slotted spoon, fine sieve, bowl of iced water
Instant-read thermometer
Thermos flask for holding the sauce
Kitchen paper

ingredients.note: heavy for their size, with tight leaves
one for acidulated water, one for cooking
made exactly as for Eggs Benedict: 3 yolks, 12 tbsp (170 g) butter

mise: Fill a large bowl with cold water and squeeze in the juice of one lemon, dropping the halves in too. This is the acidulated water that stops cut artichokes browning.
Wash the spinach in two changes of water and spin it dry.
Chop the shallot, warm the milk.
Set up the hollandaise station: separated yolks, warm melted butter, lemon, a bain-marie at a bare simmer and a warmed thermos.
Heat the poaching water with vinegar to 185°F (85°C).
Crack the poaching eggs into cups.

timeline.do: Turn the artichokes and start them cooking.
Poach the eggs and hold in iced water.
Blanch the spinach and make the creamed spinach.
Make the hollandaise.
Warm the artichoke bottoms, reheat the eggs.
Build the plates.

steps.do: Turn the artichokes. Snap off the dark outer leaves by bending them back until they break, working round until you reach pale yellow leaves. Cut off the top two thirds of the leaves with the serrated knife, and cut the stem flush with the base. Rub every cut surface with lemon.
steps.look: A squat, pale green base with a cone of short yellow leaves on top. Cut surfaces stay pale where lemon touched them.
steps.mistake: Leaving dark green leaf bases on, which stay fibrous and stringy even after cooking.
steps.fix: Pare round the base with the paring knife, turning the artichoke against the blade like peeling an apple, until only pale flesh shows.

steps.do: Drop each turned artichoke into the acidulated water as soon as it is done. Bring a large pan of water to the boil with the second lemon's juice, 1 tbsp (8 g) flour whisked in and 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Add the artichokes, cover with a plate to keep them under, and simmer 20 to 25 minutes.
steps.look: A paring knife slides into the base like into a ripe pear. The cooking liquid looks cloudy from the flour.
steps.mistake: Cooking them in plain water, so they turn grey and taste metallic.
steps.fix: The flour and lemon cooking liquid, called a blanc, keeps them pale. Grey artichokes still taste fine; serve them sauced and use the blanc next time.

steps.do: Lift the artichokes out and cool them upside down until you can handle them. Pull away the remaining leaves, then scrape out the hairy choke with the teaspoon. Trim the bottoms into neat cups. Keep them in a little of their cooking liquid.
steps.look: Smooth, pale cups about 3 inches (7 cm) across with a clean hollow, no fibres left.
steps.mistake: Leaving wisps of choke, which feel like hair in the mouth.
steps.fix: Scrape firmly in a circle with the spoon edge, then rub with a finger; any remaining fuzz comes away.

steps.do: Poach the eggs in two batches of four at 185°F (85°C) for 3 minutes, draining each through a sieve first, and hold them in iced water, exactly as for Eggs Benedict.
steps.look: Neat oval eggs, whites set, yolks soft.
steps.mistake: Water that boils and shreds the whites.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to a quiver and trim any ragged edges with scissors.

steps.do: Blanch the spinach. Plunge it into a large pan of boiling salted water for 30 seconds, drain and plunge into iced water. Drain again, then squeeze it hard in your fists or a clean cloth until no more water drips. Chop it finely.
steps.look: A tight, dark green ball about a quarter of its raw size. Chopped, it looks like moss with no liquid running from it.
steps.mistake: Not squeezing hard enough, so the creamed spinach is watery and dilutes the hollandaise.
steps.fix: Squeeze in a cloth and twist until your hands ache. If the cream sauce turns loose later, simmer it a minute longer to reduce.

steps.do: Melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter in the medium pan over medium-low heat. Sweat the shallot 3 minutes without colour. Stir in 1 tbsp (8 g) flour and cook 1 minute. Whisk in the warm milk, then the cream, and simmer 3 minutes until thick. Stir in the spinach, nutmeg, salt and white pepper, and warm through.
steps.look: A thick, glossy green mixture that holds its shape on a spoon and smells of nutmeg and warm cream.
steps.mistake: A thin sauce, so the spinach spreads across the plate instead of making a bed.
steps.fix: Simmer longer to reduce; it should be thick enough to mound.

steps.do: Make the hollandaise: sabayon of yolks, lemon and water whisked over the bain-marie to 145 to 155°F (63 to 68°C), then warm butter whisked in drop by drop and then in a thin stream, seasoned with salt and cayenne. Hold it in the warmed thermos.
steps.look: A glossy, pale yellow sauce that falls in a soft ribbon.
steps.mistake: Overheating the sabayon so it scrambles.
steps.fix: Lift the bowl off the heat often. Rescue a split sauce by whisking it into 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm water in a clean bowl.

steps.do: Warm the artichoke bottoms for 2 minutes in their simmering liquid. Reheat the eggs for 60 to 90 seconds in water at 150 to 160°F (65 to 71°C). Drain both very well on kitchen paper.
steps.look: Artichokes hot through, eggs warm on the outside with soft yolks.
steps.mistake: Wet artichoke cups that leak liquid into the sauce.
steps.fix: Turn the cups upside down on kitchen paper for 30 seconds.

steps.do: On each warm plate, spoon two mounds of creamed spinach and press an artichoke bottom into each. Set an egg in each cup and coat with 2 tbsp (30 ml) hollandaise. Serve at once.
steps.look: Two neat towers of green, pale artichoke, white egg and golden sauce, the spinach visible at the base.
steps.mistake: Building the plate before everything is hot, so it arrives lukewarm.
steps.fix: Assemble last, in a line, plates warmed in a low oven at 150°F (65°C).

dishes.science: Artichokes brown fast because cutting breaks cells and lets an enzyme, polyphenol oxidase, meet oxygen and turn the plant's phenolic compounds into brown pigments. Acid slows the enzyme, which is why lemon on the cut surfaces and acidulated water keep them pale. Cooking in a blanc, water with flour and lemon, adds a film of starch that limits contact with air and helps hold the colour, while the acid preserves the pale green. Spinach is mostly water held in thin cell walls; blanching collapses the walls and releases that water, which is why you can squeeze so much out. Shocking in iced water stops the chlorophyll turning olive. A roux-thickened cream sauce binds the spinach so it stays put under the egg.
dishes.plating: Warm round plates, two towers per plate set side by side on the diameter. Keep spinach in a neat mound no wider than the artichoke so the base looks deliberate. Sauce only the egg, letting it run onto the artichoke but not across the plate. No garnish is needed; a grain of cayenne on each is enough.

pairing.drink: A dry Grüner Veltliner or Sauvignon Blanc. Both handle artichoke, which makes many wines taste sweet, and their green, peppery edge suits spinach.
pairing.brennans: Eggs Sardou: the dish itself is on the Brennan's breakfast menu, so cooking it at home is the best preparation for describing it at the table.

variations: Use good tinned or jarred artichoke bottoms, rinsed and warmed, when fresh artichokes are not in season.
Add a spoonful of finely grated Parmesan to the creamed spinach for a deeper flavour.
Swap the hollandaise for a béarnaise for a tarragon-scented version.
safety: Use pasteurised eggs in the hollandaise for anyone vulnerable; hold the sauce warm and use it within an hour.
Turning artichokes needs a firm grip and a sharp knife; work on a damp cloth so the board cannot slide, and cut away from your hand.

dishes.title: Omelette Arnold Bennett
dishes.summary: An open omelette topped with flaked smoked haddock and a sauce of mornay lightened with hollandaise and whipped cream, then glazed under a hot overhead grill (broiler). It is here because it joins two sauces you already know into a glaze, and because cooking a flat omelette that stays soft beneath a browned top is a lesson in heat from below and above at once.
skills: a mornay lightened with hollandaise and cream
an open omelette glazed under the grill
equipment: Ovenproof nonstick frying pan, 10 inch (25 cm)
Shallow pan for poaching the fish
Small saucepan and whisk for the mornay
Heatproof bowl and saucepan for a small hollandaise
Mixing bowl and whisk for the cream
Fork and rubber spatula
Oven gloves

ingredients.note: skinned; undyed is pale cream, not bright yellow
for poaching, then used in the mornay
1 tbsp (14 g) for the roux, 1 tbsp (14 g) for the pan

ingredients.item: Egg yolk, for a small hollandaise
ingredients.note: with 1 tsp (5 ml) lemon juice and 4 tbsp (56 g) melted butter

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, melted, for the hollandaise

ingredients.note: the haddock is salty, so season lightly

mise: Heat the grill to its highest setting with a shelf 4 inches (10 cm) below the element.
Put the haddock in the shallow pan with the milk and bay leaf.
Grate the cheese.
Melt the 4 tbsp (56 g) butter for the hollandaise and keep warm; set up a small bain-marie.
Whip the cream to soft peaks and keep cold.
Beat the 5 eggs with a pinch of pepper and a very small pinch of salt until no streaks of white remain.

timeline.do: Heat the grill, poach the haddock.
Make the mornay from the poaching milk.
Make the small hollandaise, whip the cream.
Fold the sauce together and flake the fish.
Cook the omelette base.
Top, glaze under the grill, serve.

steps.do: Bring the milk with the haddock to a bare simmer over medium-low heat, then turn off the heat, cover and leave 5 minutes. Lift the fish out and strain the milk into a jug; you need 1 cup (240 ml).
steps.look: The fish turns opaque and flakes when pressed. The milk smells gently smoky.
steps.mistake: Boiling the fish, which makes it dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the first bubble breaks; the residual heat finishes it.

steps.do: Flake the fish into large pieces, removing any bones you find by running your fingers through the flakes.
steps.look: Big, moist, pale flakes, not shreds.
steps.mistake: Mashing it into threads.
steps.fix: Pull it apart along its natural layers with two forks.

steps.do: Make the mornay. Melt 1 tbsp (14 g) butter, stir in the flour and cook 1 minute without colour. Whisk in 1 cup (240 ml) of the warm poaching milk a little at a time, simmer gently 5 minutes, then off the heat stir in the cheese.
steps.look: A smooth sauce, thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, smelling of smoke and cheese.
steps.mistake: Lumps from adding the milk too fast.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; if lumps remain, push it through a sieve.

steps.do: Make a small hollandaise: whisk the yolk with the lemon juice and 1 tsp (5 ml) water over the bain-marie until thick and pale, then off the heat whisk in the 4 tbsp (56 g) warm butter in a thin stream.
steps.look: A glossy small sauce that holds a ribbon.
steps.mistake: Scrambling such a small amount of yolk, which heats very quickly.
steps.fix: Work mostly off the heat, returning the bowl only for a few seconds at a time.

steps.do: Let the mornay cool for 5 minutes until warm, not hot. Fold in the hollandaise, then fold in the whipped cream. Fold in half the haddock.
steps.look: A light, pale, airy sauce that still holds its shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Folding the hollandaise into boiling-hot mornay, which splits it.
steps.fix: Wait until the mornay is about body temperature; if it splits, whisk in a spoonful of cold cream.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the ovenproof pan over medium heat until it foams. Pour in the beaten eggs and stir with the spatula, pulling the set egg from the edges into the centre, for about 1 minute, then stop stirring and let it set for 30 seconds.
steps.look: A flat, even round of soft, barely set egg, still glossy and wet on top, pale gold underneath.
steps.mistake: Cooking it right through on the hob, so it is rubbery by the time it has been grilled.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat while the top is still runny; the grill does the rest.

steps.do: Scatter the remaining haddock over the omelette, then spoon the sauce over evenly, right to the edges.
steps.look: An even blanket of sauce covering the egg completely.
steps.mistake: Leaving bare egg at the edges, which dries and toughens under the grill.
steps.fix: Spread the sauce to the rim of the omelette with the back of a spoon.

steps.do: Slide the pan under the grill, handle facing out, for 2 to 3 minutes until the top puffs and browns in patches. Wear oven gloves; the handle will be scorching.
steps.look: A puffed, bubbling, golden glaze with darker brown spots, smelling of browned cheese.
steps.mistake: Walking away; the sauce goes from golden to burnt in under a minute.
steps.fix: Stay and watch, turning the pan once. If the edges darken first, move it further from the element.

steps.do: Slide onto a warm plate, scatter the herbs and cut into halves at the table.
steps.look: A tender omelette beneath a soufflé-like browned top.
steps.mistake: Letting it stand, so the glaze collapses.
steps.fix: Serve it the moment it leaves the grill.

dishes.science: The glaze works because each sauce adds something the others lack. Mornay brings a starch-stabilised body that will not split under fierce heat. Hollandaise adds egg yolk, whose proteins and sugars brown quickly. Whipped cream adds air and milk fat, so the sauce puffs and turns light as the trapped air expands under the grill. That browning is the Maillard reaction between proteins and sugars, which runs fast above about 300°F (150°C), a temperature only the surface reaches. The omelette below stays soft because the sauce insulates it and the grill heats only from above for a short time. Smoked haddock is cold-smoked and salted, so it needs only warming through.
dishes.plating: Serve it whole on a warm plate slightly larger than the omelette, or straight from the pan on a board for two to share. Cut into halves with a sharp knife to show the soft egg and flakes inside. A small green salad with a mustard vinaigrette on the side is the only accompaniment.

pairing.drink: A Chablis or another unoaked Chardonnay. Its crisp acidity and chalky edge match the smoked fish and cut the creamy sauce.
pairing.brennans: Crab & Corn Omelette: Brennan's own omelette, a useful comparison of a seafood omelette for the guest choosing between rich egg dishes.

variations: Use hot-smoked trout or salmon in place of the haddock.
Leave out the hollandaise and fold more whipped cream into the mornay for a simpler, still glazing sauce.
Make individual omelettes in a 7 inch (18 cm) pan for neat single portions.
safety: Use oven gloves on the pan handle after grilling, and leave a cloth draped over the handle as a reminder that it is hot.
Use a pasteurised egg yolk in the hollandaise for anyone vulnerable.

dishes.title: Rösti with Fried Eggs
dishes.summary: A single golden cake of coarsely grated potato, fried slowly in butter until crisp outside and tender within, flipped whole and served with fried eggs. It is here because getting one cake to hold together without egg or flour teaches how starch binds, and because the flip is a skill every line cook needs.
skills: a single slow-fried cake flipped whole
equipment: Medium saucepan
Box grater, coarse side
Heavy nonstick or well-seasoned cast-iron frying pan, 9 to 10 inch (23 to 25 cm)
Flat plate slightly larger than the pan
Fish slice or thin spatula
Second frying pan for the eggs

ingredients.note: such as Charlotte, Yukon Gold or Désirée, similar in size
or 2 tbsp (28 g) butter plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil
for the edges at the flip

mise: The day before, boil the whole unpeeled potatoes in salted water for 10 to 12 minutes, until a knife meets firm resistance in the centre. Drain, cool and refrigerate uncovered overnight.
Next morning peel the cold potatoes with your fingers or a small knife.
Grate them on the coarse side of the box grater into long strands.
Season with salt and pepper and toss lightly with your fingers, without squashing.

timeline.do: Parboil the potatoes and chill overnight.
Peel and grate.
Fry the first side slowly.
Flip and fry the second side.
Fry the eggs.
Slide onto a board and serve.

steps.do: Parboil the potatoes the day before as in the mise, then chill them uncovered overnight.
steps.look: Potatoes that are cooked at the rim and still firm in the middle, cold and slightly dry on the surface.
steps.mistake: Boiling them soft, so they grate into mush.
steps.fix: If they are overcooked, grate them very gently and accept a softer cake, or turn them into a mash and try again tomorrow.

steps.do: Grate the peeled cold potatoes coarsely, holding each one at a long angle so you get long strands. Season lightly and loosen with your fingertips.
steps.look: Long, separate, slightly translucent strands, not wet or pasty.
steps.mistake: Pressing hard on the grater, which breaks the strands into crumbs.
steps.fix: Use light, long strokes; the cold, firm potato should grate cleanly.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (28 g) of the clarified butter in the pan over medium heat until it shimmers. Add the potato all at once and spread it to the edges with a fork, then press gently into an even cake about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick, tidying the edges into a neat round.
steps.look: The fat sizzles steadily as the potato goes in, a gentle hiss rather than a roar.
steps.mistake: Packing the cake hard, which makes it dense and gluey.
steps.fix: Press only enough to make contact with the pan; the starch will bind it as it cooks.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium-low and fry for 12 to 15 minutes without moving it. After 8 minutes, shake the pan: the cake should slide as one piece.
steps.look: A steady quiet sizzle, a smell of toasted butter, and a golden-brown crust visible when you lift an edge with the spatula.
steps.mistake: Too much heat, which blackens the outside before the inside heats through.
steps.fix: If it smells of burning, turn the heat down; if it is still pale at 12 minutes, raise it slightly.

steps.do: Flip it. Slide the cake onto the plate, put the pan upside down over the plate, then with one hand on the plate and one on the handle (in oven gloves), turn both over together in one confident movement.
steps.look: The cake drops back into the pan browned side up, whole.
steps.mistake: Hesitating halfway, so the cake breaks.
steps.fix: Commit to the turn. If it cracks, push it back together with the spatula; the second side will glue it.

steps.do: Add the remaining 1 tbsp (12 g) clarified butter and the 1 tbsp (14 g) whole butter round the edge so it runs underneath. Fry the second side 10 to 12 minutes over medium-low heat.
steps.look: The fresh butter foams round the edges, and the cake firms and crisps again.
steps.mistake: Adding no fat, so the second side scorches in a dry pan.
steps.fix: Tilt the pan and swirl so the butter flows underneath the cake.

steps.do: Meanwhile fry the eggs in a little butter over medium-low heat, covered for the last minute, until the whites are set and the yolks still soft.
steps.look: Glossy set whites with no crisp brown edges, yolks bright and soft.
steps.mistake: Frying the eggs hot so the whites blister and toughen.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and cover the pan to set the top of the white with steam.

steps.do: Slide the rösti onto a warm board or plate, cut into wedges, top each with an egg and scatter chives.
steps.look: A deep golden crust on both faces, a tender, steaming centre when cut.
steps.mistake: Covering the rösti while it waits, which steams the crust soft.
steps.fix: Keep it uncovered in a low oven at 200°F (95°C) if the eggs are running behind.

dishes.science: A rösti holds together without egg or flour because of the potato's own starch. Parboiling swells and partly gelatinises the starch granules just beneath the skin, and chilling overnight lets that starch partly recrystallise, a process called retrogradation. The cold potato is firmer and drier, so it grates into neat strands that keep their shape. As the cake fries, the surface starch softens again and glues the strands where they touch, while the outer layer dries and browns. Clarified butter matters because its milk solids, which burn at about 250°F (120°C), have been removed, so it can fry slowly for half an hour without turning bitter. Low, steady heat lets the centre warm through before the crust overcooks.
dishes.plating: Bring it to the table whole on a wooden board, browned side up, eggs on top, and cut it there. For individual plates, cut neat wedges with a sharp knife, set an egg on the widest part and add a small pile of dressed watercress beside it.

pairing.drink: A dry Swiss Chasselas or a dry Riesling. Both have soft fruit and enough acid to refresh the palate after butter and potato.
pairing.brennans: Brabant Potatoes: Brennan's crisp fried potato side, a good comparison when you describe how texture is built from potato starch.

variations: Bernese style: fold in crisp bacon lardons and a little grated Gruyère before frying.
Raw rösti: grate raw potatoes, squeeze them very dry in a cloth and fry; quicker but crisper and more fragile.
Top with smoked salmon and soured cream instead of eggs.
safety: Flipping with a hot pan over a plate risks burns: use oven gloves and work over the hob, not over your feet.
Cooked potatoes for the next day should go into the fridge within 2 hours and be used within 2 days.

dishes.title: Hummus Msabbaha
dishes.summary: Silky hummus made from dried chickpeas cooked past soft, whipped with tahini and iced water, then topped with warm whole chickpeas in lemon and garlic. It is here because the whipped tahini is an emulsion you build by ear and eye, and because cooking dried legumes until they collapse is a lesson in what bicarbonate does to pectin.
skills: cooking dried chickpeas very soft with bicarbonate
equipment: Large bowl for soaking
Large saucepan
Slotted spoon and skimmer
Food processor
Small saucepan
Measuring jug and a few ice cubes

ingredients.note: 1/2 tsp (2.5 g) to soak, 1/2 tsp (2.5 g) to cook
a smooth, pourable Lebanese or Palestinian brand; stir the jar well
one grated for the hummus, one for the topping
plus a pinch for the topping

ingredients.item: Warm pita and raw onion wedges

mise: The night before, cover the chickpeas with at least three times their volume of cold water and stir in 1/2 tsp (2.5 g) bicarbonate. Leave 12 hours.
Drain and rinse the chickpeas.
Squeeze the lemons; grate one garlic clove finely and leave it in half the lemon juice for 10 minutes to soften its bite.
Put a few ice cubes in a jug of water.

timeline.do: Soak the chickpeas with bicarbonate.
Simmer the chickpeas until very soft.
Blend the hummus while the chickpeas are hot.
Warm the reserved whole chickpeas with lemon and garlic.
Swirl, top and serve.

steps.do: Put the drained chickpeas in the large pan with 1/2 tsp (2.5 g) bicarbonate and stir over medium heat for 3 minutes, then cover with water by 2 inches (5 cm) and bring to the boil.
steps.look: The chickpeas look slightly paler and swollen; a grey-white foam rises as the water heats.
steps.mistake: Skipping the bicarbonate, so the chickpeas stay grainy however long you cook them.
steps.fix: Add it now, even late; it works within the next hour of cooking.

steps.do: Simmer for 1 to 1 1/2 hours, skimming off foam and loose skins every 15 minutes, until they are completely soft.
steps.look: A chickpea crushes to smooth paste with no resistance when pressed between finger and thumb; many skins float on top.
steps.mistake: Stopping when they are merely tender, which gives gritty hummus.
steps.fix: Keep going; for hummus they should be past what you would serve whole, almost falling apart.

steps.do: Lift out 3/4 cup (about 120 g) of the best whole chickpeas for the topping and keep them in a little cooking liquid. Drain the rest, saving some of the liquid.
steps.look: Two piles: whole, intact chickpeas and very soft, broken ones.
steps.mistake: Draining the topping chickpeas dry, so they go leathery.
steps.fix: Keep them covered in their liquid until you need them.

steps.do: While the chickpeas are still hot, blend them in the food processor with the lemon juice and garlic mixture for 3 minutes until a thick paste forms, scraping down twice.
steps.look: A thick, warm, fairly smooth paste, smelling of garlic and lemon.
steps.mistake: Blending cold chickpeas, which gives a heavier, pastier texture.
steps.fix: Reheat them in their liquid for a minute if they have cooled.

steps.do: Add the tahini, salt and cumin and blend 1 minute. With the motor running, add iced water a tablespoon at a time, about 5 tbsp (75 ml) in all, blending for 3 to 4 minutes in total.
steps.look: The hummus suddenly lightens in colour, becomes fluffy and smooth, and spreads softly like whipped butter.
steps.mistake: Adding all the water at once, which makes it runny rather than whipped.
steps.fix: Add it slowly and stop when it is soft enough to swirl. If too thin, blend in 1 tbsp (15 g) more tahini.

steps.do: Taste and adjust: more salt, more lemon if it is flat, more tahini if it tastes thin. Blend another 30 seconds.
steps.look: Nutty, rich, bright with lemon, salted so the sesame tastes clearly.
steps.mistake: Under-salting; hummus needs more than you think.
steps.fix: Add salt a pinch at a time and taste again on a piece of bread.

steps.do: Warm the reserved whole chickpeas in a small pan with the remaining lemon juice, the second garlic clove grated, a pinch of salt and 2 tbsp (30 ml) of their liquid.
steps.look: Glossy, steaming chickpeas in a little lemony liquid, smelling of garlic.
steps.mistake: Boiling them dry so they split and toughen.
steps.fix: Keep it to a gentle warm, then take it off the heat.

steps.do: Spread the hummus on a wide plate, making a deep well with the back of a spoon by turning the plate under it. Spoon the warm chickpeas and their juice into the well, then pour the olive oil over and scatter paprika and parsley.
steps.look: A smooth, pale ring of hummus with warm chickpeas glistening in a pool of oil in the centre.
steps.mistake: Leaving the hummus flat, so the oil and topping slide off.
steps.fix: Push the spoon down and turn the plate slowly against it to make a raised rim.

dishes.science: Bicarbonate makes the cooking water alkaline, and in alkaline conditions pectin, the glue that holds plant cell walls together, breaks down far faster. The chickpeas soften completely and their skins loosen, so they blend to silk rather than grit. Tahini is ground sesame: oil plus finely ground seed solids and proteins. When you add water, the seed particles absorb it and swell while the oil disperses into tiny droplets, which is why tahini first seizes and thickens, then turns pale and smooth. Ice-cold water firms the oil and helps the mixture whip, trapping air so the hummus becomes light. Blending the chickpeas hot keeps their starch soft and spreadable.
dishes.plating: A wide, shallow plate with a raised ring of hummus, warm chickpeas in the centre, a generous pool of green olive oil and a stripe of red paprika. Serve with warm pita wrapped in a cloth and a small plate of raw onion wedges, pickles and mint leaves.

pairing.drink: A crisp dry rosé from Provence. Its red fruit and acidity cut through tahini richness and stand up to raw garlic.

variations: Hummus with spiced lamb: top with minced lamb fried with cinnamon, allspice and pine nuts.
Ful mudammas topping: crushed warm fava beans with cumin and lemon in place of the whole chickpeas.
Add a spoonful of the tahini sauce, tahini whisked with lemon and water, over the warm chickpeas for extra richness.
safety: Cooked chickpeas should be cooled and refrigerated within 2 hours; hummus keeps 3 to 4 days in the fridge, covered with a film of oil.

dishes.title: Shiozake Teishoku (Salted Salmon Breakfast)
dishes.summary: A Japanese set breakfast of salted, grilled salmon with crisp skin, served with steamed rice, miso soup and small pickles. It is here because it teaches you to cut a whole side of salmon into even portions and to dry salt fish so it firms and seasons evenly, then to grill skin until it crackles.
skills: cutting a salmon side into portions
equipment: Long sharp knife or a flexible filleting knife
Fish tweezers or clean needle-nose pliers
Cutting board with a damp cloth underneath
Wire rack set on a tray
Grill pan or an oven grill (broiler) with a foil-lined tray
Heavy saucepan with a tight lid for the rice
Small saucepan for the miso soup
Kitchen paper

ingredients.note: a centre-cut piece of an even thickness
optional, to wipe the fish before salting
made from kombu and katsuobushi, or instant dashi

mise: Rinse the rice in cold water, swirling and draining four or five times until the water is only faintly cloudy. Drain in a sieve for 30 minutes.
Make or warm the dashi.
Soak the wakame; cube the tofu; slice the spring onion.
Grate and lightly squeeze the daikon.
Line the grill tray with foil and oil the rack lightly.

timeline.do: Portion and salt the salmon, refrigerate uncovered on a rack.
Rinse and drain the rice.
Cook the rice.
Grill the salmon.
Finish the miso soup.
Serve everything at once on a tray.

steps.do: Lay the salmon skin side down. Run your fingertips along the centre line from head to tail to find the pin bones and pull each out with tweezers at the same angle it lies, towards the head.
steps.look: A row of small white bone tips appears under your fingers; each comes out with a gentle tug and no flesh attached.
steps.mistake: Pulling straight up or against the grain, which tears the flesh.
steps.fix: Press the flesh down beside the bone with one finger and pull in the direction the bone points.

steps.do: Cut the side across into 4 even portions, each about 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) wide, using one long stroke of the knife per cut, no sawing. Cut the thin belly end a little wider so all four weigh about the same.
steps.look: Four pieces of matching weight, about 5 oz (140 g) each, with clean, glossy cut faces.
steps.mistake: Sawing back and forth, which shreds the flesh, or cutting equal widths so the thin tail piece overcooks.
steps.fix: Weigh the pieces and adjust; draw the knife from heel to tip in one pull.

steps.do: Wipe the pieces with the sake if using, then sprinkle the salt evenly over both sides, a little more on the thick parts. Set skin side up on the rack over the tray and refrigerate, uncovered, overnight or at least 2 hours.
steps.look: By morning the flesh is darker, firmer and slightly translucent at the surface, with beads of liquid on the tray below, and the skin looks dry and tight.
steps.mistake: Covering the fish, which keeps the skin damp so it will not crisp.
steps.fix: If short of time, salt for 2 hours and pat very dry; the fish will be softer and less seasoned but still good.

steps.do: Put the drained rice and 1 2/3 cups (400 ml) water in the heavy pan. Bring to the boil over medium-high heat, cover tightly, reduce to the lowest heat and cook 12 minutes. Turn off the heat and leave covered 10 minutes.
steps.look: Small steam holes across a flat surface, every grain plump and glossy, sticky but not mushy.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking, which lets the steam out and leaves hard grains.
steps.fix: Keep it covered. If the top is still firm, sprinkle 1 tbsp (15 ml) water, cover and leave 5 more minutes off the heat.

steps.do: Heat the grill to high. Pat the salmon dry with kitchen paper. Grill skin side up 4 inches (10 cm) from the element for 5 to 6 minutes until the skin blisters and browns, then turn carefully and grill the flesh side 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: The skin bubbles, crackles and turns golden with darker spots; fat sizzles onto the tray. The flesh turns opaque and flakes at the thickest point.
steps.mistake: Grilling a wet fish, which steams the skin limp.
steps.fix: Dry thoroughly before grilling. If the skin is browning too fast, lower the tray a shelf.

steps.do: Check doneness: the thickest part should reach 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for moist, just opaque salmon. Let it rest 1 minute.
steps.look: Flakes separate under gentle pressure with the barest translucency in the very centre.
steps.mistake: Cooking until white fat seeps out all over the surface, a sign it is overcooked and dry.
steps.fix: Pull it at the first sign of white beads at the edges; the salt has already firmed it.

steps.do: Make the miso soup. Heat the dashi to just below a simmer, add the tofu and drained wakame and warm 1 minute. Turn off the heat. Put the miso in a ladle, lower it into the soup and whisk it in with chopsticks until dissolved. Do not boil it again.
steps.look: A cloudy, golden soup that smells sweet and savoury, tofu cubes intact.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the miso goes in, which dulls its aroma and makes it grainy.
steps.fix: If you reheat, stop just before the first bubble.

steps.do: Serve each person a tray: a bowl of rice front left, miso soup front right with spring onion, salmon on a small plate behind with a mound of grated daikon and a drop of soy, and pickles alongside.
steps.look: A neat balance of bowls, the salmon skin crisp and glossy.
steps.mistake: Setting the soup on the left, which is the reverse of the Japanese table arrangement.
steps.fix: Rice on the left, soup on the right, main dish behind.

dishes.science: Dry salting draws water from the surface of the fish by osmosis, then the salt dissolves in that moisture and slowly diffuses back into the flesh. As it travels inwards, it partly dissolves and loosens the muscle proteins, which then bind more tightly when heated, so the fish cooks up firmer and juicier rather than flaking into dry crumbs. Overnight salting also seasons the flesh evenly throughout. Leaving the fish uncovered on a rack dries the skin, and dry skin crisps because the heat goes into browning rather than evaporating water. Salmon skin has a fat layer underneath, which renders under the grill and fries the skin from below, giving the crackling surface.
dishes.plating: A traditional tray with separate dishes: a rectangular plate for the fish, skin side up and angled with the thicker end to the left, a small tidy cone of grated daikon in front of it, rice and miso in matching bowls, pickles in a tiny dish. Leave space between each dish.

pairing.drink: A cup of hot green tea, or a chilled dry junmai sake if served as a late, lazy meal. Both cleanse the palate after rich salmon.

variations: Saba shioyaki: the same salting and grilling with mackerel fillets.
Miso-marinated salmon: replace the salt with a sweet miso and mirin paste, wipe off before grilling.
Flake leftover salted salmon into onigiri with a strip of nori.
safety: Keep salting fish in the fridge below 40°F (4°C); salting for flavour does not make fish safe to eat raw.
Pin bones are a choking hazard; run your fingers over every portion before cooking.

The official guideline for fish is 145°F (63°C). Salmon is traditionally taken off at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for moist flesh; for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or unwell, cook it to 145°F (63°C).

dishes.title: Gravlax with Hovmästarsås on Rye
dishes.summary: Salmon cured for two days under salt, sugar, pepper and a thick blanket of dill, sliced thin and served on rye with a sweet mustard and dill sauce. It is here because it is the first cure in the course, where the amount of salt is a weight you measure, not a guess, and because slicing paper thin on the bias is a knife skill all of its own.
skills: a salt, sugar and dill cure by weight
equipment: Digital scale
Fish tweezers
Glass or ceramic dish just big enough for the fish
Cling film
A small board and a few tins, for weighting
Long, thin, very sharp slicing knife
Small bowl and whisk for the sauce

ingredients.item: Salmon fillet, skin on, centre cut
ingredients.note: sold for raw eating and previously frozen; cut into two matching halves
half roughly chopped with its stalks, half finely chopped for the sauce and serving

ingredients.item: Swedish or Dijon mustard, for the sauce

mise: Weigh the salmon and work out the salt: about 7.5% of the weight. For 600 g that is 45 g.
Mix the salt, sugar and crushed pepper in a bowl.
Chop half the dill roughly, stalks and all.
Clear a flat space in the fridge for the dish.

timeline.do: Pin-bone, cure, wrap, weight and refrigerate.
Turn and baste.
Turn and baste every 12 hours.
Unwrap, scrape, dry.
Make the sauce.
Slice thin and serve on rye.

steps.do: Run your fingers along each fillet and pull out the pin bones with tweezers, towards the head end. Cut the fillet into two equal pieces if it is not already halved.
steps.look: Two neat pieces of matching size with no bones left anywhere.
steps.mistake: Missing bones, which catch the knife when you slice thin.
steps.fix: Check twice; bones near the head end are larger and easy to feel.

steps.do: Lay one piece skin side down in the dish. Rub half the cure over its flesh, sprinkle with half the spirit, then pile the roughly chopped dill on top. Rub the rest of the cure over the second piece and lay it on top, flesh side down, so the two flesh sides sandwich the dill.
steps.look: A fat sandwich of salmon with dill showing at the edges and cure visible on every bit of flesh.
steps.mistake: Putting all the cure on top, so the bottom piece barely cures.
steps.fix: Divide it evenly by eye before you start; the thicker parts get slightly more.

steps.do: Wrap the whole thing tightly in cling film, set the board on top and weigh it down with two or three tins. Refrigerate.
steps.look: A flattened parcel; within a few hours liquid starts to collect in the dish.
steps.mistake: Not weighting it, so the cure works unevenly and the fish stays soft.
steps.fix: Any heavy flat weight will do: a small chopping board and a bag of sugar.

steps.do: Every 12 hours, turn the parcel over and spoon the brine that has collected back over the fish through the gap in the film. Continue for 48 hours in total.
steps.look: By the second day the flesh is deeper orange, firmer and more translucent at the edges, and there is a good pool of brine.
steps.mistake: Pouring the brine away, which takes the seasoning with it.
steps.fix: Keep it; it is the cure doing its work. A day longer gives firmer, saltier fish if you prefer.

steps.do: After 48 hours, unwrap, scrape off the dill and cure with the back of a knife and pat the fish dry with kitchen paper.
steps.look: Firm, glossy, deep coral flesh that springs back when pressed, smelling clean of the sea and dill, never fishy.
steps.mistake: Rinsing under the tap, which waterlogs the surface.
steps.fix: Scrape and pat dry only. If it tastes too salty, slice thinner; salt reads less on a thin slice.

steps.do: Press the finely chopped dill onto the flesh side of one piece if you want a green edge. Make the sauce: whisk mustard, sugar and vinegar, then whisk in the oil in a thin stream until thick, and stir in 2 tbsp (6 g) of chopped dill. Season with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: A glossy, pale yellow, thick sauce that tastes sweet, sharp and herbal.
steps.mistake: Adding the oil too fast so it splits.
steps.fix: Whisk in a teaspoon of hot water to bring a split sauce back.

steps.do: Slice. Lay the fish skin side down and start a third of the way from the tail. Hold the knife almost flat, at about 15 degrees, and draw it towards you in one long stroke to cut a slice 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, cutting down to but not through the skin. Lift each slice off with the knife.
steps.look: Long, wide, translucent slices with a darker line of flesh at the skin edge; the knife makes one clean pass each time.
steps.mistake: Sawing short strokes or holding the knife too upright, giving thick, ragged chunks.
steps.fix: Use the full length of the blade; wipe it between slices and keep it very sharp.

steps.do: Lay the slices in loose folds on buttered rye, spoon a little sauce alongside, and add a lemon wedge and a dill sprig.
steps.look: Soft folds of glossy salmon, the sauce in a neat pool beside them.
steps.mistake: Slicing too far ahead, so the slices dry and dull.
steps.fix: Slice just before serving; wrap the rest tightly and keep up to 5 days in the fridge.

dishes.science: Salt draws water out of the fish by osmosis and then diffuses into the flesh, where it partly dissolves the muscle proteins and makes them bond into a denser, firmer texture. Sugar does the same job more gently and balances the salt, so the fish tastes seasoned rather than briny. Together they lower the water available to bacteria, which is why the cure helps the fish keep. Curing by weight matters because a percentage of salt gives the same result each time, whatever size the fillet. Weighting the parcel presses the cure into close contact and squeezes out liquid, so the texture becomes silky and dense. A cure does not kill parasites, which is why fish for gravlax should be frozen first.
dishes.plating: On a long board or plate, overlapping slices on squares of rye, each topped with a frond of dill. A small bowl of the mustard sauce and lemon wedges at one end. For a smart plate, roll three slices into rosettes on a single round of rye with a dot of sauce and a sprig of dill.

pairing.drink: A cold aquavit for the Scandinavian table, or a dry sparkling rosé whose red fruit matches the salmon and whose bubbles cut the oil.
pairing.brennans: Pierre Sparr Brut Rosé Crémant d’Alsace NV: the rosé Crémant on Brennan's list is the kind of wine that works beautifully with cured salmon.

variations: Beetroot gravlax: add 1 grated raw beetroot to the cure for a magenta rim.
Citrus gravlax: replace the spirit with the zest of an orange and a lime and add a few crushed coriander seeds.
Serve on blinis with soured cream instead of rye.
safety: Curing does not kill parasites. Use salmon sold for eating raw that has been frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for at least 7 days, or freeze it yourself before curing if your freezer reaches that temperature.
Keep the fish in the fridge below 40°F (4°C) the whole time and eat within 5 days of finishing the cure.
Pregnant guests and anyone vulnerable should avoid cured raw fish.

dishes.title: Bagels with Home-Cured Lox and Schmear
dishes.summary: Proper bagels made from a stiff dough, shaped into rings, retarded overnight, boiled in malted water and baked, served with salmon you have cured yourself and a schmear of cream cheese. It is here because boiling dough before baking is a technique of its own, and because the lox cure is saltier and shorter than gravlax, a second lesson in curing by weight.
equipment: Digital scale
Stand mixer with a dough hook, or strong arms
Large bowl and cling film
Two baking trays lined with baking paper, lightly oiled
Large wide saucepan for boiling
Slotted spoon or spider
Wire rack
Glass dish for curing the salmon
Long thin slicing knife

ingredients.note: 1 tbsp (20 g) in the dough, the rest in the water; or use honey
the dough is stiff at about 58% water

ingredients.item: Salmon fillet, skin on, for the lox
ingredients.note: sold for raw eating and previously frozen

mise: Two days before serving, cure the salmon (step 1) so it is ready with the bagels.
Weigh all the dough ingredients.
Line and lightly oil the trays.
Slice the onion as thinly as you can and keep it in iced water to soften its bite.

timeline.do: Cure the salmon.
Mix, knead, shape and refrigerate the bagels.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C), boil the water.
Float test, boil, top and bake.
Cool the bagels; slice the lox.
Schmear and build.

steps.do: Cure the lox. Mix the salt and sugar and pack it all over the flesh of the salmon in the dish. Wrap tightly and refrigerate 36 to 48 hours, turning once. Then rinse briefly, pat dry and refrigerate uncovered for 2 hours to dry the surface.
steps.look: Firm, deep orange, glossy flesh that is distinctly saltier than gravlax.
steps.mistake: Leaving it far longer than 48 hours, which makes it hard and too salty to eat.
steps.fix: Soak over-salted fish in cold water for 30 minutes, dry it and taste again.

steps.do: Mix the dough. Combine flour, 1 tbsp (20 g) malt, salt, yeast and water and knead 10 minutes in the mixer on low to medium, or 15 minutes by hand.
steps.look: A stiff, smooth, slightly tacky dough that feels like firm modelling clay and stretches thin without tearing.
steps.mistake: Adding more water because it feels too dry; bagel dough is meant to be stiff.
steps.fix: Keep kneading; it smooths out. If the mixer strains, knead half the time by hand.

steps.do: Divide into 8 pieces of about 100 g each, roll into balls and rest 10 minutes under cling film.
steps.look: Smooth balls that have relaxed slightly.
steps.mistake: Unequal pieces that bake unevenly.
steps.fix: Weigh them; it takes a minute.

steps.do: Shape. Push your thumb through the centre of each ball, then rotate it round two fingers to stretch the hole to about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm). Set on the oiled trays, cover with oiled cling film and refrigerate 12 to 18 hours.
steps.look: Even rings with a hole that looks too big; it will shrink as they rise.
steps.mistake: Making the hole small, so it closes up and you get rolls.
steps.fix: Stretch the holes wider than looks right.

steps.do: Next day, heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) and bring the wide pan of water to the boil with the remaining malt and the bicarbonate. Test one bagel by dropping it into a bowl of cold water.
steps.look: The bagel floats within 10 seconds, which means it has risen enough.
steps.mistake: Boiling bagels that sink, which bake dense.
steps.fix: If it sinks, leave the bagels at room temperature 20 minutes and test again.

steps.do: Boil 3 or 4 bagels at a time for 1 minute a side, turning with the slotted spoon. Lift out, drain briefly on the rack and dip the tops in seeds if using. Set back on the lined trays.
steps.look: The bagels puff and the surface turns smooth and slightly shiny.
steps.mistake: Boiling too long, which gives a thick, wrinkled skin.
steps.fix: One minute a side for a chewy crust; 30 seconds a side for a softer one.

steps.do: Bake 18 to 22 minutes, turning the trays halfway, until deep golden brown. Cool on the rack at least 20 minutes.
steps.look: A shiny, deep brown crust, a hollow sound when tapped underneath.
steps.mistake: Cutting them hot, which squashes the crumb into gum.
steps.fix: Wait; the crumb sets as they cool.

steps.do: Slice the lox thin on the bias as for gravlax, the knife almost flat, in long strokes.
steps.look: Long, translucent, glossy slices.
steps.mistake: Thick chunky slices that taste only of salt.
steps.fix: Very thin slices balance the stronger cure.

steps.do: Split the bagels, spread with a thick schmear of cream cheese to the edges, drape the lox in loose folds and top with drained onion, capers and tomato.
steps.look: A generous, layered bagel with the salmon in soft folds.
steps.mistake: Laying the lox flat in one sheet, which makes it hard to bite through.
steps.fix: Fold each slice loosely; it tears cleanly with the teeth.

dishes.science: Boiling sets the outside of the bagel before it reaches the oven. The hot water gelatinises the starch on the surface into a thin skin, which stops the dough expanding much in the oven, so the crumb stays dense and chewy rather than airy. Bicarbonate makes the water alkaline, which speeds browning, and malt adds sugars that caramelise into the glossy brown crust. The stiff dough, low in water, develops a tight gluten network that gives the famous chew. The long cold rest in the fridge slows the yeast while enzymes break starch into sugars and build flavour. The lox cure uses more salt than gravlax, drawing out more water and making the flesh firmer and saltier.
dishes.plating: Serve open on a board: bagel halves schmeared and topped, the lox in rosettes, onion rings scattered, capers in small clusters, tomato slices overlapping on one side. Or set up a platter with the bagels, lox, cream cheese and garnishes separate so everyone builds their own.

pairing.drink: A Bloody Mary, its tomato, horseradish and citrus a natural match for salty cured fish and cream cheese.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Bloody Mary: the house's own brunch cocktail, the drink most guests reach for with a salty, savoury breakfast.

variations: Everything bagel topping: equal parts sesame, poppy, dried garlic, dried onion and flaky salt.
Use bought cold-smoked salmon in place of home-cured lox.
Whip chives and lemon zest into the cream cheese.
safety: Curing does not kill parasites: use salmon frozen to -4°F (-20°C) for at least 7 days before curing.
Lower bagels into boiling water with a slotted spoon, never by hand, and keep the pan handle turned in.
Keep the lox below 40°F (4°C) and eat within 5 days.

dishes.title: Longganisa with Garlic Rice
dishes.summary: Filipino sweet garlic pork sausage made from hand-ground shoulder and fat, cured briefly with vinegar and salt, formed into skinless links and fried, with garlic rice and a fried egg. It is here because making sausage teaches the ratio of lean to fat, keeping everything cold, and how salt binds minced meat.
skills: curing with salt, garlic and vinegar
equipment: Digital scale
Meat grinder with a 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate, or a large heavy knife
Two metal bowls, one set in a bowl of ice
Cling film or baking paper
Large nonstick frying pan with a lid
Wok or large frying pan for the rice
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Pork back fat or fatty belly

ingredients.note: about 1.8% of the meat and fat

ingredients.item: Spiced cane vinegar with chilli, to dip

mise: Put the grinder parts and both metal bowls in the freezer for 30 minutes.
Cut the pork and fat into 1 inch (2.5 cm) cubes and freeze them on a tray for 20 minutes, until firm at the edges.
Mince all the garlic.
Weigh out the seasoning in a small bowl.

timeline.do: Cook the rice and chill it; grind, season and form the sausages.
Cure the links in the fridge.
Fry the sausages.
Fry the garlic rice.
Fry the eggs.
Plate with vinegar for dipping.

steps.do: Grind the semi-frozen pork and fat together through the 1/4 inch (6 mm) plate into the bowl set over ice. If chopping by hand, chop with the heavy knife until it looks like coarse mince.
steps.look: Distinct pink and white specks of meat and fat, clean edges, the fat not smeared.
steps.mistake: Grinding warm meat, which smears the fat into a greasy paste.
steps.fix: If the fat smears or the grinder slows, put everything back in the freezer for 15 minutes.

steps.do: Add the garlic, sugar, salt, vinegar, soy, pepper and paprika. Mix with a gloved hand or the paddle of a mixer for 2 minutes, until the mixture turns sticky and binds.
steps.look: The mince turns tacky and holds together; a pinch pressed to your palm sticks when you turn your hand over.
steps.mistake: Under-mixing, so the sausage is crumbly and falls apart in the pan.
steps.fix: Mix another minute; salt needs work to draw out the sticky proteins.

steps.do: Fry a teaspoon of the mixture in a small pan, cool it a minute and taste. Adjust salt, sugar or pepper.
steps.look: Sweet, garlicky, gently sour and properly salted.
steps.mistake: Tasting raw pork; never do this.
steps.fix: Always cook the test patty through before tasting.

steps.do: Divide into 12 pieces of about 60 g. Lay each on a square of baking paper, shape into a log 4 inches (10 cm) long and roll up tightly, twisting the ends like a sweet wrapper.
steps.look: Neat, even, firm cylinders.
steps.mistake: Loose wrapping, so they lose shape in the pan.
steps.fix: Roll tightly against the worktop with the paper to compact the log.

steps.do: Refrigerate the links overnight on a tray.
steps.look: Firmer logs, slightly darker in colour, with a deeper garlic smell.
steps.mistake: Leaving them out at room temperature.
steps.fix: Keep them below 40°F (4°C); use within 2 days or freeze.

steps.do: Unwrap and put the links in the cold frying pan with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water. Cover and cook over medium heat for 8 minutes, until the water has almost gone.
steps.look: The links firm up and turn pale, and their fat begins to render into the pan.
steps.mistake: Frying on high from the start, which burns the sugar before the centre cooks.
steps.fix: The water steams them through first; then you brown them.

steps.do: Uncover and fry in the rendered fat, turning, for 5 to 7 minutes until glossy and caramelised all over. Check the centre with a thermometer.
steps.look: Sticky, dark, shiny links smelling of caramel and garlic, 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
steps.mistake: Letting the sugar blacken.
steps.fix: Lower the heat once the colour begins and keep turning.

steps.do: For the rice, fry the 6 cloves of minced garlic in the oil over medium-low heat until golden, lift half out for garnish, then add the cold rice, breaking up clumps, and fry 5 minutes over medium-high heat. Season with salt.
steps.look: Golden flecks of garlic through hot, separate grains, smelling nutty.
steps.mistake: Using hot freshly cooked rice, which turns to paste.
steps.fix: Use rice cooked and chilled the day before.

steps.do: Fry the eggs sunny side up. Plate the rice, eggs and sausages together with a bowl of spiced vinegar for dipping and the crisp garlic on top of the rice.
steps.look: A shining plate of red-brown sausage, golden rice and a bright yolk.
steps.mistake: Serving without the vinegar, which leaves it sweet and heavy.
steps.fix: The sharp vinegar is part of the dish; always put it on the table.

dishes.science: Salt dissolves certain muscle proteins, chiefly myosin, which become sticky when mixed and act as a glue. When the sausage cooks, those proteins set into a gel that traps fat and water, giving a sausage that slices cleanly and stays juicy. That is why salt must go in before thorough mixing, and why the mixture turns tacky. Fat at around a quarter of the weight carries flavour and moisture; too little and the sausage turns dry and crumbly. Keeping everything near freezing stops the fat melting and smearing, which would coat the proteins and stop them binding. The sugar caramelises in the pan, and vinegar adds a sour note while slightly lowering the pH.
dishes.plating: The Filipino breakfast plate: a dome of garlic rice pressed in a small bowl and turned out, a fried egg leaning against it, three links laid in a row, sliced tomato or atchara pickle on the side, and a small dish of spiced vinegar.

pairing.drink: A cold calamansi or lime juice, or a light lager; sweetness and acidity balance sweet-garlic pork.
pairing.brennans: Housemade Pork Sausage Patty: Brennan's own breakfast sausage, a good comparison of seasoning and fat when describing it to a guest.

variations: Longganisa de recado: less sugar and more garlic, pepper and vinegar, the savoury style.
Stuff the mixture into rinsed hog casings and twist into links.
Form into flat patties for a quicker breakfast.
safety: Cook pork sausage to 160°F (71°C) in the centre; minced meat carries surface bacteria throughout.
Wash hands, boards and the grinder in hot soapy water after handling raw pork.
Keep raw sausage in the fridge below 40°F (4°C) and use within 2 days, or freeze.

dishes.title: Jeonbok-juk (Abalone Rice Porridge)
dishes.summary: A Korean rice porridge cooked slowly with fresh abalone, coloured green-gold by the abalone's own guts and finished with sesame oil. It is here because it adds shellfish fabrication, scrubbing, shucking and cleaning a live abalone, to the congee you already know, and because the porridge depends on toasting the rice in oil first.
skills: slow-cooked rice porridge with sesame oil
equipment: Small stiff brush
Large metal spoon
Sharp paring knife and kitchen scissors
Heavy-based saucepan
Wooden spoon
Sieve and a small bowl
Blender or mortar

ingredients.note: lively, moving when touched, smelling of clean sea water
or a light anchovy and kelp stock

ingredients.item: Fine salt or soup soy sauce

mise: Rinse the rice until the water runs nearly clear and soak it for 1 hour, then drain.
Keep the abalone in the fridge in a bowl covered with a damp cloth until you prepare them.
Have the water heated in a kettle.

timeline.do: Soak the rice.
Clean and shuck the abalone.
Fry rice and abalone, add water.
Simmer, stirring, until the porridge thickens.
Season and finish.
Serve with sesame oil and seaweed.

steps.do: Scrub the abalone under cold running water with the brush, paying attention to the black foot and the edges, until the dark slime comes off and the flesh looks pale cream.
steps.look: A clean, firm, pale foot that contracts when touched.
steps.mistake: Using hot water, which kills and toughens the flesh.
steps.fix: Scrub only in cold water; a little salt rubbed on helps lift the slime.

steps.do: Shuck. Slide the large spoon between the shell and the flesh on the thin side of the shell, keeping the spoon against the shell, and lever along to release the muscle. Lift the meat out.
steps.look: The meat comes away in one piece with the guts attached at one end.
steps.mistake: Pushing the spoon into the flesh and tearing it.
steps.fix: Keep the edge of the spoon pressed against the inside of the shell all the way.

steps.do: Cut the guts away from the muscle with scissors and keep them. Cut off and discard the hard mouth parts at the narrow end. Push the guts through a sieve or blend them with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water.
steps.look: A smooth green or ochre paste and a clean, ivory muscle.
steps.mistake: Throwing away the guts, which give the porridge its colour and depth.
steps.fix: Keep them; if a gut sac looks dark and smells off, discard that one.

steps.do: Slice the abalone muscle thinly, then cut into small dice about 1/4 inch (6 mm). Keep 4 nice thin slices whole for the top.
steps.look: Neat little cubes of firm, pearly flesh.
steps.mistake: Cutting large pieces, which turn chewy.
steps.fix: Small, thin pieces stay tender in the porridge.

steps.do: Heat the sesame oil in the heavy pan over medium heat. Add the diced abalone and stir 1 minute, then add the drained rice and stir for 3 to 4 minutes until the grains turn translucent at the edges.
steps.look: The rice crackles slightly and smells nutty; the grains look glassy round the outside.
steps.mistake: Using high heat, which burns sesame oil and makes it bitter.
steps.fix: Keep it at medium and stir constantly.

steps.do: Stir in the abalone gut purée, then add about a third of the hot water. Bring to a simmer, stirring.
steps.look: The porridge turns an even pale green or golden colour.
steps.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so the rice sits in a thin soup for a long time.
steps.fix: Add it in stages, as for a risotto, so the rice releases its starch.

steps.do: Simmer gently, stirring often with the wooden spoon and scraping the bottom, adding the rest of the water in two more lots, for about 40 to 50 minutes.
steps.look: The grains swell and break, and the porridge thickens to the consistency of thick, flowing cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so it catches and burns on the base.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down and stir every few minutes; if it sticks, do not scrape the burnt layer into the porridge.

steps.do: Season with salt or soup soy sauce, add the reserved slices for the last 2 minutes, and loosen with a little hot water if it has become too thick.
steps.look: Silky, flowing porridge that settles slowly in the bowl, seasoned so the sea flavour is clear.
steps.mistake: Overseasoning, which hides the delicate abalone.
steps.fix: Season gently, then add more at the table.

steps.do: Ladle into warm bowls, lay the abalone slices on top and finish with a few drops of sesame oil, sesame seeds, crumbled gim and spring onion.
steps.look: A pale green porridge with glistening oil and dark seaweed flecks.
steps.mistake: Too much sesame oil, which overwhelms it.
steps.fix: A few drops are enough; offer more on the side.

dishes.science: Toasting the rice in oil first coats each grain and starts to break down its outer starch, which gives a nuttier flavour and helps the grains break evenly. As the rice simmers with plenty of water and is stirred, the starch granules swell and burst and amylopectin, the branched starch that dominates short grain rice, leaks out and thickens the liquid into porridge. Adding water in stages keeps the grains in contact with each other, so stirring rubs starch free. The abalone's guts hold pigments from the seaweed it eats, which colour the porridge, and amino acids that deepen its flavour. Abalone muscle is dense with collagen; cut thin and cooked briefly it stays tender, while long cooking makes it chewy.
dishes.plating: Serve in warm earthenware or white bowls. Lay the abalone slices in a fan on top, sprinkle sesame seeds in a line, add a small pile of crumbled gim and spring onion, and offer kimchi and soy on the side.

pairing.drink: Warm barley tea, or with a lazy weekend breakfast a dry, mineral white such as Muscadet.

variations: Use frozen cleaned abalone, thawed in the fridge, if you cannot buy live.
Dakjuk: chicken porridge made the same way with shredded poached chicken.
Add finely diced carrot and courgette with the rice for a vegetable version.
safety: Buy live abalone from a reputable fishmonger, keep them cold and cook them the same day; discard any that do not respond to touch.
Discard any gut that smells unpleasant.
Keep the spoon pointed away from your hand when shucking.

dishes.title: Phở Bò
dishes.summary: Vietnamese beef noodle soup with a clear, long-simmered broth scented with charred ginger, onion and toasted spices, poured over rice noodles and raw beef sliced thin enough to cook in the bowl. It is here because a clear broth demands blanched bones, a heat that never boils, and spices added late, which is stock work at a higher standard.
skills: slicing raw beef thin to cook in the bowl
equipment: Very large stockpot, at least 8 quarts (8 litres)
Large colander
Ladle and a fine skimmer
Gas burner, overhead grill (broiler) or blowtorch for charring
Small dry frying pan
Muslin or a spice bag
Fine sieve lined with muslin
Very sharp knife
Saucepan for the noodles
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Cassia bark or a cinnamon stick
Beef sirloin or eye of round
To serve: bean sprouts, Thai basil, coriander leaves, sawtooth herb, sliced chillies, lime wedges, sliced onion, hoisin and sriracha

mise: Soak the rice noodles in cold water for at least 1 hour.
Slice a small onion paper thin and soak in cold water.
Pick the herbs and wash the bean sprouts.
Put the sirloin in the freezer 30 minutes before you slice it.

timeline.do: Blanch and scrub the bones.
Char aromatics, start the broth at a bare simmer.
Lift out the brisket.
Add the toasted spice bag.
Strain and season; slice the beef; cook the noodles.
Build the bowls and pour over boiling broth.

steps.do: Put the bones and brisket in the stockpot, cover with cold water, bring to a hard boil and boil for 10 minutes. Drain everything into the colander, discard the water, then rinse the bones under the tap and scrub the pot clean.
steps.look: Thick grey foam rises in the first minutes. After rinsing the bones look clean, with no grey clinging to them.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blanch, which leaves you skimming for hours and still gives a cloudy broth.
steps.fix: Blanch even if pressed for time; it is the single biggest step to clarity.

steps.do: Char the unpeeled onions and ginger directly over a gas flame, under a hot grill or with a blowtorch, turning until blackened in patches all over, about 10 minutes. Rub off the loose burnt skin under running water and halve them.
steps.look: Blistered black skins, soft hot interiors, and a sweet smoky smell.
steps.mistake: Barely browning them, which gives a flat broth.
steps.fix: Char them properly; most of the black comes off, the flavour stays.

steps.do: Return the bones and brisket to the clean pot with the 5 quarts (5 litres) cold water and the charred onion and ginger. Bring slowly to 195°F (90°C) over medium heat and hold it there, the surface barely shivering.
steps.look: Only an occasional lazy bubble breaking. Any foam that collects is pale and easy to skim.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil, which emulsifies fat and particles into the broth and makes it cloudy for good.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer and adjust the heat, or set the lid half on to keep it steady. Skim every 20 minutes for the first hour.

steps.do: After 90 minutes, test the brisket with a skewer; when it slides in without resistance, lift it out into a bowl of cold water for 10 minutes, then refrigerate.
steps.look: Tender, grey-brown brisket that holds together when lifted.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in for the whole time, so it falls apart and goes dry.
steps.fix: Pull it as soon as it is tender; it will be sliced and served.

steps.do: Keep the bones at a bare simmer for about 5 hours in total. Top up with hot water if the level drops below the bones.
steps.look: The broth turns golden and clear, smelling deeply of beef.
steps.mistake: Topping up with cold water and then boiling hard to bring it back.
steps.fix: Add hot water from the kettle so the temperature stays steady.

steps.do: With 90 minutes to go, toast the star anise, cassia, cardamom, coriander, cloves and fennel in the dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes, shaking, until fragrant. Tie them in muslin and drop into the broth.
steps.look: A warm, sweet, liquorice smell as the spices toast; they darken very slightly.
steps.mistake: Adding spices at the start, which gives a bitter, medicinal broth after hours.
steps.fix: Add them late; if the broth smells too spiced, lift the bag out early.

steps.do: Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve into a clean pan. Skim the fat from the surface with a ladle. Season with fish sauce, sugar and salt, tasting as you go.
steps.look: A clear, amber broth you can see through, seasoned so it tastes slightly too salty on its own, which balances the unsalted noodles.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning, so the finished bowl tastes thin.
steps.fix: Season boldly; the noodles and herbs dilute it.

steps.do: Slice the semi-frozen sirloin across the grain as thinly as you can, about 1/16 inch (2 mm). Slice the cold brisket a little thicker, 1/8 inch (3 mm).
steps.look: Translucent sheets of raw beef you can almost see through.
steps.mistake: Slicing warm beef, which gives thick, ragged slices that will not cook in the bowl.
steps.fix: Freeze it longer until firm; use your sharpest knife with long strokes.

steps.do: Bring the broth to a full rolling boil. Cook the drained noodles in boiling water for 20 to 30 seconds, drain and divide between deep warm bowls. Top with brisket, raw sirloin and onion. Ladle the boiling broth straight over the raw beef.
steps.look: The raw beef turns from red to pink within seconds as the broth hits it.
steps.mistake: Pouring broth that is merely hot, so the beef stays raw.
steps.fix: The broth must be at a rolling boil when you ladle it. If you prefer, dip the sirloin in the boiling broth for 10 seconds first.

steps.do: Serve with the herb plate, lime, chillies, hoisin and sriracha on the side.
steps.look: Clear broth, glossy noodles, pink beef and green herbs.
steps.mistake: Pouring sauces into the broth before tasting it.
steps.fix: Taste the broth first; sauces are for dipping the meat.

dishes.science: Clarity is a matter of particles. Blanching removes most of the blood proteins that would otherwise coagulate into fine grey specks. After that, the broth is held below a boil because bubbling breaks fat into tiny droplets and churns proteins into suspension, where they stay and make it cloudy. At a bare simmer, impurities rise and gather on the surface where they can be skimmed. Long cooking dissolves collagen from knuckles into gelatin, which gives body. Charring the onion and ginger caramelises their sugars and adds smoky depth. Spices go in late because their aromatic oils are volatile; hours of simmering would drive off the bright notes and leave only bitter ones.
dishes.plating: Deep, wide bowls. Noodles in a loose mound, brisket fanned to one side, raw sirloin laid over the top in a single layer so the broth reaches every slice, onion slices and spring onion scattered. The herb plate goes alongside, sprouts in a pile, herbs on their stems, lime wedges cut neatly.

pairing.drink: A cold Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk after, or with the bowl a crisp lager; for wine, an off-dry Riesling handles the spice and chilli.

variations: Phở gà: the same method with a whole chicken and chicken bones, simmered 2 hours.
Add oxtail to the bones for a richer, more gelatinous broth.
Pressure cooker broth: cook the blanched bones and aromatics 90 minutes at high pressure for a quicker, slightly less clear version.
safety: The raw beef cooks only in the broth: buy it from a trusted butcher, keep it cold and make sure the broth is at a rolling boil when poured.
Cool leftover broth quickly in a shallow container or an ice bath and refrigerate within 2 hours; reboil before serving.
Use tongs and long sleeves when charring over a gas flame.
