dishes.title: Chicken Souvlaki with Tzatziki and Pita
dishes.summary: Greek chicken skewers made from thighs you bone yourself, cut into even cubes, marinated in lemon, oregano and garlic and grilled over high heat, wrapped in soft homemade pita with tzatziki. It is here because boning thighs and cubing them evenly so every piece cooks at once is basic butchery, and it adds a simple yeasted flatbread.
equipment: Boning knife or small sharp knife
Cutting board for raw meat
Metal skewers, or wooden ones soaked 30 minutes
Barbecue with hot coals, or a ridged cast-iron grill pan
Large mixing bowl
Box grater and a clean tea towel
Rolling pin
Heavy dry frying pan or cast-iron pan
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.note: gives about 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of meat

ingredients.item: Sugar and salt, for the pita
Dill, chopped, red wine vinegar and olive oil
ingredients.metric: about 3 g dill, 15 ml vinegar, 15 ml oil

mise: Make the pita dough: mix flour, yeast, sugar, salt, warm water and oil, knead 5 minutes and leave to rise 1 hour.
Grate the cucumber, toss with a pinch of salt, leave 10 minutes and squeeze dry in the tea towel. Mix with yoghurt, garlic, dill, vinegar and oil; chill.
Soak wooden skewers if using.
Slice tomato and onion.

timeline.do: Make the pita dough and the tzatziki.
Bone and cube the chicken; marinate 2 hours.
Light the coals or heat the grill pan; shape pitas.
Cook the pitas; keep warm in a cloth.
Grill the skewers.
Wrap with tzatziki, tomato and onion.

steps.do: Bone the thighs. Lay a thigh skin side down. Cut along both sides of the bone down its length, then scrape the meat away from the bone with the knife tip, working round it, and cut under the knuckle at each end to free it.
steps.look: A flat piece of thigh with the bone removed cleanly and little meat left on it.
steps.mistake: Hacking at the meat and leaving half of it on the bone.
steps.fix: Keep the knife tip against the bone and use short scraping strokes.

steps.do: Remove the skin if you like and trim away tendons and large pieces of fat. Cut the meat into even 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) cubes.
steps.look: A pile of matching cubes.
steps.mistake: Uneven pieces, so small ones dry out while big ones stay raw.
steps.fix: Cut strips of even width first, then cut across them.

steps.do: Toss the cubes with the oil, lemon, garlic, oregano, honey, salt and pepper. Cover and refrigerate 1 to 4 hours.
steps.look: Glossy cubes flecked with oregano.
steps.mistake: Marinating overnight in lots of lemon, which makes the surface mealy.
steps.fix: Keep it to a few hours.

steps.do: Thread onto skewers, pushing the pieces snugly together without crushing them.
steps.look: Even skewers with pieces touching.
steps.mistake: Packing so tightly the middle stays raw, or spacing so loosely they dry out.
steps.fix: Snug, not squashed.

steps.do: Divide the risen dough into 6, roll each to a round 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick and cook in the very hot dry pan for 1 to 2 minutes a side until puffed and spotted brown. Wrap in a cloth.
steps.look: Soft rounds that puff up and colour in patches.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thin, which makes them crisp rather than soft.
steps.fix: Keep them thicker; wrap at once to keep soft.

steps.do: Grill the skewers over hot coals or in the smoking hot grill pan for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 2 to 3 minutes, until charred at the edges.
steps.look: Sizzling, golden-brown cubes charred at the corners, smelling of lemon and oregano.
steps.mistake: Moving them constantly, so they never colour.
steps.fix: Leave them still until they release easily, then turn.

steps.do: Check a cube in the middle of a skewer with the thermometer: it should read at least 165°F (74°C), better 175°F (79°C). Rest 3 minutes.
steps.look: Juicy, opaque meat with no pink.
steps.mistake: Serving underdone chicken.
steps.fix: Return to the heat for 2 to 3 minutes more.

steps.do: Spread a warm pita with tzatziki, slide the chicken off the skewer onto it, add tomato and onion, sprinkle oregano and roll.
steps.look: A soft wrap bursting with charred chicken and white tzatziki.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so it splits.
steps.fix: A modest amount; roll it in paper for eating.

dishes.science: Even pieces cook evenly because heat travels inwards at a steady rate, so a cube twice as thick takes much longer to reach temperature. Thigh meat suits grilling because it has more fat and connective tissue than breast, which keeps it juicy at the higher temperatures it can stand. The lemon in the marinade slightly loosens surface proteins and the salt seasons and helps hold moisture. Honey's sugars brown quickly over high heat, giving the charred corners. In the tzatziki, salting the cucumber draws out water by osmosis, so the sauce stays thick. The pita puffs because steam from the dough's water forms a pocket between its two surfaces in a very hot pan.
dishes.plating: Wrapped in paper, half peeled back, for a street style plate; or on a platter with the skewers laid over warm pita, a bowl of tzatziki, tomato wedges, sliced red onion, lemon wedges and oregano sprinkled over.

pairing.drink: A crisp Greek Assyrtiko, whose bright lemony acidity mirrors the marinade.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a Santorini Assyrtiko on the Brennan's list, the classic Greek white for grilled chicken.

variations: Pork souvlaki: shoulder cubed the same way, the most common version in Greece.
Serve on a plate with lemon potatoes and Greek salad instead of in pita.
Add red pepper and onion pieces between the chicken.
safety: Cook chicken to at least 165°F (74°C).
Use a separate board and knife for raw chicken, and never use the raw marinade as a sauce.
Boning knives are sharp and narrow: cut away from your holding hand and work slowly.

dishes.title: Tacos al Pastor
dishes.summary: Mexico City's taco: thin sheets of pork shoulder marinated in a red chilli and achiote adobo, stacked into a home trompo crowned with pineapple, roasted, then carved in thin shavings and crisped onto warm tortillas. It is here because it teaches slicing a shoulder into even sheets and carving from a vertical stack, a butchery and carving lesson in one.
equipment: Very sharp chef's knife
Blender
Large bowl or container for marinating
Loaf tin or small roasting tin, and a long metal skewer or two
Half an onion, for the base of the stack
Rimmed baking tray
Instant-read thermometer
Large cast-iron frying pan or plancha
Tortilla warmer or clean cloth

ingredients.note: or a pinch of ground clove
a thick slab for the top, the rest in wedges

ingredients.item: White onion and coriander leaves, finely chopped

mise: Toast the chillies in a dry pan for 15 to 20 seconds a side until fragrant, then soak in hot water 20 minutes.
Blend the drained chillies with the achiote, pineapple juice, vinegar, garlic, oregano, cumin, cloves and salt to a smooth, thick paste.
Partly freeze the pork for 1 hour so it is firm to slice.

timeline.do: Slice the pork and marinate overnight.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C); build the trompo.
Roast 75 to 90 minutes.
Rest, then carve thin shavings.
Crisp the shavings; warm tortillas; char pineapple.
Build small tacos and eat in twos and threes.

steps.do: Slice the semi-frozen pork against its grain into broad sheets about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, working with long, even strokes.
steps.look: Even, wide slices of the same thickness.
steps.mistake: Uneven slices, which cook at different rates in the stack.
steps.fix: Firmer meat slices more evenly; return it to the freezer if it softens.

steps.do: Coat every sheet thoroughly in the adobo, cover and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: Every surface painted deep brick red.
steps.mistake: Marinating only an hour, which gives a shallow flavour.
steps.fix: At least 6 hours; overnight is best.

steps.do: Build the trompo: stand the half onion cut side down in the loaf tin and push the skewer upright through it. Thread the pork sheets onto the skewer one at a time, pressing each down firmly, turning each sheet a little so the stack is even, until you have a tight, rough cone. Top with the thick pineapple slab.
steps.look: A tall, compact stack, wider at the base, the pineapple on top.
steps.mistake: A loose stack that slumps and cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Press down firmly after every few sheets; use two skewers if it leans.

steps.do: Roast at 375°F (190°C) for 75 to 90 minutes, until the outside is charred at the edges and the centre reads 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C).
steps.look: Dark, crisp, caramelised edges and dripping juices; the pineapple caramelises and drips over the pork.
steps.mistake: Pulling it out at 145°F (63°C), when the stacked shoulder is still chewy.
steps.fix: Roast longer; the fat and connective tissue need the extra heat to soften.

steps.do: Rest 10 minutes. Holding the stack upright with tongs, carve thin shavings from the outside downwards with the sharp knife, as a taquero would.
steps.look: Thin, crisp-edged shavings falling away, glistening red.
steps.mistake: Hacking thick chunks, which loses the crisp-edge character.
steps.fix: Carve only the outside layer, then roast the stack 10 minutes more for another crisp round if needed.

steps.do: Crisp the shavings on the hot cast-iron pan with a spoonful of the drippings for 1 to 2 minutes. Char the pineapple wedges in the same pan and chop small.
steps.look: Sizzling, crisp edges and caramelised pineapple.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding the pan, so the meat steams.
steps.fix: Work in batches.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas on a dry hot pan for 30 seconds a side, stack them in the cloth. Use two tortillas per taco if they are thin.
steps.look: Soft, pliable, lightly spotted tortillas.
steps.mistake: Cold, stiff tortillas that crack.
steps.fix: Wrap them warm in a cloth so they steam soft.

steps.do: Top each tortilla with meat, a little pineapple, chopped onion and coriander, and serve with lime wedges and salsa verde.
steps.look: Small, neat tacos: red pork, gold pineapple, white onion, green herbs.
steps.mistake: Overloading, so the taco falls apart.
steps.fix: Small tacos, eaten in two or three bites.

dishes.science: Thin sheets in a tight stack behave like the vertical spit: fat renders from the upper layers and bastes those below, while the outside, exposed to dry oven heat, browns and crisps. Achiote's annatto seeds give an earthy flavour and a deep red-orange colour, and the acid in the vinegar and pineapple juice seasons the meat. Fresh pineapple contains bromelain, an enzyme that breaks down proteins, but only juice in moderate amounts is used so the meat does not turn mushy overnight; cooking destroys the enzyme. Shoulder has plenty of fat and collagen, which need a final temperature well above the minimum safe point to soften, which is why the stack is taken to 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C).
dishes.plating: Tacos served on a plate in threes, slightly overlapping, onion and coriander scattered, a lime wedge at the side and salsa in a small bowl. For a party, bring the carved trompo to the table on a board and carve to order.

pairing.drink: A cold Mexican lager with lime, or an agua fresca of pineapple; for wine, an off-dry Riesling handles the chilli and sweetness.

variations: Pan al pastor: sear the marinated sheets hard in a cast-iron pan and chop, for a weeknight.
Gringas: al pastor with melted cheese in a flour tortilla.
Use chicken thighs marinated the same way.
safety: Partially frozen meat slices more easily but is still slippery; use a sharp knife and keep fingers curled.
Pork must reach at least 145°F (63°C) with a rest; this recipe goes higher for tenderness. Use a thermometer.
The skewer and tin are very hot after roasting; use oven gloves and tongs to carve.

dishes.title: Bún Chả
dishes.summary: Hanoi's lunch: grilled pork patties and caramelised slices of pork belly served in a bowl of warm, balanced dipping sauce, with cold rice vermicelli and a mountain of herbs. It is here because the dipping sauce, nước chấm, must balance salt, sweet, sour and heat by taste alone, and because a caramel marinade teaches grilling sugar without burning it.
equipment: Small heavy saucepan for the caramel
Two mixing bowls
Charcoal grill or a hinged grilling basket, or an oven grill (broiler) with a rack
Saucepan for the noodles
Colander
Instant-read thermometer
Sharp knife

ingredients.item: Fish sauce, for the nước chấm
Garlic and bird's eye chilli, finely chopped
Green papaya or kohlrabi and carrot, thinly sliced
ingredients.note: quick pickled in a little of the sauce

ingredients.item: Lettuce, perilla, mint, coriander and Thai basil

mise: Make a caramel sauce: melt 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water in the small pan over medium heat, swirling, until deep amber, then carefully add 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water. It will spit. Cool.
Make the nước chấm: dissolve the sugar in the warm water, add fish sauce and lime, then garlic and chilli. Taste and balance. Add the sliced papaya and carrot.
Pick and wash the herbs.
Chop shallots and garlic.

timeline.do: Make caramel and nước chấm.
Marinate the pork belly and the mince for 1 to 2 hours.
Light the coals or heat the grill; cook noodles.
Shape patties and grill both porks.
Warm the meat in the sauce bowls.
Serve with noodles and herbs.

steps.do: Mix half the shallots and garlic, the fish sauce, 1 tbsp (13 g) sugar, pepper, oil and 1 tbsp (15 ml) caramel. Pour half over the belly slices and mix the other half into the mince. Marinate 1 to 2 hours in the fridge.
steps.look: Glossy, dark-tinted pork smelling of fish sauce and shallot.
steps.mistake: Adding too much caramel, which burns on the grill.
steps.fix: One spoonful in each is enough for colour.

steps.do: Taste the nước chấm with a piece of lettuce. Adjust: more lime if flat, more sugar if harsh, more fish sauce if it tastes weak, more water if strong.
steps.look: A sauce that tastes salty, sweet and sour at once, with chilli heat behind; you should want to drink a spoonful.
steps.mistake: Making it strong like a dip, when it is meant to be a light broth.
steps.fix: Dilute with warm water until you can sip it.

steps.do: Cook the vermicelli in boiling water for 3 to 4 minutes, drain, rinse under cold water and leave to drain in nests.
steps.look: Soft, separate white noodles.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in a wet heap, which sticks together.
steps.fix: Rinse well and twirl into small nests while still damp.

steps.do: Shape the mince into small flat patties about 2 inches (5 cm) across and 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick.
steps.look: Even little patties.
steps.mistake: Big thick patties that char before cooking through.
steps.fix: Small and thin cook quickly and evenly.

steps.do: Grill the belly slices and patties over hot coals or under a hot grill, 3 to 4 minutes a side, turning when charred in places.
steps.look: Caramelised, sticky, charred edges, sizzling fat and a sweet smoky smell.
steps.mistake: Grilling too close to the heat, so the sugar blackens before the pork cooks.
steps.fix: Raise the rack or move to a cooler part of the grill.

steps.do: Check a patty with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C) in the centre.
steps.look: Juicy, cooked through, no pink.
steps.mistake: Serving underdone mince.
steps.fix: Return to the grill for a minute more.

steps.do: Warm the nước chấm gently, divide into four bowls and add the grilled meats to the bowls.
steps.look: Pork pieces bobbing in a warm, amber sauce.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce, which dulls the lime.
steps.fix: Just warm it.

steps.do: Serve each person a bowl of pork in sauce, a plate of noodle nests and a shared platter of herbs and lettuce. Dip noodles and herbs into the bowl as you eat.
steps.look: A table of colour: amber sauce, white noodles, green herbs.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sauce over the noodles.
steps.fix: Keep them separate; the eater dips.

dishes.science: Caramel adds colour and a bittersweet depth because heating sugar breaks it down into hundreds of new aroma compounds. A little in the marinade helps the pork brown quickly on the grill, but sugar burns fast above about 350°F (175°C), so thin slices, moderate heat and a spoonful only. Fish sauce provides salt and savoury glutamates. Balancing nước chấm is about how tastes interact: sugar softens the perception of sour and salty, acid brightens and lifts salt, and diluting with water makes the sauce light enough to dip noodles in without overpowering. Rinsing the noodles removes surface starch so they do not clump.
dishes.plating: Each person gets a small bowl of warm sauce with the pork, a plate of noodle nests and a share of a big herb platter with lettuce leaves, mint, perilla, coriander and basil. Extra chilli and garlic in small dishes. Add fried spring rolls if you are ambitious.

pairing.drink: A cold Vietnamese lager or an off-dry Riesling whose sweetness and acidity match the sauce.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry Mosel Riesling on the Brennan's list, the classic match for sweet, sour and spicy dishes.

variations: Bún thịt nướng: the same grilled pork served in one bowl over noodles and herbs with the sauce poured over.
Add crisp fried spring rolls (nem rán) cut into pieces.
Use chicken thighs for the patties and slices.
safety: Cook minced pork to 160°F (71°C) and sliced belly until no pink remains.
Caramel is extremely hot and spits when water is added; stand back, add the water slowly and keep children away.
Keep raw pork away from the herbs and cooked noodles.

dishes.title: Mul Naengmyeon
dishes.summary: Korea's cold noodle soup: chewy buckwheat noodles in an icy, perfectly clear beef broth sharpened with radish water kimchi brine, topped with sliced beef, egg, cucumber and pear. It is here because it demands a broth that is completely clear and fat free when cold, the strictest stock test yet, and noodles rinsed until they squeak.
skills: a clear beef broth chilled and fat removed
equipment: Large stockpot
Fine sieve lined with muslin
Large container for chilling the broth
Ladle and a spoon for removing fat
Glass jar for the radish brine
Large pot for the noodles
Large bowl of iced water
Kitchen scissors
Chilled serving bowls, ideally stainless steel

ingredients.note: half in the broth, half for the brine

ingredients.item: Fine salt and sugar, for the radish brine

ingredients.note: for the brine, plus more to serve
half grated for the brine, half sliced to serve

ingredients.item: Korean hot mustard (gyeoja) or English mustard

mise: Make a quick radish brine the day before: slice half the radish thinly, toss with the salt and sugar for 30 minutes, then add 2 cups (480 ml) water, the vinegar, the grated half pear and a slice each of garlic and ginger. Refrigerate.
Soak the beef in cold water for 30 minutes to draw out blood, then drain.
Cut the cucumber into matchsticks and slice the pear just before serving.

timeline.do: Make the radish brine; make the beef broth, strain and chill overnight.
Lift off the fat; season the broth with brine.
Put the broth in the freezer until slushy.
Slice the beef; prepare toppings.
Cook and rinse the noodles.
Assemble the bowls with icy broth.

steps.do: Put the beef, 10 cups (2.4 litres) water, onion, half the radish, garlic, ginger, spring onions and peppercorns in the stockpot. Bring to the boil, skim all the foam, then reduce to a bare simmer and cook 1 1/2 hours.
steps.look: A clear, gently trembling broth, foam skimmed off as it rises.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which clouds the broth.
steps.fix: Keep it at a quiver and skim regularly.

steps.do: Lift out the beef when a chopstick slides in easily, wrap it and refrigerate. Strain the broth through the muslin-lined sieve, cool it quickly and refrigerate overnight.
steps.look: A clear golden broth that sets with a layer of fat on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving the broth warm on the worktop for hours.
steps.fix: Cool in a sink of iced water, then refrigerate within 2 hours.

steps.do: Next day, lift off every piece of solid fat with a spoon, then blot the surface with kitchen paper.
steps.look: A completely clear broth with no fat spots.
steps.mistake: Leaving specks of fat, which turn waxy and coat the mouth when cold.
steps.fix: Blot with kitchen paper laid flat on the surface.

steps.do: Mix the broth with about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the strained radish brine. Season with soup soy, sugar, a splash of vinegar and salt. Taste it cold.
steps.look: A clear, cold broth that is savoury, gently sweet and tangy all at once.
steps.mistake: Seasoning warm broth, which tastes too strong; cold dulls flavour, so season cold.
steps.fix: Taste cold and adjust; it should taste lively.

steps.do: Put the broth in the freezer for 1 to 2 hours, stirring once or twice, until icy and slushy at the edges.
steps.look: Thin ice crystals forming, broth very cold.
steps.mistake: Freezing it solid.
steps.fix: Check every 30 minutes; if solid, leave at room temperature to soften.

steps.do: Slice the cold beef very thin across the grain.
steps.look: Thin, neat slices.
steps.mistake: Thick slices that are chewy cold.
steps.fix: Cut thin with a sharp knife.

steps.do: Boil the noodles in plenty of water for 40 to 60 seconds, or as the packet says, stirring. Drain and plunge into iced water, then rub them hard between your hands under cold running water.
steps.look: Noodles turn springy and chewy and lose their surface starch; the water runs clear and they squeak.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, which makes them soft and sticky.
steps.fix: Time it exactly; rinse until they squeak.

steps.do: Twist each portion into a nest in a chilled bowl. Top with beef, half an egg, cucumber and pear. Ladle the icy broth around. Serve with scissors, mustard and vinegar.
steps.look: A clear, icy broth around a tight nest of noodles and neat toppings.
steps.mistake: Leaving noodles in long strands that are hard to eat.
steps.fix: Snip the noodles with scissors at the table.

dishes.science: A cold broth reveals every fault. Fat that is invisible in hot soup solidifies when chilled into waxy flecks that coat the tongue, so the broth is chilled overnight to let the fat rise and set into a layer that can be lifted off. Gentle simmering and skimming keep proteins and fat from being churned into suspension, so the broth stays clear. Cold also dulls our ability to taste salt and sweetness, which is why the broth is seasoned cold and more boldly than a hot one. The radish brine adds acidity and a gentle fermented tang. Buckwheat noodles blended with potato or sweet potato starch are very elastic; rinsing removes the surface starch that would make them sticky.
dishes.plating: Chilled stainless or glass bowls: a tight nest of noodles centred, beef slices fanned on one side, half an egg on top, cucumber and pear matchsticks beside it, broth poured gently around so the nest stays visible, a few ice crystals floating. Mustard and vinegar on the side.

pairing.drink: Cold barley tea, or a crisp, dry Riesling with plenty of acidity.

variations: Bibim naengmyeon: the same noodles tossed in a spicy sweet gochujang sauce, with a little broth on the side.
Use a light chicken broth instead of beef.
Use store-bought dongchimi brine to save a day.
safety: Cool the broth quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; keep it cold until serving.
Eat the cooked beef within 3 days of cooking.

dishes.title: Khao Soi
dishes.summary: Chiang Mai's curry noodle soup: chicken legs braised in coconut milk with a hand-pounded paste of dried chillies, aromatics and dry spices, served over soft egg noodles and crowned with a nest of the same noodles fried crisp. It is here because it joins a pounded paste built on toasted dry spices with two textures of noodle in one bowl.
skills: a curry paste with dry spices
frying noodles for the crisp topping
equipment: Large stone mortar and pestle, or a small blender
Small dry frying pan for toasting spices
Large heavy saucepan or casserole
Deep heavy pan for frying noodles
Thermometer for the oil
Spider or tongs
Wire rack lined with kitchen paper
Large pot for boiling noodles

ingredients.note: seeded, soaked in hot water 15 minutes
do not shake; you need the thick cream on top

ingredients.item: Palm sugar or light brown sugar
Pickled mustard greens, shallot wedges, lime wedges and roasted chilli paste

mise: Soak the dried chillies.
Toast the coriander, cumin and cardamom seeds in the dry pan over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind them in the mortar.
Spoon off the thick cream from the top of both cans of coconut milk into a bowl; keep the thin milk separate.
Set aside a quarter of the noodles for frying, loosened into a few small nests.
Prepare the condiment plate.

timeline.do: Toast spices and pound the paste.
Fry the paste in coconut cream until the oil splits.
Braise the chicken 35 to 40 minutes.
Fry the crisp noodle nests.
Season the broth; boil the soft noodles.
Assemble, crown and serve with condiments.

steps.do: Pound the drained chillies with a pinch of salt in the mortar until broken down, then add shallots, garlic, ginger and turmeric a little at a time, pounding to a paste. Add the ground spices, curry powder and shrimp paste and pound until smooth, 10 to 15 minutes in all.
steps.look: A thick, fairly smooth, deep red-orange paste, fragrant and slightly oily.
steps.mistake: Adding everything at once, so the fibrous ingredients never break down.
steps.fix: Work from the hardest to softest, pounding each before adding the next. A blender with a spoonful of oil is acceptable.

steps.do: Heat the thick coconut cream in the casserole over medium heat, stirring, for 5 to 8 minutes until it bubbles and the oil begins to separate.
steps.look: The cream thickens, turns glossy and clear oil pools at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding the paste to cream that has not split, which leaves the paste raw tasting.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and stirring; it will split.

steps.do: Add the paste and fry in the coconut oil, stirring constantly, for 5 to 7 minutes.
steps.look: The paste darkens, smells deeply toasted, and red oil separates around it.
steps.mistake: Frying on high heat, which scorches the paste.
steps.fix: Keep it at medium and keep it moving; lower the heat if it sticks.

steps.do: Add the chicken and turn to coat in the paste for 2 minutes. Add the thin coconut milk and stock, bring to a gentle simmer, and cook partly covered for 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: A rich, orange broth with red oil on top, the chicken tender enough to pull from the bone.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which makes the chicken stringy and splits the coconut milk into grains.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle bubble.

steps.do: Heat the frying oil to 350°F (175°C). Fry the reserved noodle nests one or two at a time for 1 to 2 minutes, turning once, until puffed, golden and crisp. Drain on the rack.
steps.look: The noodles hiss, puff and crisp up into a golden tangle.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, giving greasy, chewy nests.
steps.fix: Wait for the thermometer before each batch.

steps.do: Season the broth with fish sauce and palm sugar. Taste: it should be rich, savoury, gently sweet and fragrant with spice. Check the chicken at the bone reads at least 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: A balanced broth and tender chicken.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning a broth that will be diluted by noodles.
steps.fix: Add fish sauce a teaspoon at a time until it tastes full.

steps.do: Boil the remaining noodles in plenty of water for 1 to 2 minutes, drain and divide between deep bowls.
steps.look: Soft, springy noodles.
steps.mistake: Overcooking, so they turn soft in the broth.
steps.fix: Cook them just before serving.

steps.do: Set a chicken leg on each bowl of noodles, ladle the hot broth over, and crown with a crisp noodle nest. Serve with the condiment plate.
steps.look: A golden bowl topped with a crunchy tangle, red oil glistening.
steps.mistake: Adding the crisp noodles too early, so they go soggy.
steps.fix: Crown each bowl at the last second.

dishes.science: Dry spices such as coriander, cumin and cardamom carry their flavour in oils locked inside the seed. Toasting drives off moisture and starts browning reactions, creating new roasted aromas, and grinding opens the seed so those oils can escape. Pounding breaks the cells of fresh aromatics, releasing juice and aroma, more thoroughly than chopping. Coconut cream is an emulsion of fat in water; heated, the water evaporates and the emulsion breaks, freeing coconut oil. Frying the paste in that oil cooks off its raw, harsh edge and dissolves the fat-soluble flavours and colours. Deep frying the noodles drives out their water quickly, so they set crisp before they can absorb much oil.
dishes.plating: Deep bowls: soft noodles in the bottom, a chicken leg resting on top, broth ladled round so red oil pools at the surface, a crisp golden nest balanced on top. The condiments go on a shared plate: pickled greens, shallot wedges, lime and chilli paste.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or Gewurztraminer, whose sweetness and aromatics meet coconut and spice.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: a dry, aromatic Alsace Riesling on the Brennan's list that stands up to curry spice.

variations: Khao soi with beef shin, braised for 2 hours.
Use a good bought red curry paste with the toasted spices added for a quicker version.
Vegetarian: tofu and mushrooms, with soy sauce instead of fish sauce and no shrimp paste.
safety: Hot oil: fill the pan no more than a third full, add noodles carefully, and keep a lid nearby. Never use water on burning oil.
Cook chicken to at least 165°F (74°C) at the bone.
Wear gloves or wash your hands well after handling dried chillies.

dishes.title: Curry Laksa
dishes.summary: Malaysian curry laksa: a spice paste, the rempah, fried until the oil splits, cooked into a stock built from prawn shells and chicken, enriched with coconut milk and poured over two kinds of noodle with prawns, chicken, tofu puffs and cockles. It is here because frying a paste until it splits, and building stock from shells, are the two foundations of this style of cooking.
skills: a rempah fried until the oil splits
equipment: Blender or a large mortar and pestle
Large heavy saucepan or wok
Second saucepan for the prawn stock
Fine sieve
Large pot for noodles and blanching
Slotted spoon
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Raw prawns, shell on, heads on if possible
Fish sauce or salt, and sugar
Fresh yellow egg noodles and rice vermicelli
Hard-boiled eggs, laksa leaf (Vietnamese mint), sambal and calamansi or lime

mise: Peel and devein the prawns, keeping all shells and heads.
Blend the drained chillies, shallots, garlic, galangal, lemongrass, candlenuts and belacan with 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil to a smooth paste; stir in the ground spices.
Halve the tofu puffs, blanch the bean sprouts, halve the eggs.
Scrub the cockles and discard any that are open and do not close when tapped.

timeline.do: Blend the rempah; make the prawn shell stock.
Poach the chicken in the stock.
Fry the rempah 10 to 15 minutes until split.
Build the broth with stock and coconut milk.
Cook prawns, cockles and tofu in the broth; blanch noodles.
Assemble the bowls.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the second saucepan over medium-high heat and fry the prawn shells and heads for 4 to 5 minutes, pressing the heads, until bright orange and fragrant.
steps.look: Shells turn deep orange-red and the pan smells sweet and toasty.
steps.mistake: Under-frying, so the stock tastes thin.
steps.fix: Keep going until they are well coloured.

steps.do: Add the chicken stock, bring to the boil, then simmer 20 minutes. Add the chicken thighs for the last 15 minutes. Lift out the chicken and strain the stock, pressing the shells.
steps.look: A rich, orange, prawn-scented stock; chicken cooked to 165°F (74°C).
steps.mistake: Simmering the shells for hours, which turns the stock bitter.
steps.fix: Twenty minutes is enough for shells.

steps.do: Heat the remaining oil in the large pan over medium heat and add the rempah. Fry, stirring and scraping constantly, for 10 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The paste darkens to brick red, thickens, and the oil separates out and shimmers round the edge. It smells sweet, not raw.
steps.mistake: Stopping after 3 or 4 minutes, which leaves a raw, sharp, grainy broth.
steps.fix: Be patient; lower the heat if it catches. Pecah minyak, the splitting of the oil, is the sign it is ready.

steps.do: Pour in the prawn stock and simmer 10 minutes. Add the coconut milk and bring back to a gentle simmer, not a boil. Season with fish sauce or salt and a little sugar.
steps.look: A rich, glossy, orange broth with red oil floating on top.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard after the coconut milk goes in, which splits it into grains.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer.

steps.do: Add the tofu puffs and simmer 3 minutes so they soak up the broth. Add the prawns and cockles, cover and cook 3 to 4 minutes, until the prawns are pink and the cockles open.
steps.look: Pink, curled prawns; cockles gaping open; tofu puffs swollen with broth.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the prawns into rubber.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat as soon as they turn pink. Discard any cockles that stay closed.

steps.do: Slice the chicken. Blanch the noodles in boiling water: egg noodles 1 minute, vermicelli 2 to 3 minutes, then drain.
steps.look: Soft, separate noodles.
steps.mistake: Cooking noodles in the broth, which clouds and thickens it.
steps.fix: Blanch separately.

steps.do: Put both noodles in deep bowls, add bean sprouts, chicken, prawns, cockles, tofu puffs and half an egg. Ladle over the very hot broth.
steps.look: A loaded bowl swimming in rich orange broth.
steps.mistake: Using lukewarm broth, which chills the bowl.
steps.fix: Bring the broth back to a simmer before ladling.

steps.do: Top with shredded laksa leaf and a spoon of sambal, with calamansi or lime on the side.
steps.look: Green leaves, red sambal, a glossy surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the laksa leaf, which is the signature aroma.
steps.fix: Use mint and coriander if laksa leaf is unavailable.

dishes.science: Frying a rempah until the oil splits is about driving out water. The fresh paste is mostly water from shallots, garlic and aromatics; while water remains, the paste cannot rise above boiling point and simply steams. Once the water has gone, the temperature climbs, sugars caramelise and browning reactions create deep, sweet, roasted flavours, and the fat-soluble aromas and colours dissolve into the oil, which then separates out. Prawn shells and heads are rich in flavour compounds and in astaxanthin, the pigment that turns orange when heated; frying them in oil first browns them and dissolves the colour and flavour into the fat before the stock goes in.
dishes.plating: Deep, wide bowls: noodles first, toppings arranged in neat groups on top rather than mixed, broth poured over the side, laksa leaf scattered and sambal in a dollop on one side, a wedge of lime on the rim.

pairing.drink: An iced lime juice or a cold lager; for wine, an off-dry German Riesling handles chilli and coconut.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry Mosel Riesling on the Brennan's list, a reliable match for rich, spicy coconut broth.

variations: Assam laksa: a sour tamarind and fish broth from Penang, with no coconut milk.
Vegetarian: vegetable stock, more tofu, mushrooms, and soy sauce in place of belacan and fish sauce.
Add fish balls or fish cake slices.
safety: Cook shellfish until prawns are opaque and cockles have opened; discard any cockles that do not open.
Keep raw prawns and cockles cold until cooking, and use them the day you buy them.
Frying rempah spits: use a deep pan and stir with a long spoon.

dishes.title: Egusi Soup with Pounded Yam
dishes.summary: Nigerian egusi soup: ground melon seed fried into soft curds in palm oil with blended peppers, cooked into a rich stock of beef, stockfish and smoked fish, finished with greens and eaten with pounded yam. It is here because it asks for a slow, layered stock from smoked and dried fish, a delicate curd that must set before it is stirred, and a smooth swallow pounded by hand.
skills: frying ground melon seed in palm oil
pounding yam to a smooth swallow
equipment: Large heavy pot
Medium pot for the yam
Blender
Large wooden mortar and pestle, or a stand mixer with a paddle
Wooden spoon
Bowl of hot water for the pestle
Disposable gloves for peeling yam

ingredients.note: half for the meat, half for the pepper blend

ingredients.item: Smoked fish, such as catfish or mackerel

ingredients.note: a firm white African yam, not sweet potato

mise: The day before, soak the stockfish in hot water, changing it twice; it softens and loosens.
Blend the bell peppers, Scotch bonnet and half the onion with a little water to a smooth purée.
Mix the ground egusi with 1/3 cup (80 ml) water and the other half of the onion, finely chopped, into a thick paste.
Wash and chop the greens.
Wearing gloves, peel the yam and cut it into 2 inch (5 cm) chunks; keep them in cold water.

timeline.do: Soak the stockfish.
Simmer the beef and stockfish with seasoning.
Fry peppers in palm oil, add egusi in clumps.
Let the curds set, then add stock and fish.
Boil the yam, then pound.
Wilt the greens and serve with the pounded yam.

steps.do: Put the beef, stockfish, half the chopped onion, the stock cube and salt in the large pot with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water. Cover and steam in its own juices over medium heat for 10 minutes, then add 4 cups (960 ml) water and simmer 50 to 60 minutes until the beef is tender.
steps.look: Tender beef that a fork pushes through, a savoury, slightly funky stock.
steps.mistake: Adding all the water at once, so the meat never absorbs the seasoning.
steps.fix: The first dry steam seasons the meat; then add water.

steps.do: Add the smoked fish for the last 10 minutes. Lift out the meat and fish and keep the stock; you need about 3 cups (720 ml).
steps.look: A rich, smoky stock.
steps.mistake: Breaking the smoked fish into flakes by stirring.
steps.fix: Lay it in gently and lift it out with a slotted spoon.

steps.do: Heat the palm oil in the pot over medium heat until it is just hot and fluid, about 2 minutes. Do not let it smoke. Add the pepper purée and fry 10 to 12 minutes, stirring, until thick and the oil rises.
steps.look: A thick, glossy red sauce with oil separating at the edges.
steps.mistake: Burning the palm oil until it smokes and turns pale, which gives an acrid taste.
steps.fix: Medium heat only; palm oil should stay deep red.

steps.do: Drop the egusi paste into the sauce in small clumps, spaced apart. Do not stir. Cover and cook on low heat for 8 to 10 minutes.
steps.look: The clumps puff and set into soft curds, like scrambled eggs, and smell nutty.
steps.mistake: Stirring straight away, which turns it into a grainy porridge.
steps.fix: Leave it alone until the clumps have set firm on the outside.

steps.do: Gently break the curds into smaller pieces with the wooden spoon, add the crayfish and pour in about 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of stock. Return the meat and fish and simmer 10 minutes, stirring gently.
steps.look: A thick, rich soup with visible curds of egusi, oil glistening on top.
steps.mistake: A soup so thick it sticks, or so thin the curds float apart.
steps.fix: Adjust with the remaining stock until it is thick but spoonable.

steps.do: Boil the yam in salted water for 20 to 25 minutes until completely soft.
steps.look: A knife slides through with no resistance; the edges begin to crumble.
steps.mistake: Undercooked yam, which pounds into lumps.
steps.fix: Test several pieces; they must be very soft.

steps.do: Drain the yam, saving a cup of the water. Pound it hot in the mortar, wetting the pestle in hot water, pressing and folding, adding a splash of yam water if needed, for 8 to 10 minutes. Or beat in the stand mixer with the paddle on low then medium.
steps.look: A smooth, stretchy, elastic dough that pulls in long strands and has no lumps.
steps.mistake: Letting it cool, which makes it impossible to smooth.
steps.fix: Work fast while it is hot; in the mixer, add hot water a spoonful at a time.

steps.do: Stir the greens into the soup and simmer 2 to 3 minutes until just wilted. Taste and season.
steps.look: Bright green leaves through a red-orange soup.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the greens until grey and limp.
steps.fix: Add them last and serve soon after.

steps.do: Shape the pounded yam into smooth balls with wet hands and serve beside bowls of soup.
steps.look: Glossy white balls of yam and rich soup.
steps.mistake: Serving the yam cold.
steps.fix: Wrap it in cling film to keep warm while you finish.

dishes.science: Egusi is ground melon seed, rich in protein and oil. When clumps of the moistened paste meet hot liquid and are left alone, the outside proteins set first, much as egg does, forming soft curds that hold together; stirring too early breaks the setting proteins into fine grains. Frying the pepper purée in palm oil cooks off its water and caramelises its sugars, while the oil carries the carotenoid colour. Stockfish is air-dried cod, so long soaking rehydrates it and its concentrated savoury compounds flavour the stock alongside smoked fish. Pounded yam works because cooked yam starch, worked hot, forms an elastic gel; once cool, the starch sets and refuses to smooth.
dishes.plating: Serve the soup in a deep bowl with pieces of meat and fish on top, and the pounded yam as a smooth ball on a separate plate or wrapped in film. Eat by pinching off yam with the right hand, making a dent with the thumb and scooping the soup.

pairing.drink: A cold malt drink or a crisp lager; for wine, a juicy, low-tannin red served cool.

variations: Serve with eba (garri) or fufu instead of pounded yam.
Add goat meat or assorted offal in place of beef, as at celebrations.
Use pumpkin seed meal if you cannot find egusi.
safety: Raw yam can irritate the skin; wear gloves when peeling.
Palm oil heated until it smokes produces harsh compounds; keep it at medium heat.
Heavy pestles slip: work on a stable surface and keep fingers out of the mortar.

dishes.title: Feijoada
dishes.summary: Brazil's Saturday lunch: black beans slowly cooked with several cuts of salted, smoked and fresh pork, each added at the moment it needs, served with rice, garlicky greens, toasted farofa and orange slices. It is here because it teaches desalting cured meats and managing many cuts with different cooking times in one pot.
skills: farofa, couve and orange to serve
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid
Large bowls for soaking
Large frying pan
Medium saucepan for rice
Sharp knife and board
Slotted spoon

ingredients.item: Carne seca (Brazilian dried beef) or salted beef
Smoked sausage, such as linguiça or calabresa

mise: Desalt the carne seca and salted ribs: cut into large pieces and soak in cold water in the fridge for 12 to 24 hours, changing the water three or four times.
Soak the beans overnight in plenty of cold water.
Chop the onions and garlic.
Roll the collard leaves tightly and slice into very fine ribbons, 1/16 inch (2 mm) wide.

timeline.do: Desalt the cured meats; soak the beans.
Simmer the beans with bay and the cured meats.
Brown the bacon, shoulder and onions; add to the pot.
Add the sausage; make the rice and farofa.
Sauté the greens; thicken the beans.
Serve with all the sides.

steps.do: Taste a small piece of the soaked carne seca after a quick boil to check its salt.
steps.look: Mildly salty, like well seasoned cooked meat.
steps.mistake: Cooking it unsoaked, so the whole pot is far too salty.
steps.fix: Soak longer and change the water again.

steps.do: Drain the beans and put them in the large pot with the bay, the desalted carne seca and ribs, and water to cover by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring to the boil, skim, and simmer partly covered for 1 hour.
steps.look: Beans starting to soften, the liquid darkening.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which bursts the beans.
steps.fix: Keep it at a lazy simmer; top up with hot water.

steps.do: Meanwhile, cut the bacon into lardons and fry in the frying pan over medium heat until the fat runs. Brown the pork shoulder in the fat in batches, then soften the onions and garlic in the same pan.
steps.look: Well browned meat and golden, sweet onions.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, which steams the pork grey.
steps.fix: Brown in batches with space round each piece.

steps.do: Add the bacon, shoulder, onions and garlic to the beans, scraping in the browned bits from the pan with a little water. Simmer 1 hour more.
steps.look: The broth turns thick, dark and glossy, and the shoulder grows tender.
steps.mistake: Adding everything at the start, so the tender cuts fall apart.
steps.fix: Cuts go in by how long they need: cured and tough first, sausage last.

steps.do: Add the sausage and simmer 30 minutes more. Meanwhile cook the rice.
steps.look: Sausage plump and heated through, fat glistening on top.
steps.mistake: Adding sausage early, so it dries out and loses its flavour into the pot.
steps.fix: Thirty minutes is enough.

steps.do: Make the farofa: melt the butter in the frying pan over medium heat, add the manioc flour and toast, stirring, for 5 to 6 minutes, with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Golden, sandy, toasted crumbs smelling nutty.
steps.mistake: Burning the flour, which happens suddenly.
steps.fix: Keep stirring and take it off as soon as it is golden.

steps.do: Mash a ladle of beans against the side of the pot and stir in to thicken. Season, though it may need little salt.
steps.look: A thick, velvety, near-black broth.
steps.mistake: Adding salt before tasting.
steps.fix: Taste first; the cured meats carry salt.

steps.do: Sauté the greens: heat a little oil, fry a sliced garlic clove for 30 seconds, add the collard ribbons and toss over high heat for 1 to 2 minutes with a pinch of salt.
steps.look: Bright green, just wilted ribbons.
steps.mistake: Cooking them until olive green.
steps.fix: Toss quickly over high heat.

steps.do: Serve the feijoada with rice, greens, farofa, orange slices and pepper sauce.
steps.look: A table full of colour: black beans, white rice, green couve, golden farofa, orange.
steps.mistake: Serving the pot alone.
steps.fix: The sides are part of the dish; the orange cuts the richness.

dishes.science: Desalting works by diffusion: salt moves out of the meat into fresh water until the concentrations balance, so changing the water repeatedly draws more out. Cuts with lots of collagen, such as ribs, dried beef and shoulder, need long gentle simmering for collagen to melt into gelatin, while sausage is already cooked and only needs heating, so the order of addition matches each cut's needs. The gelatin and the starch released from mashed beans thicken the broth into a glossy sauce. Black beans owe their colour to anthocyanins in their skins, which tint the broth near black. Toasting manioc flour in butter browns its starch and gives a nutty crunch.
dishes.plating: Bring the feijoada to the table in its pot or a clay dish, with separate bowls of rice, couve, farofa and orange slices. On the plate: rice first, beans and meat over half of it, greens beside, farofa sprinkled over the beans and orange slices on the side.

pairing.drink: A caipirinha, cachaça with lime and sugar, whose sharp citrus cuts the rich pork and beans.

variations: Feijoada light: use fresh pork and smoked turkey for a leaner version.
Use a pressure cooker for the beans and cured meats, about 40 minutes, then finish with the rest.
Serve with fried pork crackling, torresmo, on top.
safety: Desalt cured meats in the fridge, not on the worktop.
Cool leftovers quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours; reheat until piping hot.

dishes.title: Hyderabadi Chicken Biryani
dishes.summary: Hyderabadi kacchi biryani: raw chicken marinated in spiced yoghurt, layered under basmati boiled to seventy per cent done, scented with saffron milk and fried onions, then sealed and cooked in its own steam. It is here because raw meat and part-cooked rice must finish together under a seal, a feat of timing and heat control.
skills: parboiling basmati to seventy per cent
equipment: Heavy pot with a tight lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres), ideally wide
Large saucepan for boiling rice
Frying pan for the onions
Fine sieve or colander
Heat diffuser or a flat griddle (tava)
Instant-read thermometer
Small bowl for the saffron
Large mixing bowl

ingredients.item: Bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks, skinless
ingredients.note: thighs cut in half through the bone by the butcher

ingredients.us: 2 tsp, plus 3 tbsp for the rice water

ingredients.item: Whole spices for the rice: green cardamom, cloves, cinnamon stick, bay leaf, shahi jeera
ingredients.us: 4 cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 stick, 2 bay, 1 tsp shahi jeera
ingredients.metric: 4 cardamom, 4 cloves, 1 stick, 2 bay, 2 g shahi jeera

ingredients.note: steeped in 1/4 cup (60 ml) warm milk

ingredients.item: Plain or wholemeal flour, for the seal
ingredients.note: mixed with water to a stiff dough

mise: Fry the onions in the oil over medium heat, stirring, for 15 to 20 minutes until deep brown and crisp; drain on paper and keep the oil.
Wash the rice gently 3 times and soak it in cold water for 30 minutes.
Steep the saffron in warm milk.
Make a stiff dough for the seal and roll it into a rope long enough to go round the pot rim.

timeline.do: Fry onions; marinate the chicken 4 hours or overnight.
Soak the rice; spread chicken in the pot.
Parboil the rice to seventy per cent; layer.
Seal; 5 minutes high, then 35 to 40 minutes on the lowest heat over the diffuser.
Rest sealed, check the chicken.
Break the seal at the table and serve.

steps.do: Mix the chicken with the yoghurt, ginger and garlic paste, chilli powder, turmeric, garam masala, lime, green chillies, half the mint and coriander, half the fried onions, 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the onion oil and 2 tsp (12 g) salt. Cover and refrigerate 4 hours or overnight.
steps.look: Chicken thickly coated in a pink-orange, herb-flecked marinade.
steps.mistake: Marinating less than 2 hours, which gives a bland, firmer chicken.
steps.fix: At least 4 hours; overnight is best.

steps.do: Take the chicken out 30 minutes before cooking. Spread it with all the marinade in an even layer in the heavy pot, and add 2 tbsp (28 g) ghee over it.
steps.look: A flat, even layer covering the base.
steps.mistake: Piling it in the middle, so the centre cooks more slowly than the edges.
steps.fix: Spread it flat to the edges.

steps.do: Bring 3 quarts (3 litres) water to a rolling boil with the 3 tbsp (54 g) salt and the whole spices. The water should taste as salty as the sea. Drain the rice and add it.
steps.look: A fast boil that returns quickly after the rice goes in.
steps.mistake: Under-salting the water, so the rice tastes flat.
steps.fix: Taste the water; this is the rice's only seasoning.

steps.do: Boil 4 to 5 minutes, testing a grain every 30 seconds by pressing it between finger and thumb. Drain immediately when it is about seventy per cent done.
steps.look: The grain is soft on the outside but breaks with a firm white dot in the centre, and has lengthened.
steps.mistake: Boiling until fully cooked, so the top turns to mush under the seal.
steps.fix: Drain a little early rather than late; the steam finishes it.

steps.do: Spoon the hot rice over the chicken in a loose, even layer without pressing. Scatter the rest of the fried onions, mint and coriander, drizzle the saffron milk in streaks and the remaining 2 tbsp (28 g) ghee over the top.
steps.look: A fluffy white layer streaked with gold and dotted with herbs.
steps.mistake: Pressing the rice down, which squashes it and stops steam rising.
steps.fix: Spoon it on lightly.

steps.do: Press the dough rope round the rim of the pot and press the lid down on it firmly to seal.
steps.look: A tight seal with no gaps; no steam escapes at the edges.
steps.mistake: A gap in the seal, which lets steam out and leaves dry rice over wet chicken.
steps.fix: Patch any gap with more dough.

steps.do: Cook on high heat for 5 to 7 minutes until you hear the base sizzling and see a wisp of steam at the seal, then put the heat diffuser under the pot and cook on the lowest heat for 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: A gentle sizzle, then quiet; a faint fragrant steam.
steps.mistake: Cooking on high all the way, which burns the chicken to the base.
steps.fix: Use the diffuser or a griddle under the pot to spread low, even heat.

steps.do: Turn off the heat and rest 10 minutes. Break the seal, push the thermometer into the thickest piece of chicken near the bottom.
steps.look: Chicken at 165°F (74°C) or more, tender and falling from the bone; rice fluffy and separate.
steps.mistake: Skipping the check with raw chicken under rice.
steps.fix: If under, reseal with foil and the lid and cook 10 minutes more on low.

steps.do: Serve by lifting wedges from the side with a flat spoon right to the bottom, so each serving has rice and chicken, rather than stirring.
steps.look: Layers of white and saffron rice over spiced chicken.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which breaks the rice and mixes it to a mush.
steps.fix: Dig down from the edge with a flat spoon.

dishes.science: Dum cooking finishes rice in steam rather than water. The rice is boiled until its outer starch has gelatinised but the core is still firm, about seventy per cent done, and then the steam rising from the marinade carries it the rest of the way. The seal traps that steam and builds gentle pressure, so meat below and rice above cook together. The yoghurt's acid and enzymes tenderise the surface of the chicken, and the yoghurt liquid becomes the steam. Aged basmati has dried further, so the grains absorb water evenly and lengthen rather than split. Saffron's colour and aroma compounds dissolve in warm milk, and fried onions add caramelised sweetness throughout.
dishes.plating: Bring the pot to the table, break the seal there for the burst of aroma, then serve on a large platter with saffron and white rice on top and chicken beneath. Serve with raita, a salad of onion and cucumber, and a mirchi ka salan or a simple gravy.

pairing.drink: A salted lassi or a glass of cool raita on the side; for wine, an off-dry Gewurztraminer or a light, fruity red.

variations: Mutton or goat kacchi biryani: the same method with longer cooking, 60 to 70 minutes, for the tougher meat.
Pakki biryani: cook the chicken curry first, then layer and steam for 20 minutes, a safer method while learning.
Vegetable biryani: marinate mixed vegetables and paneer in place of chicken.
safety: Raw chicken cooks under the rice: check that the thickest pieces reach 165°F (74°C) before serving.
Keep marinating chicken in the fridge and wash hands, boards and bowls after handling it.
Steam escapes fiercely when the seal is broken; open the lid away from you.

dishes.title: Siu Mai
dishes.summary: Cantonese dim sum dumplings of hand-chopped prawn and fatty pork, worked until springy, wrapped in thin open-topped wrappers and steamed. It is here because the bouncy texture Cantonese cooks prize comes from slapping and working the filling, and because the open-topped fold is a skill of its own.
skills: a springy pork and prawn filling slapped for bounce
equipment: Bamboo steamer with a lid, and a wok or wide pan it sits in
Baking paper cut into rounds with holes, or cabbage leaves
Sharp cleaver or chef's knife
Large mixing bowl
Small spoon or butter knife
Instant-read thermometer

ingredients.item: Round yellow dumpling wrappers, or square wonton wrappers trimmed into rounds
Carrot, very finely diced, or fish roe

mise: Pat the prawns dry with kitchen paper.
Drain the mushrooms, squeeze dry, discard the stems and chop finely.
Line the steamer baskets with the perforated paper.
Keep the wrappers covered with a damp cloth.

timeline.do: Soak mushrooms; prepare prawns.
Make and work the filling; chill 20 minutes.
Fold the siu mai.
Bring water to the boil under the steamer.
Steam 8 minutes.
Serve in the baskets with chilli oil and soy.

steps.do: Chop half the prawns finely with the cleaver into a coarse paste and the other half into pea-size pieces.
steps.look: A mix of sticky paste and small chunks.
steps.mistake: Mincing all the prawns to paste, which loses the bite of prawn pieces.
steps.fix: Paste binds; chunks give texture. You want both.

steps.do: Put the pork in the bowl with the salt and stir hard in one direction with chopsticks or your hand for 2 minutes.
steps.look: The pork turns sticky and stringy and clings to the bowl.
steps.mistake: Stirring in both directions, which breaks the strands forming.
steps.fix: Stir one way only; it builds the protein network.

steps.do: Add the prawns, mushrooms, sugar, cornflour, oyster sauce, wine, sesame oil, pepper and water and stir hard in the same direction for 2 minutes more.
steps.look: A thick, sticky, cohesive filling.
steps.mistake: Under-mixing, so the filling is loose and crumbly.
steps.fix: Keep stirring until it holds together as one mass.

steps.do: Pick up the whole mass and slap it back into the bowl 20 to 30 times. Chill 20 minutes.
steps.look: The filling becomes noticeably more elastic and springy.
steps.mistake: Skipping the slapping, so the dumplings are soft rather than bouncy.
steps.fix: Slap with conviction; it is the Cantonese secret to bounce.

steps.do: Make a circle with the thumb and forefinger of one hand. Lay a wrapper over it and spoon about 1 tbsp (about 20 g) of filling into the centre. Let the wrapper sink into the circle, pushing the filling down with a butter knife and squeezing gently so the wrapper pleats up the sides.
steps.look: A little open cup, the wrapper pleated round, filling level with the top.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, so the wrapper cannot hold it.
steps.fix: Use less filling; press it down and smooth the top.

steps.do: Tap the base on the worktop to flatten it so it stands up, and smooth the top with the wet knife. Top with a little carrot or roe.
steps.look: Neat, upright, waisted dumplings with flat bases.
steps.mistake: Uneven bases that topple in the steamer.
steps.fix: Tap firmly and squeeze the waist gently.

steps.do: Set the siu mai in the lined steamer 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Steam over rapidly boiling water for 8 minutes.
steps.look: The filling turns from grey-pink to opaque pink and firm, the wrapper translucent.
steps.mistake: Letting the wok boil dry.
steps.fix: Check the water halfway and top up with boiling water from the kettle.

steps.do: Check one with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C) in the centre. Serve at once in the baskets with chilli oil and soy.
steps.look: Springy, juicy dumplings that bounce back when pressed.
steps.mistake: Serving undercooked pork.
steps.fix: Steam 2 minutes more if needed.

dishes.science: The bounce comes from proteins. Salt draws out myosin from the pork and prawn muscle, and stirring in one direction lines those sticky proteins up into a connected network. Slapping the filling compresses it, drives out air pockets and further develops that network. When steamed, the network sets into a firm, elastic gel that springs back when bitten, the texture Cantonese cooks call bouncy. Fat in the pork keeps the filling juicy, and cornflour holds moisture so it does not leak out. Steam cooks gently and evenly at the boiling point of water, which sets the proteins without drying the dumplings.
dishes.plating: Serve in the bamboo baskets they steamed in, placed on a plate to catch drips, with small dishes of chilli oil and soy, and a pot of jasmine or oolong tea.

pairing.drink: Jasmine or oolong tea, the dim sum tradition; or a dry, aromatic white such as Grüner Veltliner.

variations: Har gow: prawn dumplings in translucent wheat starch wrappers.
Add chopped water chestnut for crunch.
Freeze uncooked siu mai on a tray and steam from frozen for 12 minutes.
safety: Cook pork filling to 160°F (71°C).
Lift the steamer lid away from your face; steam burns.
Keep raw prawns and pork cold until shaping.

dishes.title: Mantı
dishes.summary: Turkish mantı: a firm egg dough rolled very thin and cut into tiny squares, each holding a pinch of spiced lamb, pinched into little parcels, boiled and served on garlic yoghurt with a sizzling butter of tomato and Aleppo pepper. It is here because the dumplings are so small that rolling thin and working fast are the whole test.
skills: garlic yoghurt and Aleppo pepper butter
equipment: Large mixing bowl
Long thin rolling pin (oklava) or a regular rolling pin, or a pasta machine
Ruler and a sharp knife or pizza wheel
Large pot
Slotted spoon
Small saucepan for the butter
Trays dusted with flour

ingredients.item: Salt, black pepper and Aleppo pepper (pul biber)

mise: Grate the onion and squeeze out the juice through a sieve.
Mix the lamb, onion, parsley, salt and both peppers well and chill.
Mix the yoghurt and crushed garlic and leave at room temperature.
Dust two trays with flour.

timeline.do: Make the dough; rest 30 minutes; make the filling.
Roll very thin and cut squares.
Fill and pinch the mantı.
Boil the water; warm the yoghurt.
Boil the mantı; make the butter.
Plate on yoghurt, pour over the butter.

steps.do: Mix the flour, salt, egg and enough water to make a firm dough. Knead 8 minutes until smooth, then wrap and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A firm, smooth, satiny dough, firmer than bread dough.
steps.mistake: A soft dough, which stretches back and sticks when rolled thin.
steps.fix: Knead in a little flour; it should feel like firm pasta dough.

steps.do: Divide the dough in two. Roll one half on a lightly floured worktop into a large sheet about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm) thick, turning it often and dusting lightly. Or roll through a pasta machine to the second thinnest setting.
steps.look: A thin, even sheet you can just see your hand through.
steps.mistake: Uneven thickness, so some mantı are tough and others tear.
steps.fix: Roll from the centre outward, turning a quarter turn every few strokes.

steps.do: Cut the sheet into 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) squares with the knife or pizza wheel and a ruler.
steps.look: A grid of neat, even squares.
steps.mistake: Cutting large squares, which makes heavy, doughy mantı.
steps.fix: Small squares are the point; keep them all the same size.

steps.do: Put a pinch of filling, about 1/4 tsp (1 to 2 g), in the centre of each square.
steps.look: A tiny bead of meat on every square.
steps.mistake: Too much filling, so the corners will not meet.
steps.fix: Use less; the size of a chickpea.

steps.do: Lift two opposite corners and pinch them together over the filling, then bring the other two corners up and pinch all four into a point. Pinch the open seams closed.
steps.look: A tiny, four-cornered parcel, sealed at the top.
steps.mistake: Leaving the sides open, so the filling falls out in the pot.
steps.fix: Pinch all four seams. Work quickly so the dough does not dry.

steps.do: Set the mantı on the floured trays without touching. Repeat with the second half of dough.
steps.look: Rows of small, neat parcels.
steps.mistake: Leaving them touching, so they stick together.
steps.fix: Space them out and dust lightly with flour.

steps.do: Bring a large pot of salted water to the boil and cook the mantı for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring gently at first, until the dough is tender.
steps.look: They float and the dough turns soft; one cut open shows cooked, grey-brown lamb.
steps.mistake: Undercooking, so the corners are hard.
steps.fix: Taste one; the pinched tops take longest.

steps.do: While they boil, melt the butter in the small pan over medium heat until it foams and turns light golden and nutty, then stir in the tomato purée and Aleppo pepper for 30 seconds.
steps.look: A sizzling, brick-red, fragrant butter.
steps.mistake: Burning the butter to black.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as it smells nutty and turns golden brown.

steps.do: Spread the garlic yoghurt on warm plates, spoon the drained mantı over, pour the hot butter across and finish with dried mint and sumac.
steps.look: White yoghurt, small golden parcels, red butter and green mint.
steps.mistake: Using cold yoghurt, which chills the dish.
steps.fix: Bring the yoghurt to room temperature or warm it gently.

dishes.science: A thin, firm egg dough is strong enough to roll paper thin without tearing because egg proteins and gluten together form a resilient network, and resting lets the gluten relax so it rolls out without shrinking. Small squares mean a high ratio of dough to filling, which is what defines the dish. Squeezing the onion removes water that would otherwise make the filling wet and leak. Browning the butter cooks its milk solids until they toast, giving a nutty flavour; tomato purée and pepper fried in the hot fat release their colour and fat-soluble flavours. The cool garlic yoghurt balances the warm butter and spices.
dishes.plating: Warm shallow bowls: a thick layer of garlic yoghurt, the mantı piled in the centre, the red butter poured in a ring so it pools over yoghurt and dumplings, dried mint and sumac dusted over the top.

pairing.drink: Ayran, the salted yoghurt drink, or a light, juicy red such as a Beaujolais or a Turkish Kalecik Karası.

variations: Bake the filled mantı in a buttered tray until crisp, then pour over hot stock, the Kayseri style.
Use minced beef in place of lamb.
Fill with spiced potato or lentils for a vegetarian version.
safety: Cook the mantı until the lamb inside is cooked through, at least 160°F (71°C).
Brown butter is very hot; pour it carefully, away from your hands.

dishes.title: Pierogi Ruskie
dishes.summary: Polish dumplings of a soft sour cream dough filled with potato, curd cheese and fried onion, sealed into half moons, boiled and then fried in butter. It is here because it refines the dumpling fold with a softer, more tender dough, and adds the boil then fry finish.
equipment: Large mixing bowl
Potato ricer or masher
Medium saucepan
Large frying pan
Rolling pin
Round cutter or glass, 3 inch (7.5 cm)
Large pot
Slotted spoon
Trays dusted with flour

ingredients.note: 1 finely chopped for the filling, 1 sliced for the topping

ingredients.item: Salt and plenty of black pepper

mise: Boil the potatoes in salted water until very tender, drain well and rice or mash while hot. Cool.
Fry the chopped onion in 1 tbsp (14 g) butter over medium heat for 10 minutes until golden.
Mix the potato, cheese and fried onion and season boldly with salt and lots of pepper. Chill.
Slice the second onion for the topping.

timeline.do: Boil potatoes; fry onion; make filling.
Make the dough; rest 30 minutes.
Roll, cut, fill and seal.
Fry the topping onions slowly.
Boil the pierogi.
Fry in butter with onions; serve with sour cream.

steps.do: Mix the flour and salt, add the egg, sour cream, melted butter and most of the warm water, and mix to a soft dough, adding the rest of the water as needed. Knead 5 minutes, cover with the upturned bowl and rest 30 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, supple dough, soft like an earlobe.
steps.mistake: A stiff dough, which makes tough pierogi.
steps.fix: Add water a spoonful at a time; soft is right.

steps.do: Taste the filling cold and adjust the seasoning.
steps.look: Boldly seasoned, peppery and salty.
steps.mistake: Under-seasoning; cold filling inside dough tastes much milder.
steps.fix: Season more than you think.

steps.do: Roll half the dough on a floured worktop to 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick. Cut rounds with the cutter.
steps.look: Thin, even rounds; you can faintly see the worktop through them.
steps.mistake: Rolling too thick, which gives doughy pierogi.
steps.fix: Roll thinner; gather and re-roll scraps once.

steps.do: Put about 1 tbsp (about 20 g) of filling in the centre of each round. Fold in half and pinch the edges firmly together from one end to the other, pushing out any air.
steps.look: Plump half moons with a tight, sealed edge.
steps.mistake: Filling on the edge, which stops it sealing, or trapped air, which bursts in the pot.
steps.fix: Keep the edge clean and dry; press the air out towards the open end as you seal.

steps.do: Crimp the sealed edge with a fork or pleat it with your fingers for extra security. Set on the floured tray, not touching.
steps.look: Neat, crimped dumplings.
steps.mistake: Letting them touch, so they stick together.
steps.fix: Space them out on a floured tray.

steps.do: Fry the sliced onion in 2 tbsp (28 g) butter over medium-low heat for 15 to 20 minutes until deep golden.
steps.look: Soft, sweet, golden onions.
steps.mistake: Rushing on high heat, so they burn before they sweeten.
steps.fix: Low and slow.

steps.do: Boil the pierogi in batches in a large pot of salted water. When they float, cook 2 minutes more, then lift out with the slotted spoon.
steps.look: Pierogi rise to the surface, puffed and tender.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding the pot, so they stick and the water stops boiling.
steps.fix: Cook 10 to 12 at a time.

steps.do: Heat the remaining butter in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the boiled pierogi 2 minutes a side until golden and blistered. Toss with the onions and serve with sour cream.
steps.look: Golden, blistered edges, glossy with butter, onions spooned over.
steps.mistake: Frying wet pierogi, which spit and stick.
steps.fix: Drain them well first; let them steam dry for a minute.

dishes.science: Sour cream and butter in the dough add fat, which coats some of the flour proteins and limits gluten, so the dough is tender and soft rather than chewy. Resting under a bowl relaxes the gluten that does form and keeps the dough moist, so it rolls thin without springing back. Floury potatoes, high in starch, mash dry and fluffy, giving a filling that holds its shape. Boiling cooks the dough by gelatinising its starch, and the pierogi float as air and steam inside make them lighter than water. Frying afterwards in butter browns the surface through the Maillard reaction, giving a crisp, nutty finish over a soft interior.
dishes.plating: Warm plates: six or eight pierogi slightly overlapping, golden onions spooned over, a dollop of sour cream on the side and a sprinkle of chopped dill or chives. Crisp bacon lardons on top if you like.

pairing.drink: A cold Polish lager, or a crisp, dry white such as Grüner Veltliner.

variations: Pierogi z kapustą i grzybami: sauerkraut and wild mushroom filling, a Christmas Eve classic.
Sweet pierogi with sweetened curd cheese or blueberries, served with sugar and cream.
Freeze boiled, cooled pierogi on a tray and fry from frozen.
safety: Lift dumplings out of boiling water with a slotted spoon, not by hand.
Cooked pierogi should be cooled and refrigerated within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Brik à l'Oeuf
dishes.summary: Tunisian brik: a sheet of very thin pastry holding tuna, capers, parsley and a whole raw egg, folded and fried in seconds so the pastry crisps and the yolk stays runny. It is here because it is a race against time, handling fragile pastry and frying with confidence, and a lesson in timing a soft egg inside hot oil.
skills: a tuna, caper and parsley filling
cracking an egg onto the pastry
folding and frying so the yolk stays runny
equipment: Large deep frying pan or wide shallow pan
Thermometer for the oil
Two wide spatulas or fish slices
Small bowl for each egg
Wire rack over a tray lined with kitchen paper
Mixing bowl

ingredients.item: Brik (malsouka) sheets, or large spring roll wrappers
ingredients.note: 8 inch (20 cm) or larger; use two sheets of filo brushed with butter if neither is available

ingredients.item: Parmesan or another hard cheese, grated

ingredients.note: enough for 3/4 inch (2 cm) in the pan

mise: Mix the tuna, capers, parsley, onion, cheese and harissa, and season with pepper and a little salt.
Crack each egg into its own small bowl.
Keep the pastry sheets covered with a damp cloth so they do not dry.
Set up the pan, rack, spatulas and thermometer close together; the work is fast.

timeline.do: Make the filling; crack the eggs.
Heat the oil to 350°F (175°C).
Fill, add egg, fold and fry one at a time.
Drain briefly and serve at once with lemon.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pan to 350°F (175°C).
steps.look: Steady temperature on the thermometer; a scrap of pastry fizzes and browns in about 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Oil too cool, giving greasy, soft pastry.
steps.fix: Wait for the temperature before starting.

steps.do: Lay one pastry sheet on a plate. Spoon a quarter of the filling onto one half of the sheet and make a hollow in the middle with the back of the spoon.
steps.look: A ring of tuna filling with a well in the centre, on one half of the sheet.
steps.mistake: Spreading the filling to the edges, so it will not seal.
steps.fix: Leave a clear border of at least 1 inch (2.5 cm).

steps.do: Slide an egg gently into the hollow.
steps.look: The yolk sitting whole in the tuna well.
steps.mistake: Pouring from a height, so the egg runs everywhere.
steps.fix: Tip it in from close to the surface.

steps.do: Fold the bare half of the sheet over to make a half moon, pressing the edges lightly together. Immediately slide the brik into the hot oil, away from you.
steps.look: A puffed half moon that sizzles at once.
steps.mistake: Taking too long, so the egg soaks through the pastry.
steps.fix: Fold and fry within 30 seconds of adding the egg.

steps.do: Fry 45 to 60 seconds, spooning hot oil over the top, then turn carefully with two spatulas and fry 30 to 45 seconds more.
steps.look: Deep golden, blistered, crisp pastry; the parcel feels puffed and the egg white set near the edges.
steps.mistake: Frying too long, so the yolk sets hard.
steps.fix: About 90 seconds in all; err on the short side.

steps.do: Lift onto the rack to drain for 30 seconds.
steps.look: Golden, crisp brik with oil draining off.
steps.mistake: Leaving them stacked, so they steam soft.
steps.fix: Drain in a single layer.

steps.do: Serve immediately with lemon wedges, one per person. Eat with your hands, biting the corner first and tilting so the yolk does not run out.
steps.look: A shattering crust and a runny yolk mixing with the tuna.
steps.mistake: Letting them stand, so the pastry softens and the yolk keeps cooking.
steps.fix: Cook and serve one at a time if needed.

dishes.science: Brik pastry is extremely thin, so in hot oil its water evaporates almost instantly and the starch sets into a crisp shell within seconds. That speed is what protects the egg: the pastry crisps and the filling around the egg warms before heat has time to travel through and set the yolk. Egg white begins to set at around 145°F (63°C) and yolk thickens at around 150 to 160°F (65 to 71°C), so a short fry leaves the white near the edges set and the yolk runny. Oil at 350°F (175°C) browns the pastry quickly and keeps oil absorption low; oil that is too cool lets the pastry soak up fat before it crisps.
dishes.plating: A plain plate with the brik whole, a lemon wedge beside it and a small spoon of harissa. Offer a simple salad of tomato, cucumber and onion. Serve on paper napkins so guests can pick them up.

pairing.drink: Fresh mint tea, or a crisp, dry rosé whose acidity cuts the fried pastry.

variations: Brik with mashed potato and tuna, which helps hold the egg.
Prawn or minced lamb fillings, cooked first.
Shape into triangles or rolls for parties, without the whole egg.
safety: Hot oil: never fill more than halfway, slide each brik in away from you, and keep a lid nearby. Never use water on burning oil.
The yolk stays runny: use pasteurised eggs for pregnant guests, the very young, the elderly or anyone with a weakened immune system, or fry longer until the yolk sets.
