dishes.title: Steak Frites with Béarnaise
dishes.summary: Two thick strip steaks seared hard and rested, double fried frites and a béarnaise built from a tarragon reduction, all landing on the plate at the same moment. It opens the Sous Chef dinners because it is three disciplines on one plate: an emulsion held at a narrow temperature, a sear judged by thermometer and a fryer run at two heats, with the timing of a pass to bring them together.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast iron or carbon steel frying pan
Heavy, deep pot of at least 5 quarts (5 litres) for frying, or an electric fryer
Clip-on deep fry thermometer and an instant read probe thermometer
Spider or slotted spoon, and a wire rack set over a baking tray
Small heavy saucepan for the reduction and a fine sieve
Heatproof glass or stainless bowl that sits over a saucepan without touching the water
Balloon whisk
Small saucepan for clarifying the butter, and a ladle
Chef's knife and a large chopping board
Large bowl of iced water for the cut potatoes

ingredients.note: or ribeye; one steak sliced feeds two

ingredients.us: 2 tsp, plus more for the frites
ingredients.note: Diamond Crystal; halve if using Morton

ingredients.item: Neutral oil with a high smoke point
Thyme sprigs and a garlic clove, crushed

ingredients.note: stalks for the reduction, about 3 tbsp (8 g) leaves chopped to finish
pasteurised in shell if serving anyone vulnerable
yields about 3/4 cup (180 ml) clarified butter

ingredients.item: Fine salt and lemon juice, to season the sauce
ingredients.us: 1/2 tsp salt, a few drops lemon
ingredients.metric: 3 g salt, a few drops lemon

mise: An hour or more ahead (up to a day), season the steaks all over with the kosher salt and set them on a rack over a tray in the fridge, uncovered.
Peel the potatoes and cut into batons 3/8 inch (1 cm) square; drop them straight into the iced water and leave at least 30 minutes to wash off surface starch.
Clarify the butter: melt it over low heat, let it sit 5 minutes, skim the foam, then ladle the clear yellow fat off the milky water below. Keep it warm at about 122°F (50°C).
Mince the shallot; pick the tarragon, keeping stalks and leaves separate; chop the leaves and the chervil and keep them under a damp paper towel.
Separate the eggs; keep the whites for another day, covered in the fridge.
Take the steaks out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking and pat them dry.
Set up the fryer away from the edge of the hob, handle turned inward, with the rack and tray beside it; keep a lid and a fire blanket within reach.

timeline.at: Day before or T minus 2 hours 30 min
timeline.do: Salt the steaks and refrigerate uncovered.
Cut the potatoes and soak them in iced water.
Clarify the butter; make and strain the tarragon reduction.
Heat the oil to 300°F (150°C); blanch the frites in batches and cool on the rack.
Steaks out of the fridge. Make the béarnaise and hold it warm.
Sear and baste the steaks; rest them.
Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C); fry the frites a second time.
Slice the steaks, salt the frites, spoon the sauce and serve.

steps.do: Make the reduction: put the vinegar, wine, shallot, tarragon stalks and cracked peppercorns in the small saucepan over medium heat and simmer until only about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of liquid is left, 6 to 8 minutes. Strain through the fine sieve, pressing hard on the solids, and let it cool to blood warm.
steps.look: The sharp vinegar smell softens to a sweet, shallot and aniseed aroma; tilting the pan, the liquid moves like a light syrup.
steps.mistake: Reducing it to a dry glaze, so there is no water left to protect the yolks and the sauce turns grainy.
steps.fix: If you have less than 2 tbsp (30 ml), top it up with water to 3 tbsp (45 ml); the water is part of the recipe.

steps.do: Blanch the frites: drain the potatoes and dry them completely in a clean towel. Heat the frying oil to 300°F (150°C). Lower in a third of the potatoes and fry 5 to 6 minutes, stirring gently once, until soft right through but still pale. Lift onto the rack. Repeat, letting the oil return to temperature between batches.
steps.look: Gentle, steady bubbling, not a roar; a baton pinched between finger and thumb (once cool enough) squashes easily and has no colour.
steps.mistake: Putting wet potatoes into the oil, which makes it spit and boil up the sides of the pot.
steps.fix: Dry them again; never fill the pot more than half full of oil, and lower the basket or spider slowly so you can lift out if the foam climbs.

steps.do: Start the sabayon: set the bowl over a saucepan of water held just below a simmer, about 160°F (70°C), the base of the bowl clear of the water. Whisk the yolks and the cooled reduction together off the heat, then set the bowl on the pan and whisk continuously in a figure of eight, reaching into the edges, for 3 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: The yolks foam, then thicken until the whisk leaves trails and a ribbon dropped on the surface holds for a second; a probe reads about 149°F (65°C). It smells eggy and warm, never like scrambled egg.
steps.mistake: Letting the water boil or the bowl get too hot, so small curds form at the edges.
steps.fix: Lift the bowl off at the first sign of thickening at the rim and whisk off the heat; if specks appear, whisk in 1 tsp (5 ml) of cold water at once and pass through a sieve if needed.

steps.do: Take the bowl off the heat and set it on a folded damp cloth so it cannot spin. Add the warm clarified butter a few drops at a time, whisking constantly, for the first quarter of it; then pour in a thin, steady stream while whisking until all of it is in.
steps.look: The sauce turns glossy and thickens with each addition until a spoon dragged through it leaves a clear path; it should hold soft ribbons like mayonnaise just loosened.
steps.mistake: Pouring the butter in too fast at the start, so the yolks cannot take it and the sauce splits into greasy curds and liquid fat.
steps.fix: Put a fresh yolk and 1 tsp (5 ml) warm water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a spoonful at a time; it comes back together.

steps.do: Season the sauce with the fine salt and a few drops of lemon juice, then fold in the chopped tarragon and chervil. Keep the bowl over the saucepan with the heat OFF, or pour the sauce into a warmed thermos, at about 130°F (55°C). Use within an hour.
steps.look: Flecked green, glossy and pale gold, with a clean aniseed smell; a thin coat clings to the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Holding the sauce over live heat, where it creeps hotter and splits, or letting it go cold, where the butter sets and it turns stiff.
steps.fix: If it stiffens, whisk in a teaspoon of warm water; if it is too thick, the same. If it is too thin, it is too warm: take it off and whisk a minute.

steps.do: Sear the steaks: heat the cast iron pan over high heat until a drop of water skitters and vanishes, 4 to 5 minutes. Add the oil, swirl, then lay the steaks in away from you. Leave them untouched for 2 minutes, then turn every minute, holding them on their fat edges for 1 minute too, until a deep brown crust forms.
steps.look: A loud, steady sizzle the moment the meat lands and a smell of roasting beef; the crust is mahogany, not black, and releases easily from the pan.
steps.mistake: Moving the steaks the moment they touch the pan, or putting them into a pan that is not hot, so they grey and stew in their own juice.
steps.fix: Wait until the pan is really hot and the steak is dry. If they stick, give them another 30 seconds: a crust that is ready lets go by itself.

steps.do: When the probe in the thickest part reads about 115°F (46°C), turn the heat to medium, add the butter, thyme and garlic, tilt the pan and spoon the foaming butter over the steaks continuously for 1 minute. Take them out at 125°F (52°C) for medium rare. Note: the official guideline for whole cuts of beef is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest, if you prefer it well cooked.
steps.look: The butter foams and browns lightly and smells nutty and herby; the crust darkens a shade and glistens.
steps.mistake: Letting the butter burn black, which gives the meat a bitter coat.
steps.fix: Basting butter should be nut brown; if it starts to smoke heavily, pour it off and add a fresh tablespoon.

steps.do: Rest the steaks on a rack over a plate for 8 to 10 minutes. The internal temperature will rise 5 to 7°F (3 to 4°C) by carryover to about 130 to 132°F (54 to 56°C).
steps.look: When you finally slice, the meat is evenly pink edge to edge under the crust and only a little juice runs onto the board.
steps.mistake: Slicing at once, so the juice floods the board and the meat looks grey and wet.
steps.fix: Use the rest time to fry the frites; the steak stays hot enough for 10 minutes uncovered.

steps.do: Second fry: raise the oil to 375°F (190°C). Fry the blanched frites in two or three batches for 2 to 3 minutes each until deep golden and crisp, then lift onto paper or a rack and salt them at once while they glisten.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling that slows as the water is driven out; the frites rattle against each other on the spider and sound hollow and crisp.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pot, so the oil temperature crashes and the frites soak up oil and turn soft.
steps.fix: Fry smaller batches and wait for the thermometer to return to 375°F (190°C) each time. Hold finished frites in a 200°F (95°C) oven on the rack for a few minutes if needed.

steps.do: Slice each steak against the grain into slices 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick, season the cut faces with a pinch of flaky salt and pepper, and plate with a pile of frites and a generous spoon of béarnaise on the side or in a small warm ramekin.
steps.look: Clean slices that fan neatly; the sauce holds its shape on the plate rather than running into the frites.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sauce over the frites, which softens them in seconds.
steps.fix: Serve the sauce beside the meat or in a ramekin; dip, do not drown.

dishes.science: Béarnaise is an emulsion: tiny droplets of butterfat suspended in a little water, held apart by lecithin and proteins from the yolk. The reduction supplies the water, and that water matters, because diluted yolk proteins set at a higher temperature than neat yolk, so the sauce can be warmed to about 149°F (65°C) for body without curdling. Add fat faster than the yolks can coat it and the droplets merge and the sauce breaks. Clarified butter has no water or milk solids, so it gives a thicker, more stable sauce. A hard sear works through the Maillard reaction, which needs a dry surface well above the boiling point of water; that is why the steak is salted ahead and dried. Frites are blanched at low heat to cook the starch, then fried hot to drive surface water out and set a rigid, crisp crust.
dishes.plating: Use warm, wide plates. Lay the sliced steak slightly fanned across the front third of the plate, cut faces up so the pink shows. Pile the frites high behind it to the left, never under the meat, which would steam them. Set the béarnaise in a warm small ramekin at two o'clock, or spoon a neat quenelle beside the steak. Finish the meat with a few grains of flaky salt and a single tarragon leaf on the sauce.

pairing.drink: A red Bordeaux or a Côtes du Rhône with soft tannins: enough structure for the beef, and fruit that does not fight the tarragon and vinegar in the sauce.
pairing.brennans: Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak: on the Brennan's menu the hanger steak is served with a French béarnaise, the very sauce you make here, so you can describe its texture and tarragon edge from your own pan.

variations: Sauce Choron: whisk 1 tbsp (15 g) of thick tomato purée, cooked down until dry, into the finished béarnaise.
Sauce Foyot: whisk 1 tbsp (15 ml) of warm meat glaze or very reduced beef stock into the finished béarnaise for a darker, meatier sauce.
Oven frites: toss the soaked, dried batons in 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil and roast on a tray at 450°F (230°C) for 35 to 40 minutes, turning twice, when a deep fryer is not practical.
safety: The yolks in béarnaise reach about 149°F (65°C), not the 160°F (71°C) that fully cooks eggs; use pasteurised eggs for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or unwell.
Keep béarnaise warm for no longer than about an hour, then discard it: it sits at a temperature where bacteria grow.
Never leave hot oil unattended, keep the pot no more than half full, and have a lid ready to smother a fire. Never use water on an oil fire.
Beef steaks: the official guideline is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; medium rare is a choice for whole, intact steaks only, never minced beef.

dishes.title: New Orleans Barbecue Shrimp
dishes.summary: Head-on Gulf shrimp cooked fast in a peppery Worcestershire, garlic and rosemary base, then finished with cold butter swirled in off the heat until the sauce is glossy and clings. It follows the béarnaise because mounting butter into a hot, acidic liquid is the same emulsion lesson without an egg to help you.
skills: mounting cold butter to an emulsion
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan or skillet that can go to the table
Whisk or a wooden spoon
Small bowl for the cubed butter, kept in the fridge
Bread knife and a board
Small saucepan for warming stock or beer

ingredients.item: Large head-on Gulf shrimp, shell on
ingredients.note: the heads carry the flavour; keep them on

ingredients.item: Unsalted butter, cold, cut into 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes
ingredients.note: keep chilled until the last minute
really coarse: crush in a mortar
check its salt before adding more
juice of half, the rest in wedges

ingredients.item: Hot sauce (a Louisiana style vinegar hot sauce)

mise: Rinse the shrimp in cold water, drain well and pat dry; keep them in the fridge until the pan is hot. Pull off the thin legs if they are long, but leave heads and shells on.
Cube the cold butter and return the bowl to the fridge.
Slice the garlic, crack the pepper coarsely, juice half the lemon and cut the other half into wedges.
Measure the Worcestershire, beer and hot sauce into a small jug.
Warm the bread in a 300°F (150°C) oven for 8 minutes just before serving; set out finger bowls and plenty of napkins.

timeline.do: Prepare the shrimp, butter, garlic and liquids.
Bread into the oven. Heat the pan and build the pepper and garlic base.
Shrimp into the pan, 2 minutes a side.
Off the heat, swirl in the cold butter.
Pan straight to the table with bread and lemon.

steps.do: Set the frying pan over medium heat with the 1 tbsp (14 g) butter and the olive oil. When the butter foams, add the garlic, cracked pepper, rosemary and Creole seasoning and stir for 45 seconds to 1 minute.
steps.look: The garlic turns pale gold at the edges and the pan smells of pepper and pine; the butter is foaming but not brown.
steps.mistake: Cooking the garlic until brown, which turns it bitter and spoils the sauce.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat as soon as the garlic is pale gold and pour in the liquids to stop the cooking.

steps.do: Pour in the Worcestershire, beer, lemon juice and hot sauce. Bring to a lively simmer and let it bubble for 2 minutes to reduce by about a third.
steps.look: A dark, fragrant, slightly syrupy liquid; the alcohol smell of the beer fades and the pan smells savoury and tangy.
steps.mistake: Reducing until almost dry, which leaves too little liquid to hold the butter later and makes it bitter and salty.
steps.fix: If it looks dry, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water or stock; you want about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of liquid in the pan.

steps.do: Raise the heat to medium high and add the shrimp in a single layer. Cook 2 minutes, spooning the liquid over them constantly, then turn each one and cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes more.
steps.look: The shells go from grey to bright coral pink and the flesh at the cut end turns from translucent to opaque white; the shrimp curl into a loose C.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until the shrimp curl tight into an O, which makes them rubbery and makes the heads hard to suck.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat the moment the last grey patches turn pink; the shrimp keep cooking in the hot sauce.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and let it stand 30 seconds so the bubbling stops. Add the cold butter cubes a handful at a time, swirling the pan and stirring constantly, and add the next handful only when the last has nearly melted.
steps.look: The thin dark liquid turns into a creamy, glossy, opaque sauce that coats the shrimp and the spoon; it should look like a loose gravy, not an oil slick.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter over high heat or all at once, so it melts into clear grease that floats on top of the sauce.
steps.fix: Take the pan off completely, add a splash, 1 tbsp (15 ml), of cold water or beer and whisk hard; a broken sauce often comes back. Keep the rest of the butter cold.

steps.do: Taste the sauce on a piece of bread and adjust with a pinch of salt, a little more lemon or a dash of hot sauce. Remove the rosemary stalks.
steps.look: The sauce tastes buttery first, then peppery heat, then a tang from the lemon and Worcestershire; no single note shouts.
steps.mistake: Salting before tasting, when the Creole seasoning and Worcestershire already carry plenty.
steps.fix: If it is too salty, add a few more cubes of cold butter and a squeeze of lemon off the heat.

steps.do: Carry the pan straight to the table on a board with the warm bread, lemon wedges and napkins. Each person peels their own shrimp, squeezes the head juices into the sauce and mops with the bread.
steps.look: A glossy sauce that still clings to the shrimp after a minute or two at the table.
steps.mistake: Letting the pan sit on the heat while people gather, which overcooks the shrimp and splits the butter.
steps.fix: Serve at once; if the sauce starts to separate at the table, swirl the pan and stir in a spoon of warm water.

dishes.science: Butter is already an emulsion of fat in water held by milk proteins. Melted slowly into a small amount of hot liquid, the milk proteins and the gelatin and proteins that leak from the shrimp heads coat the fat droplets and keep them suspended, so the sauce turns opaque and creamy. If the pan is too hot, the butter melts all at once, the water boils away and the fat droplets merge into a clear layer. That is why the pan comes off the heat and the butter goes in cold and gradually: each piece softens rather than melting instantly. Shrimp protein sets between about 120 and 140°F (49 and 60°C); past that, the muscle fibres squeeze out water and turn tough, which is why the cooking time is so short. The fat in the heads carries the deepest shellfish flavour.
dishes.plating: Serve family style in the pan it was cooked in, set on a wooden board. Arrange the shrimp so the heads point outward around the edge and the sauce pools in the centre. Scatter a few torn rosemary needles and a twist of black pepper over the top. Pile the warm bread, sliced on the bias, in a basket beside it, with lemon wedges and a bowl for shells.

pairing.drink: A cold amber lager, or a crisp, slightly fuller white such as a dry Chenin Blanc; both cut through the butter and can stand up to the pepper.
pairing.brennans: Louisiana BBQ Lobster: on the Brennan's tasting menu the lobster gets the same New Orleans barbecue treatment, so cooking this teaches you what that sauce is and why it is not barbecue at all.

variations: Peeled shrimp version: peel the shrimp but simmer the shells and heads in 1 cup (240 ml) water for 15 minutes, strain and use 1/3 cup (80 ml) of this stock instead of the beer.
Over grits: serve the shrimp and sauce over creamy stone-ground grits for a main course that needs no bread.
Crawfish tails: in season, use 1 lb (450 g) peeled crawfish tails, cooked for only 2 minutes in total.
safety: Keep raw shrimp cold, below 40°F (4°C), until the moment they go in the pan, and cook within a day of buying.
Shrimp are cooked when the flesh is opaque and pearly all the way through, about 120 to 145°F (49 to 63°C); discard any that smell of ammonia before cooking.

dishes.title: Bacalao al Pil Pil
dishes.summary: Thick loins of salt cod, desalted over two days, poached gently in garlic and chilli oil and served under an ivory sauce made only of that oil and the gelatine the fish releases. It is in the course because it is the purest emulsion there is: no egg, no flour, no butter, only temperature, patience and a swirling hand.
skills: swirling until the fish gelatine emulsifies the oil
equipment: Large non-reactive container with a lid, for desalting
Wide, shallow terracotta cazuela or a heavy 10 inch (25 cm) sauté pan with sloping sides
Instant read thermometer
Heatproof jug of at least 2 cups (500 ml)
Fish slice or wide spatula
Small sieve or tea strainer
Clean tea towel and kitchen paper

ingredients.item: Salt cod loin, thick centre cut, skin on
ingredients.note: weight before soaking; ask for 'lomo' cut at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick

ingredients.item: Mild olive oil (Arbequina or a soft Picual)
Dried guindilla chilli or a small dried red chilli
ingredients.note: cut in rings, seeds shaken out

ingredients.item: Flat leaf parsley, very finely chopped

mise: Two days ahead: rinse the salt off the cod under cold running water, then lay the pieces skin side up in the container, cover with plenty of cold water and refrigerate.
Change the water every 8 to 12 hours, four or five times in all, keeping it in the fridge throughout.
After 36 hours, taste a flake from the thickest part: it should taste pleasantly seasoned, like well salted cooked fish, never briny. Give it more soaking if needed.
On the day, lift the cod out and dry it thoroughly on a clean tea towel, skin side down, for 15 minutes; pat the top with kitchen paper.
Slice the garlic and the chilli; chop the parsley; warm the serving plates in a low oven.

timeline.do: Rinse the cod and start soaking it in the fridge.
Change the water.
Lift the cod out, taste it and dry it.
Fry the garlic and chilli in the oil; let the oil cool to 140°F (60°C).
Poach the cod skin side down for 6 to 8 minutes.
Lift out the cod, cool the oil, build the pil pil by swirling.
Return the cod, warm through gently, garnish and serve.

steps.do: Put the oil, garlic and chilli in the cold cazuela and set it over low heat. Cook gently, moving the slices around, for 4 to 6 minutes until the garlic turns pale straw gold and starts to float. Lift the garlic and chilli out with the sieve onto kitchen paper.
steps.look: Small, slow bubbles around the garlic; it smells sweet and nutty, never acrid.
steps.mistake: Letting the garlic go brown, which makes the oil bitter and the finished sauce taste burnt.
steps.fix: Lift it out at pale gold; it keeps colouring for a few seconds out of the oil. If it burns, strain the oil and start with fresh garlic.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and let the oil cool until it reads 140 to 150°F (60 to 65°C) on the thermometer, about 5 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: The surface is still and calm; a drop of water flicked in barely sizzles.
steps.mistake: Adding the cod to hot oil straight after frying the garlic, which seizes the protein so the fish weeps water rather than gelatine.
steps.fix: Wait for the thermometer. If you overshoot downward, set the pan back on the lowest heat for a minute.

steps.do: Slide the cod in skin side DOWN. Keep the pan over the lowest heat, adjusting by moving it on and off the burner so the oil stays at 140 to 150°F (60 to 65°C), and poach for 6 to 8 minutes. Gently shake the pan side to side every minute or so.
steps.look: A bead of oil breaks the surface only every few seconds; a milky white curd starts to weep from under the skin and collect around the fish.
steps.mistake: Letting the oil bubble steadily, which tightens the fish, drives out water and gives you nothing to emulsify.
steps.fix: Lift the pan off the heat the moment it starts to bubble and let it settle for a minute before carrying on.

steps.do: Turn the pieces over very gently with the fish slice and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, skin up, until the flakes shift when nudged at the thickest part. Lift the cod onto a warm plate, skin side up.
steps.look: The flesh has turned opaque white and separates into large, glossy flakes under gentle pressure; a probe in the centre reads about 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C).
steps.mistake: Breaking the loins apart while turning, so they fall to pieces.
steps.fix: Use a wide slice under the whole piece and support the top with a spoon; if a piece breaks, plate it skin side up and push it back together.

steps.do: Pour the oil carefully into the jug, leaving every bit of the milky deposit in the pan. Let the pan and the oil cool until both are only hand warm, about 95 to 105°F (35 to 40°C).
steps.look: A pale, sticky, cloudy film of gelatine and juices coats the base of the pan; it is the whole sauce, so do not wipe it out.
steps.mistake: Pouring the deposit out with the oil, leaving nothing to build the sauce on.
steps.fix: Pour slowly and stop the moment the cloudy layer reaches the lip; any that slipped into the jug will settle and can be spooned back.

steps.do: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil back to the pan. Holding the handle, swirl the pan flat on the worktop or just above it in slow, steady circles, continuously, so the oil and gelatine move together. After a minute or two, as it turns opaque, dribble in more oil a teaspoon at a time while swirling, then a thin thread, until you have used about two thirds of the oil.
steps.look: The mixture goes from clear and separated to cloudy, then ivory and glossy, thickening until it coats the back of a spoon like a loose mayonnaise. You will hear a soft sticky slapping sound as it thickens.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon or whisking hard, which shears the droplets and can break the sauce, or adding oil faster than it is taken up.
steps.fix: If the sauce goes thin and oily, stop adding oil, pour out the excess and keep swirling the base; add a spoon of the juice that has collected under the resting cod. A small sieve tapped in a circular motion through the sauce also works, the Basque trick.

steps.do: Return the cod to the pan skin side up, along with any juice from the plate. Set the pan over the lowest heat for 1 to 2 minutes, swirling, just to warm the fish through without heating the sauce above about 120°F (49°C).
steps.look: The sauce laps over the fish and clings to it; it stays thick and ivory.
steps.mistake: Heating the pan too much at this stage, which melts the emulsion back into oil.
steps.fix: Keep it barely warm; if it starts to thin, take it off the heat and swirl until it thickens again.

steps.do: Taste the sauce and add a pinch of flaky salt only if needed. Scatter the reserved garlic, chilli and a little parsley over the top and serve straight from the cazuela, with bread.
steps.look: White flakes under a smooth, pale sauce studded with gold garlic and red chilli.
steps.mistake: Salting automatically, when the cod may still carry plenty.
steps.fix: Taste first; if it is too salty, serve with plain boiled potatoes and more bread and soak the next batch longer.

dishes.science: Salt cod skin and connective tissue are rich in collagen. Held in oil at about 140 to 150°F (60 to 65°C), some of that collagen dissolves into gelatine and leaks out with the fish's juices as a cloudy deposit. Gelatine and soluble fish proteins are surface active: they can wrap tiny droplets of oil and keep them from merging, which is exactly what an egg yolk does in mayonnaise. Swirling breaks the oil into small droplets slowly and evenly, while a whisk or high heat breaks the protein coating and lets the droplets coalesce. Too hot during poaching and the proteins tighten and squeeze out water rather than gel. Desalting works by diffusion: salt moves from the fish into the surrounding fresh water, and changing the water keeps that gradient steep.
dishes.plating: This dish is served in its cazuela, which holds the heat and the drama. If plating individually, warm shallow bowls, spoon a pool of pil pil in the centre, set a loin on top skin side up and nap more sauce over it so it runs down the sides. Lay three or four slices of golden garlic and a ring of chilli on top and a tiny pinch of parsley at one edge. Keep the bread on the side.

pairing.drink: A Txakoli from the Basque coast, slightly spritzy and very fresh, or a dry Albariño; their acidity cuts the olive oil and their salinity matches the cod.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: a crisp Galician Albariño from the Brennan's list, from the same Atlantic coast as the Basque fishing ports and made for cod in olive oil.

variations: Bacalao a la Vizcaína: serve the poached cod in a sauce of soaked choricero peppers and slow cooked onion instead of pil pil.
Fresh hake al pil pil: use thick, skin-on hake steaks lightly salted for 20 minutes; the gelatine is less but the method is the same.
With potatoes: slice 1 lb (450 g) boiled waxy potatoes into the cazuela before returning the cod, for a fuller supper.
safety: Soak the salt cod in the fridge, below 40°F (4°C), not on the counter, and change the water regularly.

Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C) by the official guideline; the cod here is poached gently to about 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) in the traditional way, so use fish that has been salted and stored properly and serve it at once.

dishes.title: Sole Meunière
dishes.summary: A whole Dover sole, skinned by hand, dredged lightly in flour, cooked on the bone in butter and served under a nut brown butter with lemon and parsley, filleted at the table. It moves you from portions to whole fish: skinning, cooking on the bone and lifting four clean fillets in front of a guest.
equipment: Large oval fish pan, or two 12 inch (30 cm) frying pans, one per fish
Sturdy kitchen scissors
Flexible filleting knife and a small sharp knife
Clean dry cloth or kitchen paper for gripping the skin
Shallow tray for the flour
Two fish slices or a wide offset spatula
Two dinner forks or a fish knife and fork for filleting at the table
Small saucepan for the brown butter
Instant read thermometer

ingredients.note: or whole lemon sole, plaice or flounder; ask the fishmonger to skin the dark side if you are nervous the first time
for dredging; you will use far less
juice of 1, the half cut into wedges

mise: Trim the fins all round each fish with scissors, cutting close to the body, and snip off the tail fin square. Cut off the head on the diagonal behind the gills if your pan is small; otherwise leave it on.

Skin the dark side: lay the fish dark side up, tail towards you. Make a shallow cut across the skin just above the tail, scrape a flap of skin loose with the knife tip, then salt your fingers, grip the flap in a cloth, hold the tail down firmly with the other hand and pull the skin back towards the head in one steady movement.
Turn the fish over and scale the white side with the back of a knife, or skin it too if you prefer; rinse briefly and pat completely dry.
Spread the flour in the tray, juice the lemon, chop the parsley, dry the capers.
Warm two dinner plates and a serving platter in a low oven at 200°F (95°C).

timeline.do: Trim, skin and dry the fish; prepare garnishes.
Heat the pans; season and dredge the fish.
Cook the fish 4 to 5 minutes a side; move to the warm platter.
Make the beurre noisette, add lemon and parsley.
Pour the butter over the fish at the table and fillet.

steps.do: Pat the skinned fish dry again on both sides. Season both sides with the 1 tsp (5 g) salt and the white pepper, then lay each fish in the flour, press lightly for 2 seconds, turn and coat, then lift by the tail and tap it firmly to shake off every bit of loose flour.
steps.look: A thin, even, almost translucent dusting, like a fine film; no clumps or wet patches showing through.
steps.mistake: Flouring too early, so the flour soaks up moisture and turns into a gummy paste that sticks to the pan.
steps.fix: Dredge only in the last minute before the fish goes into the pan; if it has gone pasty, wipe it, dry it and flour again.

steps.do: Heat the clarified butter in the fish pan over medium high heat until it shimmers and a pinch of flour sizzles at once, about 2 minutes. Lay the fish in, skinned side DOWN, laying it away from you.
steps.look: An immediate, even sizzle along the whole length of the fish; the fat bubbles gently around the edges.
steps.mistake: Laying the fish into fat that is not hot enough, so the flour absorbs it and turns greasy instead of crisp.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer and test with a pinch of flour before the fish goes in; if the pan cools too much, turn the heat up a notch for the first minute.

steps.do: Cook without moving for 4 to 5 minutes, shaking the pan gently once or twice so the fish slides, until the underside is evenly golden. Turn it carefully with two fish slices and cook the second side 3 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: A crisp, golden brown crust with darker lacy edges; the fish moves freely when the pan is shaken.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, so the crust tears and sticks.
steps.fix: If it resists, give it another 30 to 60 seconds. A crust that is properly set releases on its own.

steps.do: Check doneness by sliding the tip of a small knife along the backbone at the thickest point: the flesh should lift slightly from the bone and be opaque white all the way through. A probe at the thickest part reads 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C); it rises a few degrees on the platter. Lift the fish onto the warm platter, best side up.
steps.look: White, moist flesh that just comes away from the central bone; no translucent grey near the spine.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until the flesh is dry and the fillets crumble when you try to lift them.
steps.fix: Sole is thin: take it off as soon as the flesh near the bone turns opaque. Better a touch under, finished by the hot butter, than dry.

steps.do: Wipe out the pan, or use the small saucepan. Add the 6 tbsp (85 g) cubed butter over medium heat and let it melt and foam, swirling the pan, for 2 to 4 minutes.
steps.look: First loud foaming, then the foam quietens and the bubbles shrink; the milk solids on the bottom turn golden then hazelnut brown and the butter smells of toasted nuts and biscuits.
steps.mistake: Looking away during the quiet moment, so the butter goes from brown to black and bitter in seconds.
steps.fix: The moment the foam quietens, stand and watch. When it is hazelnut brown, take it off the heat immediately; if it has gone black and smells acrid, throw it away and start again.

steps.do: Off the heat, within 10 seconds of the butter turning hazelnut, add the capers (if using), then the 2 tbsp (30 ml) lemon juice; stand back, as it will spit and foam. Swirl in the parsley.
steps.look: A violent hiss, then a foaming, glossy brown butter with green flecks; it smells of nuts and lemon.
steps.mistake: Adding the lemon while the pan is still over high heat, which can make it spit dangerously and burn the solids.
steps.fix: Always off the heat, and add the juice at arm's length.

steps.do: At the table, within 30 seconds of making it, pour the foaming butter over the fish so it sizzles. To fillet: run a fork or fish knife down the central line of the fish to the bone. Push the two top fillets out to each side with the flat of the knife, then lift the whole skeleton away from the tail end, using the fork to hold the lower fillets. Lay the top fillets back over the bottom ones, or serve all four side by side.
steps.look: Four neat fillets with no bones; the skeleton comes away in one piece, with the small fin bones along the edges.
steps.mistake: Digging into the fish so the fillets break into flakes and bones go onto the plate.
steps.fix: Work with flat blades and light pressure. Scrape away the fringe of fin bones along each edge before lifting the fillets; check each with a fork before serving.

dishes.science: Flour on a wet fish surface draws in water and forms a thin starch layer that gelatinises and browns quickly in hot fat, giving a crisp coat and protecting the delicate protein underneath. Too much flour or flour left to sit forms a paste instead. Cooking on the bone slows heat reaching the centre and the gelatin rich bone and skin keep the flesh moist. Beurre noisette is butter whose water has boiled off; once the foam quietens the milk proteins and sugars sit in hot fat well above the boiling point of water and brown through Maillard reactions, creating nutty, toasty aromas. Lemon juice stops the browning by dropping the temperature sharply and adds acidity that balances the richness. Dover sole holds together well because its muscle is firm and its proteins set evenly.
dishes.plating: For individual plates, lay the four fillets slightly overlapping in a line down the centre of a warm oval plate, the larger fillets underneath. Spoon the foaming brown butter over so every fillet glistens, and let a little pool on the plate. Scatter the capers and parsley, add a lemon wedge at the side, and set three small buttered potatoes at one end. Wipe the plate rim before it goes.

pairing.drink: A white Burgundy or a Chablis: the crisp acidity matches the lemon, and the gentle richness of Chardonnay sits beside the brown butter.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Louis Michel ‘Montmains’ Chablis Premier Cru 2023 (375 ml): a half bottle of Premier Cru Chablis from the Brennan's list, the classic white for sole in brown butter.

variations: Fillets: use 4 sole or flounder fillets of 4 oz (115 g) each and cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes per side; the brown butter is the same.
Sole amandine: toast 1/4 cup (25 g) flaked almonds in the butter as it browns.
Trout meunière: use two whole trout, cooked 5 to 6 minutes a side, a classic New Orleans brasserie dish as well.
safety: Keep the fish refrigerated until it is prepared and cook it within a day of buying.

Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C) by the official guideline; sole is traditionally taken off just as it turns opaque at the bone, around 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C), and finishes under the hot butter.
Lemon juice added to hot butter spits violently: add it off the heat and keep your face back.

dishes.title: Branzino in Salt Crust
dishes.summary: Two whole sea bass, scaled and gutted at home, sealed in a crust of coarse salt and egg white and baked until a probe pushed through the crust reads the right temperature, then cracked open and filleted at the table. It teaches the preparation of a round fish and cooking something you cannot see, by thermometer alone.
skills: a salt and egg white crust
judging doneness through the crust by probe
equipment: Large rimmed baking tray, at least 16 by 12 inches (40 by 30 cm), or an ovenproof serving platter
Fish scaler or the back of a heavy knife
Sharp kitchen scissors and a small sharp knife
Large mixing bowl
Instant read probe thermometer with a long, thin stem
Wooden spoon or small hammer for cracking the crust
Pastry brush
Two serving forks or a fish knife and fork
Large plastic bag or deep sink for scaling

ingredients.note: or one 2 1/2 lb (1.1 kg) fish; or dorade or snapper. Ask for them whole and ungutted if you want the practice

ingredients.item: Coarse sea salt or kosher salt
ingredients.note: the cheapest coarse salt is fine; not fine table salt
as needed to make it like wet sand
1 sliced for the cavities, 1 in wedges to serve

ingredients.item: Fennel fronds, thyme or flat parsley

mise: Scale the fish inside a large plastic bag or deep sink to catch the flying scales: hold the tail and scrape from tail to head with the scaler, both sides, around the belly and near the fins. Rinse.

Gut the fish: insert the scissors into the vent near the tail and cut forward along the belly to just behind the gills. Pull out the innards, scrape out the dark bloodline along the spine with a teaspoon, and cut out the red gills with scissors. Rinse the cavity under cold water and pat the fish completely dry inside and out.
Trim the sharp dorsal fins with scissors to make the fish easier to wrap and handle.
Stuff each cavity with lemon slices, herbs and garlic; do not overfill.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a shelf in the middle, for 20 minutes.
Make the salmoriglio: whisk the oil, lemon juice, oregano, parsley and a pinch of salt; set aside.

timeline.do: Scale, gut and dry the fish; heat the oven.
Mix the salt crust; pack the fish in it.
Bake; begin probing at 20 minutes.
Out when the probe reads 135°F (57°C); rest in the crust 5 minutes.
Crack the crust at the table, lift the skin, fillet and dress.

steps.do: In the large bowl, beat the egg whites until frothy, then work them into the salt with your hands. Add the 1/4 cup (60 ml) water a tablespoon at a time until the mixture holds together when squeezed, like wet sand for building a sandcastle.
steps.look: A damp, mouldable mass that keeps its shape when pressed in your fist and does not drip.
steps.mistake: Making it too wet, so it slumps off the fish and bakes into a soggy layer that sticks to the skin.
steps.fix: Add more salt a handful at a time until it holds a firm shape.

steps.do: Spread a bed of the salt mixture 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick on the tray, roughly the shape of the fish and a little larger. Lay the fish on it. Pack the rest over and around, pressing firmly, so the fish is completely sealed with a layer about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick; leave the tail exposed if you like as a handle and a visual guide.
steps.look: Two smooth white mounds with no cracks or gaps where skin shows through.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so steam escapes and the flesh near the gap dries out and becomes salty.
steps.fix: Patch any thin spots with extra mixture and smooth with a wet hand.

steps.do: Bake in the middle of the oven. After 20 minutes, push the thermometer through the crust into the thickest part of the back, just behind the head, until it reaches the bone, then pull it back a fraction. Bake until it reads 135°F (57°C), usually 25 to 30 minutes for 1 1/4 lb (560 g) fish, 35 to 40 minutes for one 2 1/2 lb (1.1 kg) fish.
steps.look: The crust turns hard, pale gold at the edges and slightly cracked; a sweet smell of herbs and steamed fish escapes from the probe hole.
steps.mistake: Cooking by the clock alone, when fish sizes and ovens vary, and ending with dry or raw flesh.
steps.fix: The probe is the only judge here. If unsure, check two places. Pull it a few degrees early rather than late: carryover in the crust is significant.

steps.do: Take the tray out and let it rest 5 minutes. The temperature inside will climb to about 140 to 145°F (60 to 63°C).
steps.look: The probe reading climbs steadily for a few minutes, then levels off.
steps.mistake: Cracking the crust immediately, losing the gentle carryover that finishes the centre.
steps.fix: Use the five minutes to set the table, warm the plates and bring the salmoriglio.

steps.do: Bring the tray to the table. Crack the crust all round, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) up from the tray, with the back of a heavy spoon, then lift it off in large slabs and put them aside on a board. Brush any loose salt off the fish with the pastry brush.
steps.look: The crust breaks in satisfying slabs; the skin often comes away with it, revealing white, glossy, steaming flesh.
steps.mistake: Letting salt crumbs fall onto the flesh, which makes bites salty.
steps.fix: Lift slabs away from the fish rather than over it; brush thoroughly and peel off any remaining skin with a fork before filleting.

steps.do: Fillet: run a knife along the lateral line from head to tail, then slide a fork and spoon under the top fillets and ease them off the bones in two pieces. Lift the backbone away from the tail end in one piece, taking the head with it. Check the bottom fillet for pin bones and lift it off the skin.
steps.look: Moist, white flesh that separates in large flakes from the bone; the spine lifts cleanly.
steps.mistake: Pressing down hard so the flesh breaks up and mixes with bones.
steps.fix: Work gently with flat utensils; if the flesh clings, it may be a little under, so return the exposed fish to the oven for 3 minutes.

steps.do: Plate two fillets per person on warm plates, spoon about 1 tbsp (15 ml) of salmoriglio over each portion and serve with lemon wedges within 5 minutes of opening the crust.
steps.look: Pearly fillets glistening with green flecked oil.
steps.mistake: Seasoning heavily with more salt, when the crust has already seasoned the skin side gently.
steps.fix: Taste a flake first, then add a pinch of flaky salt only if needed.

dishes.science: The salt crust works as a sealed, insulating oven within the oven. It slows the heat reaching the fish, so the flesh cooks evenly from edge to centre rather than overcooking outside before the middle is done, and it traps the fish's own moisture so it steams gently. Very little salt passes through the skin in this time because salt needs water to dissolve and move, and the skin acts as a barrier. Egg white proteins set into a firm network as they bake, binding the salt grains into a hard shell that cracks off in slabs. Because the crust holds so much heat, the internal temperature keeps rising after the tray leaves the oven, so the fish is pulled early. Whole fish cooked on the bone stay moister because the bone and skin limit moisture loss.
dishes.plating: Present the cracked crust at the table first: it is the show. Then plate on warm white plates: two fillets per person, laid slightly overlapping at an angle, the best side up. Spoon the salmoriglio over the fish and a little onto the plate. Add a lemon wedge and a small sprig of fennel frond. Simple sides such as boiled potatoes in olive oil or a green salad go on a separate plate.

pairing.drink: A mineral, saline white such as Assyrtiko from Santorini, Vermentino or Greco di Tufo; they mirror the sea and the lemon.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: a salty, citrus driven Greek white from the Brennan's list, a natural match for a whole fish baked in salt.

variations: Herb salt crust: mix 3 tbsp (10 g) chopped rosemary and the zest of 2 lemons into the salt for an aromatic crust.
Snapper or dorade: use the same method; a 2 lb (900 g) red snapper takes about 30 to 35 minutes.
Salt baked celeriac: a whole 2 lb (900 g) celeriac in the same crust bakes in 90 minutes at 400°F (200°C) for a vegetable side or main.
safety: Wash the board, knife and sink with hot soapy water after gutting raw fish, and wash your hands.
The official guideline for fish is 145°F (63°C); pull at 135°F (57°C) and the rest in the crust carries the centre up to about 140 to 145°F (60 to 63°C).
Egg white binds the salt; the crust is not eaten.

dishes.title: Chả Cá Lã Vọng
dishes.summary: Hanoi's turmeric fish: a whole firm white fish filleted at home, cut into even chunks, marinated in turmeric, galangal and fish sauce, fried until golden and then tossed at the table with armfuls of dill and spring onion over rice noodles. It follows the whole fish lessons because you now fillet a round fish yourself and portion it into pieces that hold together through two cookings.
equipment: Flexible filleting knife and a heavy chef's knife
Fish tweezers or clean small pliers for pin bones
Large chopping board with a damp cloth underneath
Mortar and pestle or a small food processor
Non-reactive bowl for marinating
12 inch (30 cm) non-stick or well seasoned frying pan
Second pan or a tabletop burner for the dill toss
Large saucepan for the noodles and a colander
Fish slice, chopsticks or tongs

ingredients.item: Whole firm white fish (catfish, monkfish, snakehead, hake or cod)
ingredients.us: 1 fish, about 3 lb, or 1 1/2 lb skinless fillets
ingredients.metric: 1 fish, about 1.4 kg, or 700 g skinless fillets

ingredients.note: ginger will do, but loses the piney note

ingredients.item: Fermented shrimp paste (mắm tôm) or extra fish sauce
ingredients.note: traditional and pungent; optional in the marinade

ingredients.item: Dill, thick stalks removed, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) lengths
ingredients.note: the dill is a vegetable here, not a garnish

ingredients.item: Spring onions, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) lengths
Fresh herbs: coriander, mint, Thai basil

ingredients.note: 1 for the dipping sauce, 1 in wedges

ingredients.item: Fish sauce, for the dipping sauce

mise: Fillet the fish if whole: lay it on its side, cut behind the head down to the spine, then run the knife along the backbone from head to tail in long, smooth strokes, keeping the blade angled flat against the bones. Lift the fillet, turn the fish and repeat.

Skin each fillet: lay it skin down, tail end towards you, cut down to the skin at the tail, then hold the skin firmly and push the knife forward with the blade angled slightly down, wiggling the skin side to side.
Run your fingers along each fillet against the grain to find pin bones and pull them out with tweezers in the direction they point.
Cut the fillets into even pieces about 2 by 1 1/2 inches (5 by 4 cm) and 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick, so every piece cooks at the same rate.
Pound the turmeric, galangal, shallots and garlic to a paste; stir in the fish sauce, shrimp paste (if using) and sugar.
Make the dipping sauce: stir the water, fish sauce, sugar and juice of 1 lime until the sugar dissolves; add the chilli.
Wash and dry the dill and spring onions very well; pick the herbs; chop the peanuts.

timeline.do: Fillet, skin, pin bone and portion the fish.
Make the paste and marinate the fish in the fridge for 1 to 2 hours.
Cook the noodles, rinse and drain; make the dipping sauce; prepare herbs.
Fry the fish in batches until golden.
Toss the dill and spring onion with the fish at the table and serve.

steps.do: Toss the fish pieces with the paste in the non-reactive bowl until every piece is coated yellow. Cover and refrigerate for 1 to 2 hours, no longer.
steps.look: Bright golden yellow pieces with the paste clinging; the bowl smells earthy, gingery and savoury.
steps.mistake: Marinating overnight, so the salt in the fish sauce draws out moisture and the flesh turns firm and dry.
steps.fix: Keep it to 2 hours at most; if you must hold it longer, scrape off the paste and keep the fish covered and chilled.

steps.do: Cook the noodles: drop them into a large pan of boiling water and cook 3 to 5 minutes (follow the packet), until soft but springy. Drain, rinse under cold running water while lifting them with your fingers, drain well and arrange in small nests on a plate.
steps.look: White, separate strands that hold together in a nest without being sticky.
steps.mistake: Leaving them unrinsed, so the surface starch glues them into a solid mass.
steps.fix: Rinse thoroughly and shake them dry; a sticky nest loosens under a quick pour of hot water.

steps.do: Heat 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the oil in the frying pan over medium high heat until it shimmers, about 2 minutes. Lift the fish from the marinade, letting excess drip off, and lay half the pieces in a single layer, each with space around it.
steps.look: A steady sizzle as each piece goes in; the oil stays bubbling around the edges.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the fish steams, the paste slides off and the pieces stick together.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches; if the pan falls quiet, turn the heat up and wait for the sizzle to return before adding more.

steps.do: Fry undisturbed for 2 1/2 to 3 minutes until a golden crust forms underneath, then turn each piece once with chopsticks or a fish slice and fry another 2 to 3 minutes. Lift onto a plate. Repeat with the second batch.
steps.look: Deep golden brown on two sides with crisp, slightly charred edges; the flesh is opaque through and flakes under gentle pressure.
steps.mistake: Turning the fish repeatedly, which breaks the pieces apart.
steps.fix: Turn once only, when the crust releases by itself. Broken pieces still taste right: gather them together on the plate.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil, or move to a clean pan with 2 tbsp (30 ml) fresh oil, ideally on a tabletop burner. Heat over high heat, add the spring onions and half the dill and toss for 20 seconds, then return the fish and toss gently for another 30 seconds. Add the rest of the dill off the heat.
steps.look: The dill wilts and turns glossy dark green and the kitchen fills with an anise and grass smell; some leaves stay bright and fresh.
steps.mistake: Cooking the dill for minutes until it collapses into a dark, stringy mass.
steps.fix: Thirty seconds is enough; the residual heat finishes it. Keep half the dill raw for freshness.

steps.do: Serve at once: each person puts noodles in a bowl, adds fish and dill, then peanuts, fresh herbs, a squeeze of lime and a spoon of dipping sauce.
steps.look: Yellow fish, dark green dill, white noodles and a scatter of peanuts and herbs; the bowl smells of turmeric, dill and lime.
steps.mistake: Assembling the bowls in the kitchen ahead, so the noodles go cold and the fish softens.
steps.fix: Bring everything to the table and let people build their own, as it is eaten in Hanoi.

dishes.science: Turmeric's colour comes from curcumin, which dissolves in fat rather than water, so frying in oil blooms its colour and earthy flavour much more than poaching would. Galangal contains aromatic compounds that are pine-like and peppery, which is why ginger tastes softer in its place. Salt in the fish sauce dissolves some muscle proteins on the surface, which helps the paste cling and seasons the outer layer, but over many hours it pulls water out and firms the flesh, so the marinade is short. A firm, thick white fish has dense muscle with enough connective tissue to hold together through frying and a second toss. Dill's aroma is volatile and fades with long heat, so it is wilted briefly and part is left raw.
dishes.plating: Bring the frying pan to the table on a board, the golden fish heaped in the centre under a crown of dill and spring onion. Around it set a plate of noodle nests, a bowl of chopped peanuts, a plate of herbs and lime wedges, and a small bowl of dipping sauce per person. For a plated version, put a noodle nest in a warm bowl, lay five pieces of fish against it, top with a tangle of dill and scatter peanuts on one side only.

pairing.drink: A dry or off dry Riesling or a Grüner Veltliner: crisp acidity lifts the oily fish, and the aromatic grape matches the dill and turmeric.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Alte Reben’ Grüner Veltliner 2023: a peppery, fresh Austrian white from the Brennan's list that loves fresh herbs and bright spice.

variations: Salmon chả cá: use skinless salmon fillet, cut a little thicker, and fry for 2 minutes a side.
Shrimp paste dip: the traditional sauce is mắm tôm whisked with lime juice, sugar and a splash of hot oil until it foams; try it beside the fish sauce dip.
Lettuce wraps: serve with soft lettuce leaves and wrap fish, noodles and herbs at the table.
safety: Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C); the pieces are done when opaque and flaking in the centre.
Keep the marinating fish in the fridge, below 40°F (4°C).
Wash and dry the dill and herbs well: water in hot oil spits.

dishes.title: Shui Zhu Yu (Sichuan Water-Boiled Fish)
dishes.summary: Thin slices of white fish, velveted with egg white and starch, poached for a minute in a fiery broth of chilli bean paste and stock over a bed of vegetables, then crowned with dried chillies, Sichuan pepper and garlic and blasted with smoking oil at the table. It teaches slicing fish thin and velveting, the Chinese technique that keeps delicate protein silky, together with a hot oil finish you must handle with respect.
skills: velveting with egg white and starch
equipment: Very sharp chef's knife or a Chinese cleaver
Large chopping board
Wok, or a large deep frying pan
Small saucepan for the finishing oil
Large, deep heatproof serving bowl of at least 3 quarts (3 litres)
Spider or slotted spoon
Mortar and pestle or spice grinder
Instant read or deep fry thermometer

ingredients.item: Firm white fish fillets, skinless (sea bass, tilapia, cod, haddock or flounder)
ingredients.note: grass carp or black carp are traditional
or celtuce, napa cabbage or celery

ingredients.item: Napa cabbage, cut in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces

ingredients.note: half for the broth, half for the topping

ingredients.item: Spring onions, white parts cut in 1 inch (2.5 cm) lengths
Dried red chillies, snipped in 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces, seeds shaken out
Neutral oil, for the finishing pour

mise: Put the fish in the freezer for 15 to 20 minutes to firm it; this makes thin slicing much easier.

Toast the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns in a dry wok over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and the chillies are a shade darker, not black. Tip out to cool. Grind half the peppercorns and a quarter of the chillies coarsely; keep the rest whole.
Slice the fish: hold the knife at a 45 degree angle and cut slices 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick and about 2 by 3 inches (5 by 7.5 cm), slicing across the fillet so each piece is wide and flat.

Velvet: put the slices in a bowl with the salt, white pepper and Shaoxing wine and massage gently for 30 seconds. Add the egg white and mix until absorbed, then the cornflour, until each slice wears a thin, silky coat. Refrigerate while you make the broth.
Prepare the vegetables, ginger, garlic and spring onions; measure the stock, soy and sugar.
Clear a heatproof space on the table, on a board or trivet, for the serving bowl.

timeline.do: Firm the fish in the freezer; toast and grind the spices.
Slice and velvet the fish; refrigerate.
Blanch the vegetables into the serving bowl.
Fry the bean paste, build and simmer the broth.
Poach the fish, pour over the vegetables, add the spice topping.
Heat the oil and pour it over at the table.

steps.do: Bring the stock to a boil in the wok. Add the bean sprouts and cabbage, blanch for 1 minute until just wilted, then lift them with the spider into the serving bowl in an even bed. Pour the stock into a jug and wipe the wok dry.
steps.look: Vegetables just softened but still crisp and bright; the bed covers the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Cooking the vegetables until limp, so they turn watery and dilute the broth.
steps.fix: One minute is enough; they keep cooking under the hot broth.

steps.do: Heat the 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil in the wok over medium low heat. Add the chilli bean paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes until the oil turns red. Add the ginger, half the garlic and the spring onion whites and stir for 30 seconds.
steps.look: The oil turns a deep brick red and separates from the paste; the wok smells rich, savoury and fermented.
steps.mistake: Frying the paste over high heat, so it burns and goes bitter and brown.
steps.fix: Keep the heat moderate and keep stirring. If it catches and blackens, start again; burnt bean paste cannot be rescued.

steps.do: Pour in the stock, add the soy and sugar, bring to a boil and simmer 3 minutes. Taste and adjust with salt; it should taste slightly too salty and spicy, as the fish and vegetables will absorb it. Turn the heat down until the broth barely bubbles.
steps.look: A cloudy red broth with spots of chilli oil on the surface, smelling deeply savoury.
steps.mistake: Under seasoning, so the finished fish tastes flat.
steps.fix: Season boldly now; add more soy or a pinch of salt and taste again.

steps.do: Slide the fish slices into the broth one at a time, spreading them out so they do not clump. Leave them for 30 seconds without stirring, then gently nudge them apart with chopsticks and cook 1 to 1 1/2 minutes more, keeping the broth at a gentle simmer.
steps.look: The slices turn from translucent to opaque white, curl slightly at the edges and stay silky and whole; the coating looks smooth, not frayed.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard or stirring immediately, which tears the slices and strips off the velvet coating.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and wait 30 seconds before touching them. Lift out any slices as soon as they are opaque.

steps.do: Pour the fish and broth carefully over the vegetables in the serving bowl. Scatter the remaining garlic, the ground pepper and chilli, then the whole toasted chillies and peppercorns, in a thick layer over the surface.
steps.look: A red broth with white fish just under the surface, crowned by a heap of dark red chillies and garlic.
steps.mistake: Burying the spices under the broth, so the hot oil cannot reach and bloom them.
steps.fix: Make sure the spices sit on top of the fish, not in the liquid.

steps.do: Heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) finishing oil in the small saucepan until it reads 375°F (190°C), just beginning to smoke, 3 to 4 minutes. Carry the bowl to the table first, then the pan with an oven glove, and pour the oil steadily over the spice topping, standing back.
steps.look: A loud crackle and hiss; the garlic sizzles gold and the chillies and peppercorns release a cloud of fragrance.
steps.mistake: Carrying a pan of smoking oil across a crowded kitchen, or pouring from a height so it splashes.
steps.fix: Pour from just above the bowl, in a slow circle, with a clear path to the table. Never let children near.

steps.do: Scatter the spring onion greens and coriander and serve at once with rice. Diners lift fish and vegetables from beneath the chillies with a slotted spoon; the chillies and broth are not meant to be eaten in quantity.
steps.look: Glistening red oil, white silky fish and green herbs; a numbing tingle from the Sichuan pepper with the heat.
steps.mistake: Serving the broth as soup, which is mostly chilli oil.
steps.fix: Lift the fish and vegetables out; a spoon of broth over rice is enough.

dishes.science: Velveting coats each slice in a thin layer of egg white and starch. In the hot broth the starch gelatinises and the egg white sets into a soft film that insulates the fish, slowing heat transfer and holding juices in, so the slices stay tender and silky rather than tightening and flaking apart. Freezing the fish briefly firms the muscle, so the knife cuts cleanly instead of pushing soft flesh. Chilli bean paste must be fried in oil because its colour and aroma compounds dissolve in fat; frying also deepens its flavour through browning. The final pour of very hot oil briefly heats the surface spices well above boiling, releasing volatile aromatics from the chillies, garlic and Sichuan pepper, whose hydroxy alpha sanshool causes the tingling, numbing sensation.
dishes.plating: This is a communal dish, served in the deep bowl it was finished in. Bring it to the table still crackling, set on a board, with a slotted spoon for serving and individual bowls of steamed rice. For a plated version, lay a nest of vegetables in a warm deep bowl, arrange six or seven slices of fish overlapping on top, ladle over a little broth and finish with a small heap of the bloomed chillies and a few coriander leaves.

pairing.drink: An off dry Riesling or a cold, light lager: sweetness and chill calm the heat and the numbing pepper, where a tannic red would make it burn harder.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Palmberg-Terrassen’ Riesling Spätlese-Feinherb 2014: an off dry Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list whose touch of sweetness and acidity tame chilli and Sichuan pepper.

variations: Shui zhu niu rou: use thinly sliced beef flank, velveted the same way with a little bicarbonate of soda, poached 1 minute.
Milder version: halve the dried chillies and peppercorns and use only 2 tbsp (35 g) bean paste.
With tofu and mushrooms: add 7 oz (200 g) silken tofu cubes and a handful of enoki mushrooms to the vegetable bed.
safety: Heating oil to smoking point is dangerous: use a heavy saucepan, never fill it more than a third full, keep a lid nearby and pour it only where everyone can see.
Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C): the slices are done when opaque all the way through.
Toast chillies in a ventilated kitchen; the fumes sting the eyes and throat.

dishes.title: Pla Rad Prik (Crisp Whole Fish with Chilli Sauce)
dishes.summary: A whole fish, scored deep to the bone, dried and fried until even the fins crunch, then covered in a glossy chilli, garlic, tamarind and palm sugar sauce and crisp Thai basil. It teaches deep frying at scale, with the oil safety a whole fish demands, and scoring so a thick fish cooks evenly.
skills: a sweet, sour and hot chilli sauce
equipment: Large wok of at least 14 inches (36 cm), set securely on a wok ring, or a wide heavy pot big enough for the fish
Deep fry thermometer
Two large spiders or fish slices, and long tongs
Heat resistant gloves or a thick oven glove
Sharp chef's knife and kitchen scissors
Wire rack over a tray, lined with paper
Mortar and pestle
Small saucepan or frying pan for the sauce
Fire blanket or a large lid kept within reach

ingredients.item: Whole fish, scaled and gutted (sea bass, snapper, tilapia or pomfret)
ingredients.note: it must fit flat in your wok
groundnut, rice bran or rapeseed; enough to come halfway up the fish

ingredients.item: Red chillies (long, such as Fresno or cayenne), roughly chopped

ingredients.note: seedless, the thick pulp diluted to a ketchup texture

mise: Rinse the fish inside and out, cut away any remaining gills and trim the sharp fins with scissors. Pat it completely dry with paper, inside the cavity too.

Score the fish: on each side make 3 or 4 deep diagonal cuts about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) apart, cutting down until the knife touches the bone. Then cut a second set the other way for a diamond pattern on thick fish.
Rub the fish with the salt, including inside the cuts, and leave it on the rack uncovered in the fridge for 30 minutes to 1 hour to dry the skin.
Pound the chillies, garlic, shallots and coriander roots to a coarse paste in the mortar.
Mix the palm sugar, tamarind, fish sauce and water in a small bowl.
Set up the frying station: the wok secure on its ring at a back burner, the rack and tray beside it, tongs, spiders, gloves and the lid or fire blanket to hand. Clear the area of children and pets.

timeline.do: Clean, score, salt and dry the fish in the fridge.
Pound the paste and mix the sauce liquids; cook the rice.
Make the chilli sauce; keep it warm.
Heat the oil to 360°F (182°C); dust and fry the fish.
Fry the basil; plate the fish and pour over the sauce.

steps.do: Make the sauce: heat the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil in the small pan over medium heat, add the pounded paste and fry, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and softened. Add the sugar and tamarind mixture, bring to a boil and simmer 3 to 4 minutes until syrupy.
steps.look: A glossy, brick red sauce that coats a spoon and drips in slow, thick drops; it smells hot, sweet and tangy at once.
steps.mistake: Reducing it too far, so it becomes a hard caramel as it cools.
steps.fix: If it thickens too much, loosen it with a tablespoon of water at a time. Taste: it should be equally sweet, sour, salty and hot; adjust with sugar, tamarind or fish sauce.

steps.do: Heat the frying oil in the wok over medium high heat to 360°F (182°C), checking with the thermometer. The oil should come about halfway up the thickness of the fish; it does not need to cover it.
steps.look: The surface shimmers; a chopstick dipped in releases a steady stream of small bubbles.
steps.mistake: Filling the wok too full, so it overflows when the fish goes in.
steps.fix: Keep the oil at no more than a third of the wok's depth: the fish displaces a great deal.

steps.do: Pat the fish dry once more. Dust it all over with the rice flour, working it into the scores and cavity, then shake off the excess so only a thin coat remains.
steps.look: A thin, powdery white film over the skin and inside the cuts; no thick patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving wet patches or clumps of flour, which splatter violently in the oil.
steps.fix: Dry any damp areas with paper first and tap off loose flour.

steps.do: Wearing a glove, hold the fish by the tail and lower it into the oil head first and AWAY from you, laying it down gently rather than dropping it. Do not touch it for 5 minutes, keeping the oil between 340 and 360°F (171 and 182°C).
steps.look: A rush of large bubbles that settles into a steady, vigorous fry; the scores open up as the flesh cooks.
steps.mistake: Dropping the fish from a height or lowering it towards yourself, which splashes oil onto your hand and the hob.
steps.fix: Lower it slowly, away from you, until it rests on the oil. If oil splashes onto the flame, turn the heat off and let it settle.

steps.do: Use two spiders or slices to turn the fish over carefully, lifting it rather than flipping it, and fry the second side 5 to 6 minutes. If the top is not submerged, ladle hot oil over it repeatedly as it fries. Total frying time is 10 to 14 minutes for a 1 1/2 to 2 lb (700 to 900 g) fish.
steps.look: Deep golden brown all over, the fins and tail crisp and rigid; the bubbling slows noticeably as the moisture is driven out.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, so the skin tears and sticks to the spider.
steps.fix: Wait until the first side is golden and firm before turning; if it sticks, slide a spider gently under the whole fish.

steps.do: Check doneness: the flesh in the deepest score should be opaque white and pull away from the bone, and a probe at the thickest point reads 145°F (63°C). Lift the fish out with both spiders, holding it over the wok for a moment to drain, and lay it on the rack.
steps.look: The cuts have opened into crisp ridges; the flesh is white and flakes away from the spine.
steps.mistake: Lifting the fish in one go with a single utensil, so it breaks in half.
steps.fix: Support it at both ends; a broken fish still tastes right, so plate the halves together and cover the join with sauce.

steps.do: Turn off the heat under the wok. Drop the dried basil leaves into the hot oil for 10 to 15 seconds, standing back as they spit, then lift them onto paper.
steps.look: The leaves turn translucent, deep green and crisp; they stop crackling when ready.
steps.mistake: Frying wet leaves, which splatter hot oil everywhere.
steps.fix: Dry the basil completely beforehand and add a small handful at a time.

steps.do: Lay the fish on a warm platter, rewarm the sauce until it bubbles and spoon it over the fish just before serving, letting it run into the scores. Scatter the fried basil and serve at once with jasmine rice.
steps.look: A crisp, golden fish under a shining red sauce, with dark green basil on top; it crackles when cut.
steps.mistake: Pouring sauce over the fish long before serving, which softens the crust.
steps.fix: Sauce at the last moment, or serve some sauce on the side so the tail and fins stay crisp.

dishes.science: Scoring a whole fish exposes more surface to the hot oil and creates channels for heat to reach the thickest flesh near the bone, so the thin tail and thick shoulder finish closer together. Drying the skin and salting it in advance pulls surface moisture out; less water at the surface means less violent spitting and a faster, crisper crust. Rice flour contains no gluten and fries to a glassy, brittle coat that stays crisp longer than wheat flour. When the fish enters oil at about 360°F (182°C), surface water turns to steam and bubbles out; as the surface dries, its temperature rises past boiling and browning begins. The bubbling slows as less water is left. The sauce balances sweet palm sugar, sour tamarind, salty fish sauce and hot chilli, the four corners of Thai seasoning.
dishes.plating: Use a long oval platter warmed in the oven. Lay the fish in the centre, slightly curved as if swimming, the best side up. Spoon the sauce along the spine so it runs down into the scores and pools around the fish, but leave the tail and fin edges bare so they stay crisp. Heap the fried basil along the top and add a few slices of fresh red chilli. Rice goes in a separate bowl.

pairing.drink: An off dry, aromatic white such as a Riesling Kabinett or a Gewürztraminer: the sweetness matches the palm sugar and calms the chilli.
pairing.brennans: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Kabinett 2020: a delicate, off dry Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list that pairs well with sweet, sour and hot sauces.

variations: Fillets: use 4 thick skin-on fillets, scored through the skin, dusted and shallow fried 3 to 4 minutes a side, an easier first attempt.
Pla sam rot: add 1 tbsp (15 ml) more tamarind and a little more sugar for a sweeter three flavour sauce.
Oven crisp: brush the scored, dusted fish with oil and roast at 450°F (230°C) on a rack for 25 to 30 minutes, then crisp under the overhead grill (broiler); less crunchy, but no deep frying.
safety: Deep frying a whole fish uses a large volume of hot oil: keep the wok stable on a ring, fill it no more than a third, lower the fish away from you, wear a glove, and never leave it unattended.
If the oil catches fire, turn off the heat and cover with a lid or fire blanket. Never use water.
Let the oil cool completely, for several hours, before moving or straining it.
Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point.
